# SearchFn Documentation (Full)

> Full-text search engine and adapter system for TypeScript, Python, and Swift. Ships a built-in BM25 engine for in-process and browser-persistent search, plus thin adapters for Postgres, Meilisearch, Elasticsearch, and OpenSearch.

This document contains the full content of the SearchFn documentation, optimized for LLM consumption.


================================================================================
## Ai Resources
================================================================================


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Claude Setup

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/ai-resources/claude
Description: Use SearchFn effectively with Claude Code and Claude Projects.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Claude Code

Add the MCP server:

```bash
claude mcp add searchfn https://searchfn.com/api/mcp
```

Drop this into `CLAUDE.md` at the repo root:

```markdown
# SearchFn

Use the `searchfn` MCP server for documentation lookups.

## Adapter selection
- Tests, CLIs, in-process server search → `@searchfn/adapter-memory`
- Browser apps, PWAs, offline-first → `@searchfn/adapter-indexeddb`
- Production server, already on Postgres → `@searchfn/adapter-postgres`
- Production server, dedicated search → `@searchfn/adapter-meilisearch`
- Large-scale search clusters → `@searchfn/adapter-elasticsearch` or `@searchfn/adapter-opensearch`

## Conventions
- Always call `initialize({ resources: [...] })` before indexing or searching.
- `search()` returns matching IDs; load full records separately.
- For DataFn integration, use `@searchfn/datafn-provider`.
- Server errors follow the envelope shape `{ ok, result | error }`.
- Codes: `DFQL_INVALID`, `LIMIT_EXCEEDED`, `DFQL_ABORTED`, `DFQL_UNSUPPORTED`, `FORBIDDEN`, `INTERNAL`.

## Don'ts
- Don't write a custom inverted index when `@searchfn/core` exists.
- Don't pass adapter credentials in client code; the server adapter owns them.
- Don't reuse the same adapter instance across tenants in multi-tenant mode without isolation.
```

## Claude Projects

Create a project, attach `https://searchfn.com/llms-full.txt` as a knowledge document. Pin a system prompt with the same adapter selection matrix as above.

## See also

- [MCP server](/docs/ai-resources/mcp)
- [Architecture](/docs/architecture)

### Codex Setup

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/ai-resources/codex
Description: Use SearchFn with OpenAI Codex CLI and Codex agents.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Codex CLI

In `~/.codex/AGENTS.md`:

```markdown
## SearchFn

Documentation: https://searchfn.com/llms-full.txt

When working in a repo with @searchfn/* dependencies:
- Pick adapters from this matrix:
  - In-process, tests, CLIs → @searchfn/adapter-memory
  - Browser, offline-first → @searchfn/adapter-indexeddb
  - Server + Postgres → @searchfn/adapter-postgres
  - Dedicated search → @searchfn/adapter-meilisearch
  - Large scale → @searchfn/adapter-elasticsearch / @searchfn/adapter-opensearch
- Always call `initialize({ resources: [...] })` before indexing.
- Don't hand-roll a tokenizer; use @searchfn/core.
- DataFn integration: @searchfn/datafn-provider, never custom.
- Errors follow envelopes: { ok: true, result } or { ok: false, error: { code, message } }.

Patterns to copy:
- Server bootstrap: createSearchFnServer({ adapter, basePath, authorize, logger })
- Client bootstrap: createSearchClient({ adapter, defaults })
- Provider bootstrap: createSearchProvider(adapter, { resourceFields })
```

## Pinning specific docs

Have the agent fetch `https://searchfn.com/llms.txt` first to get the outline, then specific pages as needed:

```
@web https://searchfn.com/docs/quickstart/hono
@web https://searchfn.com/docs/reference/adapters/postgres
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Cursor Setup

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/ai-resources/cursor
Description: Pin SearchFn docs in Cursor and prompt the agent effectively.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Cursor reads documentation through MCP. Set it up once, then mention SearchFn naturally in chat.

## 1. Install the MCP server

`~/.cursor/mcp.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "searchfn": {
      "url": "https://searchfn.com/api/mcp"
    }
  }
}
```

Restart Cursor.

## 2. Add to project rules

`.cursor/rules/searchfn.mdc`:

```markdown
---
description: Conventions when working with SearchFn
globs: ["**/*.ts", "**/*.tsx", "**/*.py", "**/*.swift"]
alwaysApply: false
---

# SearchFn

When working with @searchfn/* packages:

- Use the SearchFn MCP server to fetch docs before generating code.
- Pick the adapter from this matrix:
  - In-process / tests / CLI → `@searchfn/adapter-memory`
  - Browser, offline-first → `@searchfn/adapter-indexeddb`
  - Existing Postgres → `@searchfn/adapter-postgres`
  - Dedicated search service → `@searchfn/adapter-meilisearch` (most cases) or `@searchfn/adapter-elasticsearch` / `@searchfn/adapter-opensearch` (large scale)
- Always call `initialize()` with `resources` and `searchFields` before `index()` or `search()`.
- `search()` returns IDs only. Fetch full records from your store of truth.
- Validation errors are `DFQL_INVALID`; rate/limit errors are `LIMIT_EXCEEDED`.
- For DataFn integration use `@searchfn/datafn-provider`, never roll your own bridge.
```

## 3. Prompt patterns

For setup tasks:

> Set up SearchFn in this Next.js app using the PostgresAdapter. Use the SearchFn MCP server to fetch docs as needed.

For indexing tasks:

> Generate a batch indexer that reads all `articles` from Drizzle and indexes them into SearchFn with fields `title`, `subtitle`, `body`.

For relevance tuning:

> Tune the SearchFn config so `title` weighs 3x the body. Add a stop word list for German.

- [MCP server](/docs/ai-resources/mcp)
- [Architecture](/docs/architecture)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### llms.txt and llms-full.txt

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/ai-resources/llms-txt
Description: Plain-text documentation feeds for AI coding tools.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

SearchFn publishes two LLM-optimized feeds on every build:

| File | Size | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/llms.txt` | ~10 KB | Outline of all docs pages with deep links and one-line descriptions. Cheap to paste into an agent's context. |
| `/llms-full.txt` | ~300 KB+ | Full body of every page concatenated, organized by section. For agents that can ingest the whole corpus. |

## Where to find them

- `https://searchfn.com/llms.txt`
- `https://searchfn.com/llms-full.txt`

Or, when you self-host the docs, `<your-site>/llms.txt` and `<your-site>/llms-full.txt`.

## How they're generated

`scripts/generate-llms.mjs` walks `content/docs/`, parses MDX frontmatter, and emits both files into `public/` during `prebuild`. The script is self-contained (no Fumadocs runtime dependency) and runs before `next build`.

Regenerate manually with:

```bash
npm --prefix searchfn/docs run generate:llms
```

## Format

### `llms.txt`

```
# SearchFn Documentation

> Full-text search engine and adapter system for TypeScript, Python, and Swift...

## Top Level
- [SearchFn](https://searchfn.com/docs): A full-text search engine and adapter system...
- [Architecture](https://searchfn.com/docs/architecture): Built-in engine, package layers...

## Quickstart
- [Quickstart Overview](https://searchfn.com/docs/quickstart)
- [Hono](https://searchfn.com/docs/quickstart/hono)
...
```

### `llms-full.txt`

Same outline plus the full markdown body of every page, including code blocks, tables, and Mermaid diagrams.

## Using these in your agent

Paste `llms.txt` into the agent's system prompt as a navigation aid; fetch specific pages from the listed URLs when the agent needs detail. Or load `llms-full.txt` once at session start for self-contained context.

## See also

- [MCP server](/docs/ai-resources/mcp)
- [Cursor setup](/docs/ai-resources/cursor)

### MCP Server

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/ai-resources/mcp
Description: Connect Claude, Cursor, and other MCP clients to SearchFn documentation.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) lets AI agents fetch live documentation through a typed tool interface. SearchFn exposes its docs through a hosted MCP endpoint and a self-hostable variant.

## Hosted endpoint

```
https://searchfn.com/api/mcp
```

This is what you'll add to MCP-aware clients.

## Claude Code

```bash
claude mcp add searchfn https://searchfn.com/api/mcp
```

## Cursor

In `~/.cursor/mcp.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "searchfn": {
      "url": "https://searchfn.com/api/mcp"
    }
  }
}
```

Restart Cursor; the SearchFn tools appear under the MCP menu.

## Factory Droid

```bash
droid mcp add searchfn https://searchfn.com/api/mcp --type http
```

## Tools exposed

| Tool | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `searchfn_docs.list` | List all documentation pages with titles and descriptions |
| `searchfn_docs.read` | Read the full content of a specific page by URL |
| `searchfn_docs.search` | Search the docs corpus by text query |

## Self-hosting

If you fork SearchFn and run your own docs site, the MCP route lives at `app/api/mcp/route.ts`. It reads `public/llms.txt` and `public/llms-full.txt` so as long as `generate-llms.mjs` runs at build, the MCP endpoint stays current.

## See also

- [llms.txt and llms-full.txt](/docs/ai-resources/llms-txt)
- [Claude setup](/docs/ai-resources/claude)
- [Cursor setup](/docs/ai-resources/cursor)

### Skills

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/ai-resources/skills
Description: Factory Droid skills for SearchFn setup, indexing, and adapter selection.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

If you use [Factory Droid](https://factory.ai), the following skills are available out of the box.

## Available skills

| Skill | Use when |
| --- | --- |
| `searchfn-setup` | Pick an adapter and bootstrap server+client+initialize in one pass |
| `searchfn-indexing` | Generate batch indexing code for an existing data source (DB, CSV, API) |
| `searchfn-relevance` | Tune BM25 weights, field boosts, and stop word lists for a specific corpus |
| `searchfn-datafn` | Wire SearchFn as a DataFn search provider end-to-end |
| `searchfn-migrate` | Migrate between adapters (Memory → Postgres, etc.) |

## Invocation

In a Droid session:

```
/skill searchfn-setup
```

The skill drives a short questionnaire (runtime, persistence, tenancy, scale) and produces the matching scaffold.

### AI Resources

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/ai-resources
Description: Use SearchFn with AI coding tools — Cursor, Claude, Codex, Windsurf, and any LLM that consumes llms.txt.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

SearchFn ships first-class resources for AI coding tools. Everything on this site is also available as plain text optimized for LLM consumption, plus prompt patterns and integration guides for the most common agents.

## What's here

- **[llms.txt + llms-full.txt](/docs/ai-resources/llms-txt)** — the entire documentation as plain text, auto-generated at build time.
- **[MCP server](/docs/ai-resources/mcp)** — connect Claude, Cursor, or any MCP-compatible client to a live SearchFn documentation server.
- **[Skills](/docs/ai-resources/skills)** — Factory Droid skills for end-to-end SearchFn setup.
- **[Cursor setup](/docs/ai-resources/cursor)** — pin docs, prompt scaffolding, code-mode notes.
- **[Claude setup](/docs/ai-resources/claude)** — Projects and Code instructions tuned for SearchFn.
- **[Codex setup](/docs/ai-resources/codex)** — system prompts for OpenAI Codex / Codex CLI.

## Why this matters

SearchFn has three runtimes (built-in engine, Postgres, external search services), five external adapters, and two non-TS targets (Python, Swift). An LLM that doesn't know which adapter to pick or how the SearchProvider boundary works will generate plausible-looking but wrong code. The resources here give AI tools enough context to make the right decisions without hallucinating.

## See also

- [Quickstart](/docs/quickstart) for first-hand setup
- [Architecture](/docs/architecture) for the canonical mental model
- [Adapter reference](/docs/reference/adapters) for picking the right backend



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Architecture

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/architecture
Description: Built-in search engine, package layers, adapter contract, and response semantics.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

SearchFn has two core pieces: a **built-in search engine** (`@searchfn/core`) that handles tokenization, indexing, scoring, and ranking in-process, and an **adapter contract** (`SearchAdapter`) that provides a uniform interface across the built-in engine and external backends. Both tiers are production-ready — the built-in engine powers offline-first apps and in-process search, while external backends serve use cases that need shared state or backend-specific capabilities.

## Built-in Search Engine

The Memory and IndexedDB adapters are not thin wrappers — they run SearchFn's own full-text search engine, implemented in `@searchfn/core`. This is a complete search runtime comparable to libraries like FlexSearch or MiniSearch.

### Text Pipeline

Every document and query passes through a configurable text pipeline:

1. **Tokenize** — splits text into tokens using Unicode-aware regex (`[\p{L}\p{N}]+`)
2. **Normalize** — lowercases all tokens
3. **Stop words** — removes common words (built-in sets for English, Spanish, French)
4. **Stem** — reduces words to root forms (custom English stemmer; optional)
5. **Edge n-grams** — generates prefix tokens for autocomplete support (optional)

### Inverted Index

Documents are stored in an inverted index: each unique term maps to a posting list of `(docId, termFrequency)` pairs.

- **MemoryAdapter** stores postings in an in-memory `Map` keyed by `field::term`.
- **IndexedDbAdapter** stores postings in IndexedDB object stores with LRU caches for hot term lookups.

### BM25 Scoring

Search queries are scored using a BM25-inspired algorithm:

- **IDF** (inverse document frequency) — terms that appear in fewer documents score higher.
- **TF** (term frequency) — terms that appear more often in a document contribute more.
- **Length normalization** — shorter documents get a slight relevance boost.
- **Prefix penalty** — edge n-gram matches score lower than exact matches (0.7x multiplier).

### Fuzzy Matching

Fuzzy search uses Wagner-Fischer Levenshtein distance. When enabled, query terms are expanded against the vocabulary to find terms within the configured edit distance (max 3). Terms are pre-filtered by length difference for performance.

### Field Boosts

The built-in engine supports per-field relevance boosting — for example, weighting `title` matches higher than `description` matches.

## Package Layers

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph Engine ["@searchfn/core — Built-in Search Engine"]
        PL[Text Pipeline]
        IX[Inverted Index]
        BM[BM25 Scoring]
    end

    subgraph Adapters ["Adapter Packages (@searchfn/adapter-*)"]
        MA["MemoryAdapter"]
        IA["IndexedDbAdapter"]
        PA["PostgresAdapter"]
        MEI["MeilisearchAdapter"]
        EA["Elasticsearch / OpenSearch"]
    end

    subgraph Wrappers ["Application Layer"]
        CL["@searchfn/client"]
        SV["@searchfn/server"]
        DP["@searchfn/datafn-provider"]
    end

    MA -->|"uses"| Engine
    IA -->|"uses"| Engine
    PA -->|"delegates to"| PG["Postgres tsvector"]
    MEI -->|"delegates to"| MS["Meilisearch API"]
    EA -->|"delegates to"| ES["ES/OS API"]
    CL --> MA
    CL --> IA
    SV --> Adapters
    DP --> Adapters
```

| Layer | Package | Responsibility |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Engine | `@searchfn/core` | Text pipeline, inverted index, BM25 scoring, fuzzy matching, stemming |
| Contracts | `@searchfn/adapter-contracts` | Shared `SearchAdapter` contract, request/response params, and capability types |
| Adapters | `@searchfn/adapter-memory`, `@searchfn/adapter-indexeddb`, `@searchfn/adapter-postgres`, `@searchfn/adapter-meilisearch`, `@searchfn/adapter-elasticsearch`, `@searchfn/adapter-opensearch` | Adapter implementations. Memory and IndexedDB use the built-in engine; Postgres, Meilisearch, and ES/OS delegate to external backends. |
| Client | `@searchfn/client` | Validates inputs, applies defaults, and delegates to an adapter |
| Server | `@searchfn/server` | Validates HTTP requests, runs authorization, delegates to an adapter, and returns canonical response envelopes |
| Integration | `@searchfn/datafn-provider` | Maps a `SearchAdapter` into a DataFn `SearchProvider` |

## Adapter Contract

`SearchAdapter` is the boundary between application code and search implementation. Every adapter — built-in or external — implements this interface:

```typescript
interface SearchAdapter {
  readonly name: string;
  readonly capabilities?: SearchAdapterCapabilities;

  initialize?(params: InitializeParams): Promise<void>;
  index(params: IndexParams): Promise<void>;
  search(params: SearchParams): Promise<Array<string | number>>;
  searchAll?(params: SearchAllParams): Promise<SearchAllResult[]>;
  remove(params: RemoveParams): Promise<void>;
  clear(resource: string, signal?: AbortSignal): Promise<void>;
  dispose?(): Promise<void>;
}
```

| Method | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `initialize` | Optional | Declare resources and their searchable fields before indexing |
| `index` | Yes | Index a batch of documents into a resource |
| `search` | Yes | Search a single resource, returns matching IDs |
| `searchAll` | Optional | Search across multiple resources, returns IDs with scores |
| `remove` | Yes | Remove documents by ID from a resource |
| `clear` | Yes | Remove all documents from a resource |
| `dispose` | Optional | Release resources (connections, caches, handles) |

### Capabilities

Adapters declare their capabilities so clients and servers can adapt behavior:

```typescript
interface SearchAdapterCapabilities {
  persistent?: boolean;
  searchAll?: boolean;
  fuzzy?: boolean;
  fieldBoosts?: boolean;
  maxBatchSize?: number;
}
```

| Capability | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `persistent` | Data survives process restarts (IndexedDB, Postgres, Meilisearch, Elasticsearch) |
| `searchAll` | Adapter natively supports cross-resource search |
| `fuzzy` | Adapter supports fuzzy/approximate matching |
| `fieldBoosts` | Adapter supports per-field relevance boosting |
| `maxBatchSize` | Maximum documents per `index` call |

## Response Envelope

The server wraps all responses in a canonical envelope:

**Success:**
```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "result": { "ids": ["t-1", "t-3"] }
}
```

**Failure:**
```json
{
  "ok": false,
  "error": {
    "code": "DFQL_INVALID",
    "message": "Query must be a non-empty string",
    "details": { "path": "query" }
  }
}
```

### Error Codes

| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `DFQL_INVALID` | Malformed request or missing required fields |
| `LIMIT_EXCEEDED` | Query, limit, or batch size exceeds configured maximums |
| `DFQL_ABORTED` | Request was cancelled via AbortSignal |
| `DFQL_UNSUPPORTED` | Adapter does not support the requested operation or dialect |
| `FORBIDDEN` | Authorization callback denied the request |
| `INTERNAL` | Unexpected backend or runtime failure |

## Data Flow

### Built-in engine (Memory / IndexedDB)

1. **Pipeline** — text is tokenized, normalized, filtered for stop words, and stemmed.
2. **Index** — terms are inserted into the inverted index with term frequencies.
3. **Search** — query text passes through the same pipeline, optional fuzzy expansion runs against the vocabulary, postings are retrieved, and BM25 scoring produces ranked results.

### External backends (Postgres / Meilisearch / ES)

1. **Validation** — client or server validates the request shape and limits.
2. **Authorization** — server checks the `authorize` callback (if configured).
3. **Delegation** — the request is translated into the backend's native API.
4. **Response** — backend results are mapped back to SearchFn's response format.

For `searchAll`, if the adapter does not implement `searchAll` natively, the client and datafn-provider run per-resource searches concurrently and merge results with deterministic score-based ordering.



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Comparison

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/comparison
Description: SearchFn vs Algolia, Typesense, Meilisearch direct, Elasticsearch direct, Postgres FTS direct, FlexSearch, MiniSearch, Lunr.js, Orama, Pagefind.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

SearchFn is two things: a complete in-process search engine (BM25, tokenization, fuzzy, stemming) **and** a thin adapter layer over external search services. Where it fits depends on what you're solving for.

## At-a-glance

| | Self-hosted | In-process engine | Offline-first | Multi-language | TypeScript-native | Pluggable backends |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **SearchFn** | yes | yes (`@searchfn/core`) | yes (IndexedDB, SQLite) | yes (en/es/fr stemmers) | yes | yes (5 backends) |
| Algolia | no | no | no | yes | wrapper | no |
| Typesense | yes | no | no | yes | wrapper | no |
| Meilisearch | yes | no | no | yes | wrapper | no |
| Elasticsearch | yes | no | no | yes | wrapper | no |
| Postgres FTS | yes | no (in-DB) | no | partial | wrapper | no |
| FlexSearch | n/a | yes | partial | yes | yes | no |
| MiniSearch | n/a | yes | partial | yes | yes | no |
| Lunr.js | n/a | yes | yes (stale) | partial | yes | no |
| Orama | yes (own engine) | yes | yes | yes | yes | no |
| Pagefind | n/a (static) | yes (per-page) | yes | yes | yes | no |

## When to pick SearchFn

- You want **one search abstraction** that works across browser-local, in-process server, and external services. Most other tools commit you to one runtime.
- You need **offline-first browser search** with proper BM25 ranking (not just substring matching).
- You're already on the SuperFunctions stack (DataFn, AuthFn, FileFn).
- You want to start with zero infra (`MemoryAdapter`) and upgrade to Postgres/Meilisearch/Elasticsearch without rewriting application code.
- You need **TypeScript + Swift + Python parity** for the same search semantics.

## When to pick something else

### Algolia / hosted search-as-a-service

Pick if you want a managed service, are happy paying per record/query, and don't have data residency concerns. SearchFn doesn't try to be Algolia — there's no hosted offering. The `MeilisearchAdapter` is the closest analog when you want a dedicated search service you control.

### Typesense / Meilisearch / Elasticsearch direct

Pick when you want the backend's full feature set (advanced filtering, facets, geo, vector search) **and** you're committed to that one backend. SearchFn's adapters expose the common subset. If you find yourself reaching past the adapter API, use the backend SDK directly.

### Postgres FTS direct

Pick if you only need server-side search, you have one specific text shape, and you want to write the `tsvector` triggers by hand. `PostgresAdapter` is the SearchFn-flavored version: same idea, lifted into a portable API.

### FlexSearch / MiniSearch / Lunr.js

Pick if you only need browser-side search, your dataset is small, and you don't need a unified API across runtimes. These are perfectly good in their lane. SearchFn's `IndexedDbAdapter` covers the same case but with the same API as the server adapters.

### Orama

Closest to SearchFn in philosophy — a TypeScript-native search engine with persistence and a hosted Cloud variant. Pick Orama if you prefer its specific API or want the hosted offering. Pick SearchFn if you want the explicit Postgres/Meilisearch/Elasticsearch path or first-class Swift / Python parity.

### Pagefind

Pick for static sites — Pagefind indexes at build time and runs entirely on the client. SearchFn is for apps with mutable data.

## Migration tips

### From MiniSearch / FlexSearch

The mental model is nearly identical. Map:

- `MiniSearch.add()` → `client.index({ resource, documents })`
- `MiniSearch.search()` → `client.search({ resource, query })`

Switch to `IndexedDbAdapter` if you want persistence; switch to `PostgresAdapter` later if you outgrow browser-only.

### From Algolia

Index your existing Algolia objects by mapping `objectID` → SearchFn `id`. Use `MeilisearchAdapter` for a managed-feeling alternative or `PostgresAdapter` if you want infra simplicity.

### From bare Postgres FTS

`PostgresAdapter` runs migrations that create the same `tsvector` columns and GIN indexes you'd write by hand. You can keep both running side by side during migration — SearchFn's tables are namespaced under `_searchfn_*`.

### From Elasticsearch

Use `ElasticsearchAdapter` to keep the same backend with a portable client API. If you want to also retire ES, run both adapters in parallel and shift traffic.

## What SearchFn doesn't try to do

- Vector / semantic search — not in scope today. Hybrid lexical + vector is on the roadmap.
- Faceted aggregations — partially supported per adapter; not unified.
- Geo search — backend-specific. Use the backend SDK directly.
- Spell-correction-as-a-service — the built-in engine has fuzzy matching; for richer correction use Meilisearch or ES.

## See also

- [Architecture](/docs/architecture)
- [Adapter reference](/docs/reference/adapters)
- [DataFn integration](/docs/integrations/datafn)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Getting Started with Swift

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/getting-started-swift
Description: Build local Swift search with the standalone SearchFn Swift package.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

SearchFn Swift is a standalone Swift Package Manager package for local search in native Apple apps and other Swift runtimes where in-process or SQLite-backed search is the right fit.

It ships:

- `SearchFnCore` for tokenization, prefix indexing, fuzzy expansion, and BM25-style scoring
- `SearchFnMemoryAdapter` for ephemeral in-process search
- `SearchFnSQLiteAdapter` for persisted SearchFn-owned local indexes
- `SearchFnClient` for validation and deterministic `searchAll`
- `SearchFnConvenience` for `InMemorySearchFn` and `SearchFn(sqlite:)`

## Build From Repo Root

```bash
swift test --package-path searchfn/swift
swift build --package-path searchfn/swift --target SearchFnInMemoryExample
swift build --package-path searchfn/swift --target SearchFnSQLiteExample
```

## In-Memory Example

```swift
import SearchFnAdapterContracts
import SearchFnConvenience

let search = InMemorySearchFn(
    defaults: SearchFnDefaults(limit: 20, limitPerResource: 10, fuzzy: .enabled, prefix: true)
)

let client = search.client()

try await client.initialize(
    SearchFnInitializeParams(
        resources: [
            SearchFnInitializeResourceConfig(name: "tasks", searchFields: ["title", "body"])
        ]
    )
)

try await client.index(
    SearchFnIndexParams(
        resource: "tasks",
        documents: [
            SearchFnDocument(id: "t1", fields: ["title": "Hybrid search", "body": "Swift local index"]),
            SearchFnDocument(id: "t2", fields: ["title": "Groceries", "body": "Milk and bread"])
        ]
    )
)

let ids = try await client.search(
    SearchFnSearchParams(resource: "tasks", query: "hybrid")
)
```

## SQLite Example

```swift
import Foundation
import SearchFnAdapterContracts
import SearchFnConvenience
import SearchFnSQLiteAdapter

let rootURL = FileManager.default.temporaryDirectory
    .appendingPathComponent("searchfn-swift-demo", isDirectory: true)

let search = try SearchFn(
    sqlite: SearchFnSQLiteAdapterConfiguration(
        rootURL: rootURL,
        indexKey: "project-docs"
    )
)

let client = search.client()
```

The SQLite adapter owns its persisted index state. The store layout is:

```text
<rootURL>/<slug(indexKey)>-<hash16(indexKey)>/
  searchfn.sqlite
  manifest.json
```

This is SearchFn-owned persistence, not Core Data-owned persistence.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Getting Started

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/getting-started
Description: Install SearchFn, index documents, and run your first search query in minutes.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Packages

SearchFn is split into focused packages. Install only what you need:

| Package | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `@searchfn/core` | Built-in search engine (text pipeline, BM25 scoring, inverted index, fuzzy matching) |
| `@searchfn/adapter-contracts` | Shared adapter interface and types (`SearchAdapter`, params, capabilities) |
| `@searchfn/adapter-memory` | In-process adapter backed by `@searchfn/core` |
| `@searchfn/adapter-indexeddb` | Browser-persistent adapter backed by `@searchfn/core` |
| `@searchfn/adapter-postgres` | Postgres adapter (`tsvector`/`tsquery`) |
| `@searchfn/adapter-meilisearch` | Meilisearch adapter |
| `@searchfn/adapter-elasticsearch` | Elasticsearch adapter |
| `@searchfn/adapter-opensearch` | OpenSearch adapter |
| `@searchfn/client` | Client API for app code that calls search directly (browser or Node) |
| `@searchfn/server` | HTTP server exposing `/searchfn/*` endpoints with authorization and logging |
| `@searchfn/datafn-provider` | DataFn integration — maps any adapter into a DataFn SearchProvider |

## Installation

For client-side or in-process search (uses the built-in search engine):

```bash
npm install @searchfn/client @searchfn/adapter-memory
```

For server-side HTTP search API:

```bash
npm install @searchfn/server @searchfn/adapter-memory
```

## Quick Start

The quickstart uses `MemoryAdapter`, which runs SearchFn's built-in search engine in-process. No external services required — this is the same engine that powers production in-process and offline-first search.

### 1. Create a Client

```typescript
import { createSearchClient } from "@searchfn/client";
import { MemoryAdapter } from "@searchfn/adapter-memory";

const client = createSearchClient({
  adapter: new MemoryAdapter(),
  defaults: {
    limit: 20,
    limitPerResource: 10,
    fuzzy: true,
  },
});
```

### 2. Initialize Resources

Before indexing, declare which resources exist and which fields are searchable:

```typescript
await client.initialize?.({
  resources: [
    { name: "tasks", searchFields: ["title", "description"] },
    { name: "notes", searchFields: ["content"] },
  ],
});
```

### 3. Index Documents

```typescript
await client.index({
  resource: "tasks",
  documents: [
    { id: "t-1", fields: { title: "Ship docs", description: "Write getting started guide" } },
    { id: "t-2", fields: { title: "Fix bug", description: "Handle retry logic" } },
    { id: "t-3", fields: { title: "Plan launch", description: "Coordinate docs and release" } },
  ],
});
```

### 4. Search

```typescript
const ids = await client.search({
  resource: "tasks",
  query: "docs",
  limit: 5,
});

console.log(ids); // ["t-1", "t-3"]
```

### 5. Search Across Resources

```typescript
const results = await client.searchAll({
  query: "docs",
  resources: ["tasks", "notes"],
  limitPerResource: 5,
});

// [{ resource: "tasks", id: "t-1", score: 1.2 }, ...]
```

## Server Quick Start

The server wraps any adapter behind HTTP endpoints with built-in validation, authorization, and structured logging.

```typescript
import { createSearchFnServer } from "@searchfn/server";
import { MemoryAdapter } from "@searchfn/adapter-memory";

const server = await createSearchFnServer({
  adapter: new MemoryAdapter(),
  basePath: "/searchfn",
});

// Mount server.router with your @superfunctions/http adapter (Express, Fastify, Hono, etc.)
```

The server exposes these endpoints under the configured `basePath`:

| Endpoint | Method | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/searchfn/status` | GET | Health check and adapter info |
| `/searchfn/index` | POST | Index documents into a resource |
| `/searchfn/search` | POST | Search a single resource |
| `/searchfn/search-all` | POST | Search across multiple resources |
| `/searchfn/remove` | POST | Remove documents by ID |
| `/searchfn/clear` | POST | Clear all documents in a resource |

## Convenience Constructors

For common setups, use the built-in shorthand constructors:

```typescript
import { createMemorySearchClient, createIndexedDbSearchClient } from "@searchfn/client";

const memoryClient = createMemorySearchClient({
  defaults: { limit: 20, fuzzy: true },
});

const browserClient = createIndexedDbSearchClient({
  adapterConfig: { dbName: "my-app-search" },
  defaults: { limit: 20, fuzzy: true },
});
```

## Breaking Change and Migration

The legacy aggregate adapters package has been removed. SearchFn now ships one package per adapter plus `@searchfn/adapter-contracts`.

### Package Mapping

| Legacy package (aggregate) | New package(s) |
| --- | --- |
| `searchfn adapters aggregate` | `@searchfn/adapter-contracts` + one or more leaf adapter packages |

### Import Mapping

| Legacy import (aggregate package path) | New import |
| --- | --- |
| `import { MemoryAdapter } from "<legacy-adapters-package>"` | `import { MemoryAdapter } from "@searchfn/adapter-memory"` |
| `import { IndexedDbAdapter } from "<legacy-adapters-package>"` | `import { IndexedDbAdapter } from "@searchfn/adapter-indexeddb"` |
| `import { PostgresAdapter, getPostgresMigrationSQL } from "<legacy-adapters-package>"` | `import { PostgresAdapter, getPostgresMigrationSQL } from "@searchfn/adapter-postgres"` |
| `import { MeilisearchAdapter } from "<legacy-adapters-package>"` | `import { MeilisearchAdapter } from "@searchfn/adapter-meilisearch"` |
| `import { ElasticsearchAdapter } from "<legacy-adapters-package>"` | `import { ElasticsearchAdapter } from "@searchfn/adapter-elasticsearch"` |
| `import { OpenSearchAdapter } from "<legacy-adapters-package>"` | `import { OpenSearchAdapter } from "@searchfn/adapter-opensearch"` |

### Dependency Mapping

| Legacy dependency (aggregate package) | New dependency |
| --- | --- |
| `searchfn adapters aggregate` | `@searchfn/adapter-memory` (if using `MemoryAdapter`) |
| `searchfn adapters aggregate` | `@searchfn/adapter-indexeddb` (if using `IndexedDbAdapter`) |
| `searchfn adapters aggregate` | `@searchfn/adapter-postgres` (if using `PostgresAdapter`) |
| `searchfn adapters aggregate` | `@searchfn/adapter-meilisearch` (if using `MeilisearchAdapter`) |
| `searchfn adapters aggregate` | `@searchfn/adapter-elasticsearch` (if using `ElasticsearchAdapter`) |
| `searchfn adapters aggregate` | `@searchfn/adapter-opensearch` (if using `OpenSearchAdapter`) |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### SearchFn

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/index
Description: A full-text search engine and adapter system for TypeScript applications.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

SearchFn is a full-text search engine for TypeScript applications. It ships its own search runtime — with BM25 scoring, inverted indexes, fuzzy matching, stemming, and a configurable text pipeline — that runs in-memory or in the browser via IndexedDB. The same adapter contract also connects to Postgres, Meilisearch, or Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, so you can choose the right runtime for your use case without changing application code.

## System Architecture

SearchFn has two layers: a **built-in search engine** that handles indexing, tokenization, and ranking in-process, and **backend adapters** that delegate to external search services.

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph Core ["Built-in Search Engine (@searchfn/core)"]
        PL["Text Pipeline — tokenize, normalize, stem"]
        IX["Inverted Index"]
        SC["BM25 Scoring & Ranking"]
        FZ["Fuzzy Matching — Levenshtein"]
    end

    subgraph BuiltIn ["Built-in Adapters"]
        MA["MemoryAdapter — in-process"]
        IA["IndexedDbAdapter — browser-persistent"]
    end

    subgraph External ["External Backend Adapters"]
        PA[PostgresAdapter]
        MEI[MeilisearchAdapter]
        EA["Elasticsearch / OpenSearch"]
    end

    subgraph App ["Application Layer"]
        CL["SearchClient"]
        SV["SearchFnServer (HTTP)"]
        DP["DataFn Provider"]
    end

    MA --> Core
    IA --> Core
    CL --> MA
    CL --> IA
    SV --> PA
    SV --> MEI
    SV --> EA
    SV --> MA
    DP --> MA
    DP --> PA
    DP --> MEI
    DP --> EA
```

SearchFn is composed of seven package groups:

| Package | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `@searchfn/core` | Built-in search engine — text pipeline, inverted index, BM25 scoring, fuzzy matching, stemming |
| `@searchfn/adapter-contracts` | Shared adapter interface and request/response types |
| `@searchfn/adapter-memory` / `@searchfn/adapter-indexeddb` | Built-in engine adapters (in-process + browser-persistent) |
| `@searchfn/adapter-postgres` / `@searchfn/adapter-meilisearch` / `@searchfn/adapter-elasticsearch` / `@searchfn/adapter-opensearch` | External backend adapters |
| `@searchfn/client` | Client with validation, defaults, and convenience constructors |
| `@searchfn/server` | HTTP server with authorization, structured logging, and secret redaction |
| `@searchfn/datafn-provider` | Bridge that maps any SearchAdapter into a DataFn SearchProvider |

## Built-in Engine vs External Backends

| | Built-in engine (Memory, IndexedDB) | External backends (Postgres, Meilisearch, ES/OS) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Search logic** | SearchFn's own BM25 scoring, inverted index, fuzzy matching, stemming | Delegates to the backend's native search |
| **Infrastructure** | Zero — runs in-process or in the browser | Requires running the external service |
| **Use cases** | Offline-first apps, PWAs, browser-local search, in-process server search, tests | Multi-client shared search, very large datasets, backend-specific features (facets, custom analyzers) |

Both tiers are production-ready. The built-in engine powers offline-first apps and in-process search; external backends serve use cases that need shared state across clients or backend-specific capabilities. The adapter contract means you pick the right runtime for your requirements without changing application code.

### Quickstart

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/quickstart
Description: Get SearchFn indexing and serving queries in 5–10 minutes for your stack.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Pick your runtime. Each guide installs the right packages, picks a sensible default adapter for that environment, mounts the server, and runs a first search.

| Runtime | Default adapter | Guide |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hono | Memory (dev) / Postgres (prod) | [Hono](/docs/quickstart/hono) |
| Express | Memory / Postgres | [Express](/docs/quickstart/express) |
| Fastify | Memory / Postgres | [Fastify](/docs/quickstart/fastify) |
| Bun | Memory / Postgres | [Bun](/docs/quickstart/bun) |
| SvelteKit | IndexedDB (browser) + Postgres (server) | [SvelteKit](/docs/quickstart/sveltekit) |
| Next.js | IndexedDB (browser) + Postgres (server) | [Next.js](/docs/quickstart/nextjs) |
| FastAPI | Postgres | [FastAPI](/docs/quickstart/fastapi) |
| Starlette | Postgres | [Starlette](/docs/quickstart/starlette) |
| Flask | Postgres | [Flask](/docs/quickstart/flask) |
| Swift | Memory / SQLite | [Swift](/docs/quickstart/swift) |

## What gets installed

A SearchFn deployment is three layers:

1. **An adapter** — picks where the index lives.
2. **A server** — `createSearchFnServer({ adapter, basePath, ... })` mounted onto your HTTP framework.
3. **A client** — either the SearchFn client SDK (`@searchfn/client`) or the DataFn search provider (`@searchfn/datafn-provider`) if you're using DataFn.

The Quickstart pages stitch all three for your framework, but each layer is independently swappable. You can change adapters without changing client code, and you can switch from direct client use to the DataFn provider without changing the server.

## Decisions you'll make

When the guide asks you to pick an adapter, this is the short version:

- **In dev or for a CLI:** `@searchfn/adapter-memory`. Zero infra.
- **In a browser app:** `@searchfn/adapter-indexeddb` on the client + your choice of server adapter.
- **Already on Postgres:** `@searchfn/adapter-postgres`. Reuse your DB.
- **Need a dedicated search service:** `@searchfn/adapter-meilisearch`. Best dev ergonomics.
- **Big production scale:** `@searchfn/adapter-elasticsearch` or `@searchfn/adapter-opensearch`.

See the [Adapter comparison](/docs/reference/adapters) for the full breakdown.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Migrating Between Adapters

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/documentation/advanced/adapter-migration
Description: Move from Memory → Postgres → Meilisearch → Elasticsearch without downtime.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Switching adapters is mostly a one-line code change. The hard parts are: (1) moving the index data, (2) keeping queries serving traffic during the move, and (3) verifying parity afterwards.

## The pattern

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant App
    participant Old as Old adapter
    participant New as New adapter

    App->>Old: queries (live)
    App->>New: dual-write
    App->>App: backfill
    App->>App: verify parity
    App->>New: queries (live)
    App->>Old: optional rollback window
    App->>Old: decommission
```

The whole sequence is the same shape regardless of the source/destination pair.

## Step 1 — dual-write

Add the new adapter alongside the old one and write to both:

```typescript
import { MemoryAdapter } from "@searchfn/adapter-memory";
import { PostgresAdapter } from "@searchfn/adapter-postgres";

class DualAdapter implements SearchAdapter {
  readonly name = "dual";
  constructor(public read: SearchAdapter, public write: SearchAdapter) {}

  async initialize(p) { await this.read.initialize?.(p); await this.write.initialize?.(p); }
  async index(p)      { await Promise.all([this.read.index(p), this.write.index(p)]); }
  async remove(p)     { await Promise.all([this.read.remove(p), this.write.remove(p)]); }
  async clear(r, s)   { await Promise.all([this.read.clear(r, s), this.write.clear(r, s)]); }
  async search(p)     { return this.read.search(p); }
}
```

Wire it in:

```typescript
const sf = await createSearchFnServer({
  adapter: new DualAdapter(oldAdapter, newAdapter),
  basePath: "/searchfn",
});
```

New documents flow into both indices. Queries still hit the old one.

## Step 2 — backfill

For data already in the old index, copy it across.

**Memory → Postgres / Meilisearch / Elasticsearch**: re-index from your source-of-truth DB. The memory adapter doesn't expose a snapshot iterator; the original data lives in DataFn (or your DB), so you re-run the indexer.

**Postgres → another adapter**: stream rows from the SearchFn `_searchfn_*` tables and re-index. Or, for parity, re-index from the source DB.

**Cross-adapter**: re-index from the canonical source (DataFn, your DB, etc.). Don't try to ship the indexed form across — formats differ.

```typescript
import { rebuildFromSource } from "./backfill";

for await (const batch of streamFromSource()) {
  await newAdapter.index({ resource: "articles", documents: batch });
}
```

See [backfill from DB](/docs/recipes/backfill-from-db) for the throttle-and-resume pattern.

## Step 3 — verify parity

Run a small batch of queries against both adapters and compare:

```typescript
const queries = ["ranking", "bm25 swift", "fuzzy"];

for (const q of queries) {
  const oldIds = await oldAdapter.search({ resource: "articles", query: q });
  const newIds = await newAdapter.search({ resource: "articles", query: q });

  const overlap = oldIds.filter((id) => newIds.includes(id)).length;
  const pct = (overlap / oldIds.length) * 100;
  console.log(`"${q}": ${pct.toFixed(1)}% overlap`);
}
```

Don't expect 100% — different scoring algorithms produce different rankings. Aim for:

- >90% overlap in the top 10
- >70% overlap in the top 50

If overlap is lower, the new adapter is doing something wildly different — investigate before cutover.

## Step 4 — flip the read

Once you're satisfied:

```typescript
class DualAdapter implements SearchAdapter {
  ...
  async search(p) { return this.write.search(p); }  // was: this.read
}
```

Or remove the dual wrapper entirely:

```typescript
const sf = await createSearchFnServer({
  adapter: newAdapter,                              // direct
  basePath: "/searchfn",
});
```

Deploy. Queries now hit the new adapter.

## Step 5 — keep a rollback window

For at least one full reindex cycle:

- Keep the old adapter's data fresh (continue dual-writing).
- Have a feature flag to flip reads back to the old adapter.

If you see post-cutover problems, flip the flag and roll forward at your own pace.

## Step 6 — decommission

After the rollback window:

- Stop dual-writing.
- Drop the old adapter's tables / indices.
- Remove the dual-adapter code.

## Special cases

### Postgres → Meilisearch

Meilisearch wants documents in its own JSON shape. The SearchFn `MeilisearchAdapter` does the mapping for you — just use it.

### Elasticsearch → OpenSearch

The two adapters are nearly identical. Switching is `import` change + cluster swap. No backfill needed if you're forking an ES cluster as OS (OpenSearch is forked from ES 7).

### Memory → IndexedDB

This isn't a server change; it's a client/embedded change. Re-index from your source. Same pattern.

### TypeScript → Python

Different engines (BM25 vs term-count). Parity isn't possible. Use this migration as an opportunity to evaluate whether term-count meets your needs.

## See also

- [Writing an adapter](/docs/documentation/advanced/writing-an-adapter)
- [Reindex with no downtime](/docs/recipes/reindex-no-downtime)
- [Backfill from DB](/docs/recipes/backfill-from-db)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Writing an Adapter

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/documentation/advanced/writing-an-adapter
Description: Implement SearchAdapter against your own backend — full guide.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

A SearchFn adapter is the layer between the SearchFn server and a storage backend. The contract is intentionally small. If your backend can index text and return ranked IDs, you can write an adapter for it.

## The contract

From `@searchfn/adapter-contracts`:

```typescript
export interface SearchAdapter {
  readonly name: string;
  readonly capabilities?: SearchAdapterCapabilities;

  initialize?(params: InitializeParams): Promise<void>;
  index(params: IndexParams): Promise<void>;
  search(params: SearchParams): Promise<Array<string | number>>;
  searchAll?(params: SearchAllParams): Promise<SearchAllResult[]>;
  remove(params: RemoveParams): Promise<void>;
  clear(resource: string, signal?: AbortSignal): Promise<void>;
  dispose?(): Promise<void>;
}
```

Six required methods (plus two optional). The server calls these; you do the work.

## Step 1 — pick capabilities

```typescript
const capabilities: SearchAdapterCapabilities = {
  persistent: true,        // does the index survive process restarts?
  searchAll: false,        // do you implement searchAll natively?
  fuzzy: true,             // do you support fuzzy queries?
  prefix: true,            // do you support prefix queries?
  fieldBoosts: true,       // do you respect field weights?
  maxBatchSize: 1000,      // max docs per index() call
};
```

If you set `searchAll: false`, the server falls back to running `search` per resource in parallel — fine for most cases.

## Step 2 — implement initialize

```typescript
async initialize(params: InitializeParams): Promise<void> {
  for (const config of params.resources) {
    // create per-resource storage (table, index, mapping)
    await this.createResourceIfNeeded(config.name, config.searchFields);
  }
}
```

Idempotent — called every time the server boots. If the resource already exists, no-op.

## Step 3 — implement index

```typescript
async index(params: IndexParams): Promise<void> {
  const { resource, documents, signal } = params;

  for (let i = 0; i < documents.length; i += BATCH_SIZE) {
    if (signal?.aborted) throw new Error("aborted");
    const batch = documents.slice(i, i + BATCH_SIZE);
    await this.writeBatch(resource, batch);
  }
}
```

Important details:

- **Upserts, not appends.** Re-indexing the same `id` must replace, not duplicate.
- **AbortSignal.** Respect it — bail out cleanly.
- **Field set.** Use the `searchFields` from `initialize`. Index only those.
- **Multi-line atomic writes.** A failed batch should either fully apply or fully rollback.

## Step 4 — implement search

```typescript
async search(params: SearchParams): Promise<Array<string | number>> {
  const { resource, query, fields, limit, fuzzy, prefix, fieldBoosts } = params;

  const ids = await this.backendQuery({
    resource,
    query,
    fields: fields ?? this.resourceConfig[resource].searchFields,
    limit: limit ?? 20,
    fuzzy,
    prefix,
    fieldBoosts,
  });

  return ids;
}
```

Returns **IDs only**, ranked. The server hydrates records separately.

For backends that don't support fuzzy/prefix natively (Postgres FTS doesn't do edit-distance fuzzy):

- Either degrade gracefully (treat fuzzy as exact) and document the limitation.
- Or run a parallel n-gram match and merge results.

## Step 5 — implement remove

```typescript
async remove(params: RemoveParams): Promise<void> {
  const { resource, ids } = params;
  await this.backendDelete(resource, ids);
}
```

If a backend rejects unknown IDs, swallow that — `remove` should be idempotent.

## Step 6 — implement clear

```typescript
async clear(resource: string, signal?: AbortSignal): Promise<void> {
  if (signal?.aborted) throw new Error("aborted");
  await this.backendDeleteAll(resource);
}
```

Removes all documents for a resource. Resource configuration (from `initialize`) is preserved.

## Step 7 — implement dispose

```typescript
async dispose(): Promise<void> {
  await this.connection?.close();
  this.disposed = true;
}
```

After `dispose`, subsequent methods should throw `SEARCH_ADAPTER_DISPOSED`. The server detects this code and emits a clean error.

## Step 8 — implement searchAll (optional but recommended)

```typescript
async searchAll(params: SearchAllParams): Promise<SearchAllResult[]> {
  const resources = params.resources ?? this.allResources();
  const perResourceLimit = params.limitPerResource ?? 10;

  // Native multi-resource query if your backend supports it
  const rows = await this.backendMultiQuery({
    resources,
    query: params.query,
    perResourceLimit,
    fieldBoosts: params.fieldBoosts,
  });

  // Merge & rank
  return rows
    .sort((a, b) => b.score - a.score)
    .slice(0, params.limit ?? 20);
}
```

Don't implement this if your backend can't do it efficiently — the server's fallback (parallel `search` per resource) is fine for `<10` resources.

## Step 9 — wire up errors

Use `SearchAdapterError`:

```typescript
import { SearchAdapterError } from "@searchfn/adapter-contracts";

throw new SearchAdapterError("MY_CUSTOM_CODE", "human-readable message");
```

Standard codes the server already knows:

- `SEARCH_ADAPTER_DISPOSED`
- `SEARCH_ADAPTER_NOT_INITIALIZED`
- `SEARCH_ADAPTER_RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND`

Beyond these, define your own codes — the server passes them through.

## Step 10 — test

Use the shared test suite:

```typescript
import { runAdapterContractTests } from "@searchfn/adapter-contracts/testing";
import { MyAdapter } from "./my-adapter";

describe("MyAdapter contract", () => {
  runAdapterContractTests({
    name: "my-adapter",
    create: async () => new MyAdapter({ /* config */ }),
    teardown: async (adapter) => adapter.dispose?.(),
  });
});
```

The contract suite exercises every method, edge case, abort handling, idempotency, and concurrent access. If your adapter passes, the server can use it.

## Skeleton

```typescript
import {
  SearchAdapter,
  SearchAdapterCapabilities,
  SearchAdapterError,
  IndexParams,
  SearchParams,
  RemoveParams,
  InitializeParams,
  SEARCH_ADAPTER_DISPOSED,
} from "@searchfn/adapter-contracts";

export class MyAdapter implements SearchAdapter {
  readonly name = "my-adapter";
  readonly capabilities: SearchAdapterCapabilities = {
    persistent: true,
    fuzzy: false,
    prefix: true,
    fieldBoosts: true,
    maxBatchSize: 1000,
  };

  private disposed = false;
  private resources = new Map<string, { searchFields: string[] }>();

  constructor(private readonly config: { /* your config */ }) {}

  async initialize(params: InitializeParams): Promise<void> {
    this.assertNotDisposed();
    for (const r of params.resources) {
      this.resources.set(r.name, { searchFields: r.searchFields });
      // create backend storage
    }
  }

  async index(params: IndexParams): Promise<void> {
    this.assertNotDisposed();
    // write docs
  }

  async search(params: SearchParams): Promise<Array<string | number>> {
    this.assertNotDisposed();
    // query backend, return ranked IDs
    return [];
  }

  async remove(params: RemoveParams): Promise<void> {
    this.assertNotDisposed();
    // delete docs
  }

  async clear(resource: string): Promise<void> {
    this.assertNotDisposed();
    // delete all docs for resource
  }

  async dispose(): Promise<void> {
    this.disposed = true;
    // close handles
  }

  private assertNotDisposed(): void {
    if (this.disposed) {
      throw new SearchAdapterError(SEARCH_ADAPTER_DISPOSED, "Adapter disposed");
    }
  }
}
```

Copy this, fill in the backend logic, run the contract suite.

## Publishing

Conventions across `@searchfn/adapter-*` packages:

- Package name: `@searchfn/adapter-<backend>`.
- Default export and named export both expose the adapter class.
- Peer-dependency on `@searchfn/adapter-contracts`.
- Tests in `__tests__/` directory.
- Include a `README.md` with usage example.

See `searchfn/adapter-postgres/` for a reference implementation.

## See also

- [Adapter migration](/docs/documentation/advanced/adapter-migration)
- [Capabilities reference](/docs/reference/capabilities)
- [Errors reference](/docs/reference/errors)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Diagnostics

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/documentation/apple/diagnostics
Description: Opt-in event sink for observing SearchFn lifecycle on Apple.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

`SearchFnDiagnosticsSink` is the Apple equivalent of the TypeScript server's logger. It's opt-in, redacted, and gives you per-event counts and timings.

## Wiring

```swift
let sink = SearchFnDiagnosticsSink { event in
    print(event)
}

let client = search.client(configuration: SearchFnClientConfiguration(diagnostics: sink))
```

The same sink can be attached to the adapter directly:

```swift
let adapter = SearchFnMemoryAdapter(configuration: SearchFnMemoryAdapterConfiguration(
    diagnostics: sink
))
```

When attached at both layers, client events and adapter events fire independently — useful for debugging.

## Event groups

| Source | Group | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Client | `initialize`, `index`, `search`, `searchAll`, `searchAll.fallback`, `remove`, `clear`, `dispose` | One per client method call |
| Adapter | `initialize`, `index`, `search`, `searchAll`, `remove`, `clear`, `dispose` | Adapter-level operations |
| Persistence | `open`, `reopen`, `close` | Only for `SQLiteAdapter` |

## What's included

Per-event payloads contain counts and metadata:

- `resource` (string)
- `query` length (Int) — **not** the query content
- `documentCount` (Int) for indexing
- `indexKey` (string, hashed)
- `directoryName` (string, deterministic from indexKey)
- `schemaVersion` (string)
- `durationNanoseconds` (Int)

Raw field values, full query strings, and document content are **not** emitted. Diagnostics are safe to forward to a remote logger.

## Routing to a logger

```swift
import OSLog

let logger = Logger(subsystem: "com.example.MyApp", category: "searchfn")

let sink = SearchFnDiagnosticsSink { event in
    switch event {
    case .client(let group, let detail):
        logger.info("client.\(group, privacy: .public): \(detail, privacy: .public)")
    case .adapter(let group, let detail):
        logger.info("adapter.\(group, privacy: .public): \(detail, privacy: .public)")
    case .persistence(let group, let detail):
        logger.info("persistence.\(group, privacy: .public): \(detail, privacy: .public)")
    }
}
```

Privacy markers (`.public`, `.private`) are honored by OSLog — diagnostic detail is safe to mark public because it's already redacted.

## Performance tracking

```swift
let sink = SearchFnDiagnosticsSink { event in
    if case .client(let group, let detail) = event,
       group == "search" {
        if let ns = detail.durationNanoseconds {
            let ms = Double(ns) / 1_000_000.0
            metrics.search.latency.record(ms)
        }
    }
}
```

Hook into Apple's Metrics framework or your own telemetry pipeline.

## Disabling

Don't pass a `diagnostics` to the configuration — diagnostics are off by default.

For production builds where you want diagnostics only when the user reports an issue:

```swift
let config = SearchFnClientConfiguration(
    diagnostics: userOptedIn ? sink : nil
)
```

## See also

- [Events reference](/docs/reference/events)
- [Swift reference](/docs/reference/swift)
- [Memory adapter](/docs/documentation/apple/memory-adapter)

### Apple Runtime

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/documentation/apple
Description: SearchFn on iOS, macOS, watchOS, and tvOS — standalone Swift package.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The Swift package is a standalone search runtime. It ships:

- `SearchFnCore` — the BM25 engine, ported to Swift.
- `SearchFnMemoryAdapter` — in-memory adapter.
- `SearchFnSQLiteAdapter` — SQLite-backed persistent adapter.
- `SearchFnClient` — validating client facade.
- `SearchFnConvenience` — one-liner constructors.

It does **not** depend on DataFn or the TypeScript server. You can use it standalone, or pair it with DataFn's Apple runtime via the WebView bridge.

## When to use which adapter

| Use case | Adapter |
| --- | --- |
| Tests / CLI tools | `SearchFnMemoryAdapter` |
| App with persistent search | `SearchFnSQLiteAdapter` |
| App embedded in a WebView with DataFn | `SearchFnSQLiteAdapter` under the DataFn Apple runtime |

## Sub-pages

- [Setup](/docs/documentation/apple/setup) — installation and bootstrap.
- [Memory adapter](/docs/documentation/apple/memory-adapter) — ephemeral, in-process.
- [SQLite adapter](/docs/documentation/apple/sqlite-adapter) — persistent storage.
- [SwiftUI](/docs/documentation/apple/swiftui) — binding search results into a SwiftUI view.
- [Diagnostics](/docs/documentation/apple/diagnostics) — opt-in observability.

## See also

- [Swift quickstart](/docs/quickstart/swift)
- [Swift reference](/docs/reference/swift)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Memory Adapter

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/documentation/apple/memory-adapter
Description: SearchFnMemoryAdapter — in-process, ephemeral, fastest.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The Memory adapter holds the inverted index in RAM. State is lost when the process exits. Use for tests, CLI tools, and short-lived processing.

## Bootstrap

```swift
import SearchFnConvenience
import SearchFnAdapterContracts

let search = InMemorySearchFn(
    defaults: SearchFnDefaults(
        limit: 20,
        limitPerResource: 10,
        fuzzy: .enabled,
        prefix: true
    )
)

let client = search.client()
```

`InMemorySearchFn` constructs the adapter, the client, and wires defaults in one step.

## Initialize resources

```swift
try await client.initialize(
    SearchFnInitializeParams(
        resources: [
            SearchFnInitializeResourceConfig(name: "tasks", searchFields: ["title", "body"])
        ]
    )
)
```

Resource initialization is optional but recommended. Without it, indexing falls back to all fields as searchable.

## Index

```swift
try await client.index(
    SearchFnIndexParams(
        resource: "tasks",
        documents: [
            SearchFnDocument(id: "t-1", fields: ["title": "Hybrid search", "body": "Swift local index"]),
            SearchFnDocument(id: "t-2", fields: ["title": "Groceries", "body": "Milk and bread"]),
        ]
    )
)
```

Documents have `id: String` and `fields: [String: SearchFnFieldValue]`. The field value type covers string, integer, double, boolean, and string array.

## Search

```swift
let ids = try await client.search(
    SearchFnSearchParams(resource: "tasks", query: "hybrid")
)
```

Returns `[String]` (or `[Int64]` for integer IDs — depends on how you indexed).

## searchAll

```swift
let results = try await client.searchAll(
    SearchFnSearchAllParams(query: "milk", resources: ["tasks", "notes"])
)

for hit in results {
    print(hit.resource, hit.id, hit.score)
}
```

## remove / clear

```swift
try await client.remove(resource: "tasks", ids: ["t-2"])
try await client.clear(resource: "tasks")
```

## Dispose

```swift
try await client.dispose()
```

After disposal, calling any method throws `SEARCH_ADAPTER_DISPOSED`. Re-initialize to use again.

## Threading

Methods are `async` and safe to call from any actor. Internally the adapter serializes mutations via an actor; concurrent reads are allowed.

For SwiftUI:

```swift
@MainActor
class SearchVM: ObservableObject {
    @Published var ids: [String] = []
    let client: SearchFnClient

    func search(_ q: String) async {
        do {
            ids = try await client.search(SearchFnSearchParams(resource: "tasks", query: q))
                .map(String.init(describing:))
        } catch {
            print(error)
        }
    }
}
```

## When to switch to SQLite

Memory is fine for:

- Single-session use (process restarts re-build the index from scratch).
- Datasets that comfortably fit in RAM (a few hundred MB max).
- Tests where determinism is more important than persistence.

For everything else, use [SQLiteAdapter](/docs/documentation/apple/sqlite-adapter).

## See also

- [SQLite adapter](/docs/documentation/apple/sqlite-adapter)
- [Swift reference](/docs/reference/swift)

### Setup

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/documentation/apple/setup
Description: Add SearchFn to a Swift project.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Package.swift

```swift
.package(url: "https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions", from: "0.2.0"),
.product(name: "SearchFnConvenience", package: "super-functions"),
```

`SearchFnConvenience` re-exports the adapter types and provides the one-liner constructors. For lower-level control, import the products you need directly:

```swift
.product(name: "SearchFnClient", package: "super-functions"),
.product(name: "SearchFnSQLiteAdapter", package: "super-functions"),
.product(name: "SearchFnAdapterContracts", package: "super-functions"),
```

## In Xcode

File → Add Package Dependencies → enter `https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions`. Pick the products you need.

## Min platform

- iOS 17 / macOS 14 (Observation framework dependency for SwiftUI binding).
- iOS 16 / macOS 13 (without SwiftUI bindings — pure client).

Older platforms aren't supported. SearchFn relies on Swift 5.9 features.

## App permissions

None required. SearchFn writes to the app's container; no external network or capability needed.

For SQLite mode, ensure the app supports write access to the path you choose:

```swift
let rootURL = FileManager.default
    .urls(for: .applicationSupportDirectory, in: .userDomainMask)[0]
    .appendingPathComponent("searchfn-store", isDirectory: true)
```

Application Support is the standard location. iCloud Backup includes it by default; if you want to exclude:

```swift
var url = rootURL
try url.setResourceValues({
  var v = URLResourceValues()
  v.isExcludedFromBackup = true
  return v
}())
```

## Build verification

From the repo root:

```bash
swift test --package-path searchfn/swift
swift build --package-path searchfn/swift --target SearchFnInMemoryExample
swift build --package-path searchfn/swift --target SearchFnSQLiteExample
```

These compile and execute the in-package examples.
