- [Docker](/docs/documentation/deploy/docker)
- [Scaling](/docs/documentation/deploy/scaling)
- [Production checklist](/docs/documentation/security/production-checklist)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Deploy: Railway

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/documentation/deploy/railway
Description: SearchFn on Railway with Railway Postgres or external Meilisearch.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Railway's templated Postgres + auto-deploy fit SearchFn well.

## Provisioning

1. Create a new Railway project.
2. Add a **Postgres** plugin. Railway sets `DATABASE_URL` automatically.
3. Add a **Node** service. Point it at your repo's `searchfn-server` directory.

## Server code

```typescript
import { createServer } from "node:http";
import { createSearchFnServer } from "@searchfn/server";
import { PostgresAdapter } from "@searchfn/adapter-postgres";

const sf = await createSearchFnServer({
  adapter: new PostgresAdapter({
    connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL!,
  }),
  basePath: "/searchfn",
});

await sf.adapter.initialize?.({
  resources: [{ name: "articles", searchFields: ["title", "body"] }],
});

const httpServer = createServer(async (req, res) => {
  if (!req.url?.startsWith("/searchfn/")) {
    res.writeHead(404);
    res.end();
    return;
  }

  const chunks: Buffer[] = [];
  for await (const chunk of req) chunks.push(chunk);
  const body = Buffer.concat(chunks).toString("utf8");

  const response = await sf.router.handle({
    method: req.method ?? "GET",
    url: `http://${req.headers.host}${req.url}`,
    headers: new Headers(req.headers as Record<string, string>),
    body: body || undefined,
  });

  res.writeHead(response.status, Object.fromEntries(response.headers));
  res.end(await response.text());
});

httpServer.listen(parseInt(process.env.PORT ?? "8080"));
```

## Migrations

Run the Postgres migration on first deploy:

```bash
railway run npx @searchfn/adapter-postgres migrate
```

Or programmatically at app start (idempotent):

```typescript
import { getPostgresMigrationSQL } from "@searchfn/adapter-postgres";
import postgres from "postgres";

const sql = postgres(process.env.DATABASE_URL!);
await sql.unsafe(getPostgresMigrationSQL());
```

## Meilisearch on Railway

Railway has a one-click Meilisearch template. After deploying it:

- `MEILI_HOST` and `MEILI_MASTER_KEY` are exposed to the SearchFn service via Railway's internal variable wiring.
- Use `MeilisearchAdapter` instead of `PostgresAdapter`.

## Health check

In the Railway service settings, set the health check path to `/searchfn/status`. Railway auto-restarts unhealthy instances.

## See also

- [Postgres adapter](/docs/reference/adapters/postgres)
- [Meilisearch adapter](/docs/reference/adapters/meilisearch)
- [Production checklist](/docs/documentation/security/production-checklist)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Scaling

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/documentation/deploy/scaling
Description: Capacity planning, bottlenecks, and how to scale a SearchFn deployment.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

A SearchFn deployment scales along three axes: server replicas, adapter-backend capacity, and index storage. Each has its own bottleneck.

## Server replicas

SearchFn's server is stateless when paired with an external adapter — scale horizontally. Typical sizing:

| Replicas | RPS (queries) | RPS (indexing) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 100–500 | 10–100 |
| 3 | 300–1500 | 30–300 |
| 10 | 1000–5000 | 100–1000 |

Numbers depend heavily on query complexity (single-term vs multi-term, fuzzy vs exact, single-resource vs `searchAll`).

The server is CPU-bound on queries (BM25 scoring) and memory-bound on indexing (token buffering). For a typical 8-core, 16 GB instance:

- 1 CPU per ~500 queries/sec sustained
- 256 MB of working memory per parallel index batch

## Adapter backend capacity

This is usually the real bottleneck.

### Postgres

- `tsvector` GIN index queries are ~1 ms with cache warm, ~50 ms with cache cold.
- Index writes are ~10 ms each; batches amortize.
- Postgres connection pool size caps concurrent operations.

Scale: bigger Postgres instance, then read replicas for query traffic.

### Meilisearch

- Queries ~5 ms typical.
- Indexing throughput ~10k docs/sec on a single Meilisearch instance.
- Single-node only out of the box; for HA use Meilisearch Cloud or roll your own replication.

Scale: vertically (more CPU + RAM). Meilisearch doesn't shard.

### Elasticsearch / OpenSearch

- Queries ~10 ms typical with cache.
- Indexing ~20k docs/sec on a 3-node cluster.
- Sharded; scales horizontally.

Scale: add data nodes; tune `number_of_shards`.

## Memory adapter

In-memory, in-process. Scales only by adding more (independent) processes. Use only for:

- Dev / tests
- Single-instance workloads where the dataset fits in RAM
- CLI tools

For anything that needs HA, pick an external adapter.

## Bottleneck diagnosis

1. **Watch p99 latency.** If query latency is `<10 ms` and server CPU is `>60%`, you're CPU-bound on the server — add replicas.
2. **Watch backend latency.** If query latency is `>50 ms` and backend latency is `>40 ms`, you're backend-bound — scale the backend, not the server.
3. **Watch index throughput.** If indexing keeps timing out, you're write-bound — batch larger, scale the backend, or reduce indexed fields.

## Cold-start considerations

For serverless deployments (Vercel, Cloudflare Workers, Lambda):

- `initialize()` runs on first request. Keep the resource list small.
- Adapter connection setup adds 100–500 ms to cold start. Pool with warmers (cron pings to `/searchfn/status`).
- MemoryAdapter on cold start = empty index. Don't use it on serverless.

## Cache warming

For Postgres adapter, the OS file cache warms after a few queries. Cold-cache p99 can be 10x higher than warm-cache p99. Mitigations:

- Pre-warm by running representative queries on deploy.
- Move hot indices to faster storage (NVMe vs spinning disk).
- Increase `shared_buffers` in Postgres.

## Index size estimates

| Corpus | Memory adapter | Postgres adapter | Meilisearch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1k docs × 100 chars/field × 2 fields | ~1 MB | ~5 MB | ~3 MB |
| 100k docs × 500 chars/field × 5 fields | ~500 MB | ~3 GB | ~2 GB |
| 1M docs × 1000 chars/field × 5 fields | OOM | ~50 GB | ~30 GB |
| 10M docs | ES/OS only | ~500 GB | tight | depends |

These are rough; measure with your own corpus before sizing.

## Per-resource limits

A common pattern is one giant `messages` resource and many small ones (`users`, `channels`, etc.). The big resource dominates index size and query CPU. Mitigations:

- Shard the big resource by time (`messages_2026_q1`, `messages_2026_q2`) and search across them with `searchAll`.
- Use a separate adapter for the big resource (Elasticsearch) and a cheaper one for the rest (Postgres).

## See also

- [Performance overview](/docs/documentation/performance/index)
- [Indexing throughput](/docs/documentation/performance/indexing-throughput)
- [Query latency](/docs/documentation/performance/query-latency)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Deploy: Vercel

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/documentation/deploy/vercel
Description: Run SearchFn server-side on Vercel using Next.js API routes or serverless functions.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Vercel runs SearchFn well if you pick an external adapter (Postgres, Meilisearch, Elasticsearch). The MemoryAdapter is wrong for serverless — every cold start rebuilds.

## Recommended adapter

| Use case | Adapter |
| --- | --- |
| Mostly read-heavy, already on Postgres | `@searchfn/adapter-postgres` (with Neon, Supabase, or Vercel Postgres) |
| Dedicated search service | `@searchfn/adapter-meilisearch` |
| Large scale | `@searchfn/adapter-elasticsearch` (managed Elastic Cloud) |

## Next.js App Router

```typescript
// app/searchfn/[...path]/route.ts
import { createSearchFnServer } from "@searchfn/server";
import { PostgresAdapter } from "@searchfn/adapter-postgres";

let sfPromise: ReturnType<typeof createSearchFnServer> | null = null;

function getServer() {
  if (!sfPromise) {
    sfPromise = createSearchFnServer({
      adapter: new PostgresAdapter({
        connectionString: process.env.SEARCH_DB_URL!,
      }),
      basePath: "/searchfn",
    }).then(async (sf) => {
      await sf.adapter.initialize?.({
        resources: [{ name: "articles", searchFields: ["title", "body"] }],
      });
      return sf;
    });
  }
  return sfPromise;
}

const handler = async (request: Request) => {
  const sf = await getServer();
  return sf.router.handle({
    method: request.method,
    url: request.url,
    headers: request.headers,
    body: request.body,
  });
};

export const GET = handler;
export const POST = handler;
```

The `sfPromise` cache makes the adapter survive within a single Lambda invocation — across invocations it might not, depending on Vercel's container reuse.

## Database connection pooling

Vercel Functions are stateless and ephemeral. Use a pooler:

- **Neon**: built-in connection pool — connect with `pooler` host.
- **Supabase**: built-in pgBouncer.
- **Vercel Postgres**: pre-pooled.

Without a pooler, Postgres exhausts max_connections under traffic.

```typescript
const adapter = new PostgresAdapter({
  connectionString: process.env.SEARCH_DB_URL!, // pooler URL
  poolSize: 1, // one connection per Lambda
});
```

## Edge runtime

Vercel's Edge runtime is V8 isolates, not Node. Direct DB drivers don't work. For Edge:

- Use `@searchfn/adapter-meilisearch` (HTTP) or `@searchfn/adapter-elasticsearch` (HTTP).
- Don't use `@searchfn/adapter-postgres` on Edge.

## CORS

If the SearchFn server is on a different domain than your app, configure CORS:

```typescript
const handler = async (request: Request) => {
  if (request.method === "OPTIONS") {
    return new Response(null, {
      status: 204,
      headers: {
        "Access-Control-Allow-Origin": process.env.APP_ORIGIN!,
        "Access-Control-Allow-Methods": "GET, POST, OPTIONS",
        "Access-Control-Allow-Headers": "Content-Type, Authorization",
      },
    });
  }
  // ... regular handler
};
```

## Logs

Vercel's logs are Datadog-flavoured by default. Send structured JSON; Vercel parses it:

```typescript
const sf = await createSearchFnServer({
  adapter,
  logger: {
    info: (msg, ctx) => console.log(JSON.stringify({ level: "info", msg, ...ctx })),
    warn: (msg, ctx) => console.warn(JSON.stringify({ level: "warn", msg, ...ctx })),
    error: (msg, ctx) => console.error(JSON.stringify({ level: "error", msg, ...ctx })),
    debug: () => {},
  },
});
```

## See also

- [Next.js quickstart](/docs/quickstart/nextjs)
- [Postgres adapter](/docs/reference/adapters/postgres)
- [Scaling](/docs/documentation/deploy/scaling)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Cache Tuning

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/documentation/performance/cache-tuning
Description: LRU caches in the built-in engine, OS cache for Postgres, and how to size both.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Caches are where SearchFn pays for the difference between disk and memory. The defaults are reasonable; for high-throughput deployments you'll want bigger ones.

## IndexedDbAdapter LRU caches

```typescript
new IndexedDbAdapter({
  dbName: "search",
  cache: {
    terms: 1024,    // term docFrequency
    postings: 2048, // posting lists
  },
});
```

| Cache | Default | Purpose | When to raise |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `terms` | 1024 | Hot term docFrequency lookups | Queries hit many distinct terms |
| `postings` | 2048 | Hot posting lists | Queries on same terms repeatedly |

Memory per entry is roughly:

- `terms`: ~50 bytes per entry → 1024 entries ≈ 50 KB
- `postings`: ~200 bytes per entry (typical posting list) → 2048 entries ≈ 400 KB

A 10x bump uses ~5 MB — fine for any modern device.

## MemoryAdapter

`MemoryAdapter` doesn't use LRU — everything lives in a Map. There's no cache to tune; size your process memory to fit the working set.

For a 1M-document corpus with 50 tokens/doc average, expect ~1.5 GB of working set. Bigger than that, switch to IndexedDB or external adapter.

## Postgres OS cache

Postgres caches data in two layers:

1. `shared_buffers` (configured) — Postgres's own cache.
2. OS page cache — the file system cache. Postgres reads through this.

For a SearchFn-heavy workload:

- `shared_buffers` = 25% of system memory (typical Postgres rule).
- Reserve another 50% for OS page cache by not over-provisioning Postgres.
- For dedicated DB hosts, `shared_buffers` up to 40% can help with very read-heavy workloads.

After a fresh start, run representative queries to warm the cache. Cold p99 can be 10x higher than warm p99.

## Meilisearch caches

Meilisearch caches the entire index in RAM by default. If your index is `<RAM`, Meili is fast. If the index outgrows RAM, latency spikes.

```bash
# Check Meili memory usage
curl http://localhost:7700/stats
```

Scale: vertically. Meili doesn't shard.

## Elasticsearch caches

ES has three caches:

- **Field data cache** — used by sort and aggregations.
- **Query cache** — caches frequent queries.
- **Request cache** — caches search responses.

Default sizing is fine for most workloads. For very read-heavy:

```json
PUT _cluster/settings
{ "persistent": { "indices.queries.cache.size": "20%" } }
```

Track cache hit rates via `_nodes/stats?metric=indices`.

## Cache invalidation

LRU caches in the built-in engine are invalidated on writes — index, remove, clear all flush the relevant entries. You don't need to reset them manually.

For Postgres, `VACUUM` and `ANALYZE` rebuild planner statistics; run them after big bulk changes.

For Meilisearch, an `updateDocuments` invalidates the index cache transparently.

For ES, deletes invalidate the query cache for the index.

## When caches don't help

- **High-cardinality queries.** If every query is unique (search-as-you-type with long unique queries), nothing repeats — caches don't help, but they don't hurt either.
- **Indexing-heavy workloads.** Caches are flushed by writes; under heavy write load, the cache hit rate stays low.

## Monitoring

For IndexedDB / Memory:

```typescript
adapter.cacheStats(); // { terms: { hits, misses, size }, postings: { ... } }
```

For Postgres:

```sql
SELECT relname, heap_blks_read, heap_blks_hit
FROM pg_statio_user_tables
WHERE relname LIKE '_searchfn_%';
```

For Meili: `/stats`.

For ES: `_nodes/stats?metric=indices`.

A hit ratio below 80% is a sign to raise the cache; above 99% means you could lower it without harm.

## See also

- [Query latency](/docs/documentation/performance/query-latency)
- [Inverted index](/docs/documentation/core/inverted-index)
- [Scaling](/docs/documentation/deploy/scaling)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Performance

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/documentation/performance
Description: Where to look when SearchFn is slow.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Performance work on SearchFn falls into three buckets. The right move depends on which bucket your workload is in.

| Symptom | Bucket | Read |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Indexing takes hours | Indexing throughput | [Indexing throughput](/docs/documentation/performance/indexing-throughput) |
| Search latency over budget | Query latency | [Query latency](/docs/documentation/performance/query-latency) |
| Memory or storage growing too fast | Cache tuning | [Cache tuning](/docs/documentation/performance/cache-tuning) |

## Profile before tuning

Before changing constants, measure:

- Server `durationMs` p50 / p95 / p99 per operation (from the structured logger).
- Backend latency (Postgres EXPLAIN ANALYZE, Meilisearch slow-query log, ES profile API).
- Memory usage during indexing.

A 30-minute profiling session beats a week of guessing.

## Targets

For most apps:

- Query p99 `<100 ms`.
- Indexing throughput `>1000 docs/sec` per server.
- Memory usage stable under sustained load.

If you're way off these numbers, something's wrong before tuning — almost always (a) wrong adapter pick, (b) missing index on Postgres, or (c) indexing too many fields.

## When the engine is the bottleneck

The built-in engine (`@searchfn/core`) is fast but not Rust-fast. Practical limits:

- ~50k docs/sec indexing on a single core (text-only, average field size).
- ~10k queries/sec exact match, single core, warm cache.
- Fuzzy queries are 5–20x slower than exact.

If you need more than that out of the JS engine, look at:

- `@searchfn/core-wasm` (Rust+WASM build of the same engine — see [WASM core](/docs/documentation/core-wasm/index)).
- Switching to an external adapter (Postgres / Meilisearch / Elasticsearch).

## See also

- [Scaling](/docs/documentation/deploy/scaling)
- [Core engine overview](/docs/documentation/core/index)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Indexing Throughput

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/documentation/performance/indexing-throughput
Description: Make backfills and bulk indexing fast.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

A 10 M-record backfill at 100 docs/sec takes 28 hours. At 5000 docs/sec it's 33 minutes. The difference is usually three things: batch size, concurrency, and pipeline cost.

## Pick the right batch size

```typescript
// Too small — round-trip overhead dominates
await adapter.index({ resource: "articles", documents: [oneDoc] });

// Sweet spot
await adapter.index({ resource: "articles", documents: docs.slice(0, 500) });

// Too big — memory pressure, transaction risk
await adapter.index({ resource: "articles", documents: docs.slice(0, 50000) });
```

| Adapter | Batch sweet spot |
| --- | --- |
| `MemoryAdapter` | 500–5000 (memory only) |
| `IndexedDbAdapter` | 100–500 (per IDB transaction) |
| `PostgresAdapter` | 500–2000 (per Postgres transaction) |
| `MeilisearchAdapter` | 1000–5000 (per Meili task) |
| `Elasticsearch` / `OpenSearch` | 500–2000 (per `_bulk` call) |

## Parallel batches

Sequential batches leave the backend idle while the next batch is being constructed. Parallelize:

```typescript
import pLimit from "p-limit";

const limit = pLimit(4); // 4 concurrent batches

const batches = chunk(allDocs, 500);
await Promise.all(
  batches.map((batch) =>
    limit(() => adapter.index({ resource: "articles", documents: batch }))
  )
);
```

Concurrency higher than 4 usually saturates the backend without further throughput gains.

## Reduce pipeline cost per doc

Each indexed token costs time. Per doc:

- Tokenize all `searchFields`
- Normalize each token
- Filter stop words
- Stem each token
- Generate edge n-grams (if enabled)
- Write postings

Cuts:

- **Index fewer fields.** Only what you search.
- **Disable edge n-grams** if you don't need autocomplete.
- **Drop the stemmer** for short / structured fields.
- **Lower `maxBatchSize`** — but only if you're memory-pressured. Otherwise batch larger.

## Streaming source

If the source is a paginated DB query, paginate with cursors, not `OFFSET`:

```typescript
// BAD — Postgres scans + skips every batch
for (let off = 0; ; off += 500) {
  const batch = await db.articles.findMany({ skip: off, take: 500 });
  if (!batch.length) break;
  await indexBatch(batch);
}

// GOOD — keyset pagination
let lastId = "";
while (true) {
  const batch = await db.articles.findMany({
    where: { id: { gt: lastId } },
    orderBy: { id: "asc" },
    take: 500,
  });
  if (!batch.length) break;
  await indexBatch(batch);
  lastId = batch[batch.length - 1].id;
}
```

## Postgres-specific tuning

The PostgresAdapter writes use `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT`. For bulk loads:

- Disable GIN auto-vacuum during the load, run `VACUUM ANALYZE` after.
- Set `maintenance_work_mem` to 1 GB+ for the bulk load session.
- Use `COPY` directly instead of the adapter (for one-time massive backfills) — bypass the abstraction.

## Meilisearch-specific tuning

- Send batches to the same index; Meilisearch batches them internally before applying.
- Disable typo tolerance during the load (`updateTypoTolerance`), re-enable after.
- Watch the task queue (`/tasks?status=processing`) — if it's backing up, slow down indexing.

## Elasticsearch-specific tuning

- Disable refresh during the load (`index.refresh_interval = -1`), set it back to `1s` after.
- Reduce `number_of_replicas` to 0 during the load, restore after.
- Use the `_bulk` API; ES indexes in parallel internally.

## Measuring

```typescript
const t0 = Date.now();
let count = 0;

for await (const batch of stream) {
  await adapter.index({ resource: "articles", documents: batch });
  count += batch.length;
  if (count % 10000 === 0) {
    const rate = count / ((Date.now() - t0) / 1000);
    console.log(`${count} docs in ${(Date.now() - t0) / 1000}s = ${rate.toFixed(0)} docs/sec`);
  }
}
```

Stable rate after the first minute is your real throughput.

## See also

- [Backfill from DB](/docs/recipes/backfill-from-db)
- [Reindex with no downtime](/docs/recipes/reindex-no-downtime)
- [Scaling](/docs/documentation/deploy/scaling)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Query Latency

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/documentation/performance/query-latency
Description: Where the milliseconds go and how to claw them back.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

A typical SearchFn query budget:

| Stage | Memory adapter | Postgres adapter | Meilisearch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Network in | 1–5 ms | 1–5 ms | 1–5 ms |
| Validate | `<1 ms` | `<1 ms` | `<1 ms` |
| Authorize | 0–5 ms | 0–5 ms | 0–5 ms |
| Adapter | 1–10 ms | 5–50 ms | 5–30 ms |
| Network out | 1–5 ms | 1–5 ms | 1–5 ms |
| **Total p99** | **5–30 ms** | **10–80 ms** | **10–50 ms** |

The adapter time is where you'll spend most of your tuning budget.

## Fuzzy is expensive

A 2-edit fuzzy on a 100k-vocab corpus typically adds 30–100 ms per query. If fuzzy is on by default, turn it off for autocomplete (where prefix is correct) and reserve fuzzy for the final "no results" fallback.

```typescript
// First try exact
let ids = await client.search({ resource: "articles", query });

// Only if no results, try fuzzy
if (ids.length === 0 && query.length >= 4) {
  ids = await client.search({ resource: "articles", query, fuzzy: 1 });
}
```

## Limit the result size

```typescript
// 10k results means 10k records scored, sorted, serialized
await client.search({ resource: "articles", query, limit: 10000 });

// 10 results — same scoring work, but tiny serialization
await client.search({ resource: "articles", query, limit: 10 });
```

The scoring stage doesn't short-circuit at `limit` (it has to score all candidates to rank them), but serialization, network, and downstream record fetching scale linearly with the limit.

For UI: `limit: 50` is almost always enough.

## fieldBoosts and field restriction

```typescript
// Search all fields
await client.search({ resource: "articles", query });

// Only title — faster, more relevant
await client.search({ resource: "articles", query, fields: ["title"] });
```

Field restriction is a 2–10x speedup for queries that don't actually want body matches.

## Cache hits

The built-in engine (Memory, IndexedDB) reads postings through an LRU cache. Hits are O(1); misses go to IndexedDB or the underlying map.

```typescript
new IndexedDbAdapter({
  dbName: "search",
  cache: { terms: 4096, postings: 8192 },
});
```

Default caches handle most workloads. Bump them if you see cold queries dominating p99.

For Postgres, the OS file cache holds index pages. After ~30 minutes of representative load, the cache is warm. Cold-cache p99 is 5–10x higher.

## searchAll merge cost

```typescript
await client.searchAll({
  query,
  resources: ["articles", "products", "users", "categories"], // 4 resources
});
```

Per-resource searches run in parallel (up to 10 concurrent in the default fallback). The merge sort is O(N log N) where N is total results. With `limitPerResource: 10` and 10 resources, that's 100 results sorted — trivial.

The cost goes up if resources differ wildly in size — large resources can dominate the merge. See [cross-resource ranking](/docs/recipes/cross-resource-ranking).

## Postgres EXPLAIN

If a Postgres-adapter query is slow:

```sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT id, ts_rank(search_tsv, plainto_tsquery('english', 'ranking')) AS score
FROM _searchfn_articles
WHERE search_tsv @@ plainto_tsquery('english', 'ranking')
ORDER BY score DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

What you want to see: `Bitmap Heap Scan` on the GIN index. If you see `Seq Scan`, the GIN index is missing or the query plan is off — vacuum/analyze the table.

## Meilisearch latency

Meilisearch has built-in latency in its task queue. Search queries don't go through the task queue, but index writes do. If the queue is backed up, query latency stays low but writes take seconds-to-minutes.

Monitor via `/stats` and `/tasks?status=processing`.

## Elasticsearch profile

ES has a profile API:

```json
{ "query": { ... }, "profile": true }
```

The profile shows per-shard breakdown. Look for high `rewrite_time_in_nanos` (often a sign of bad query shape).

## See also

- [BM25 scoring](/docs/documentation/core/bm25)
- [Cache tuning](/docs/documentation/performance/cache-tuning)
- [Indexing throughput](/docs/documentation/performance/indexing-throughput)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### HTTP Mount

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/documentation/python/http-mount
Description: Mount the SearchFn routes on FastAPI, Starlette, or Flask.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

`create_searchfn_server` returns a dict of route handlers in the format:

```python
{
    "routes": {
        "POST /searchfn/index":  async_handler,
        "POST /searchfn/search": async_handler,
    }
}
```

Each handler has the signature `async def handler(ctx, payload) -> dict`. `ctx` is unused (reserved); `payload` is the parsed JSON body.

## FastAPI

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request, HTTPException
from searchfn import create_searchfn_server

app = FastAPI()

plugin = create_searchfn_server({"schema": schema, "db": db})
routes = plugin["routes"]

@app.post("/searchfn/index")
async def search_index_route(request: Request):
    payload = await request.json() if await request.body() else {}
    result = await routes["POST /searchfn/index"](None, payload)
    if not result.get("ok"):
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail=result.get("error"))
    return result

@app.post("/searchfn/search")
async def search_search_route(request: Request):
    payload = await request.json()
    result = await routes["POST /searchfn/search"](None, payload)
    if not result.get("ok"):
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail=result.get("error"))
    return result
```

A small wrapper translates `{"ok": False, "error": ...}` into HTTP 400. Successful responses pass through.

## Starlette

```python
from starlette.applications import Starlette
from starlette.responses import JSONResponse
from starlette.routing import Route
from searchfn import create_searchfn_server

plugin = create_searchfn_server({"schema": schema, "db": db})
routes_map = plugin["routes"]

async def handle(spec: str):
    handler = routes_map[spec]

    async def endpoint(request):
        body = await request.body()
        payload = await request.json() if body else {}
        result = await handler(None, payload)
        if not result.get("ok"):
            return JSONResponse(result, status_code=400)
        return JSONResponse(result)

    return endpoint

app = Starlette(routes=[
    Route("/searchfn/index", endpoint=await handle("POST /searchfn/index"), methods=["POST"]),
    Route("/searchfn/search", endpoint=await handle("POST /searchfn/search"), methods=["POST"]),
])
```

## Flask

Flask is sync; bridge with `asyncio.run`:

```python
import asyncio
from flask import Flask, request, jsonify
from searchfn import create_searchfn_server

app = Flask(__name__)
plugin = create_searchfn_server({"schema": schema, "db": db})
routes = plugin["routes"]

def _bridge(handler):
    def view():
        payload = request.get_json(silent=True) or {}
        result = asyncio.run(handler(None, payload))
        return jsonify(result), (200 if result.get("ok") else 400)
    return view

app.add_url_rule("/searchfn/index", view_func=_bridge(routes["POST /searchfn/index"]),
                 methods=["POST"], endpoint="sf_index")
app.add_url_rule("/searchfn/search", view_func=_bridge(routes["POST /searchfn/search"]),
                 methods=["POST"], endpoint="sf_search")
```

For high-throughput Flask deployments, prefer Quart (Flask-API-compatible, async-native).

## Auth wrapper

The handlers don't authenticate. Wrap them:

```python
def require_admin(handler):
    async def wrapped(ctx, payload):
        # ctx carries request-derived auth in your wrapper
        if not ctx or not ctx.get("is_admin"):
            return {"ok": False, "error": "Forbidden"}
        return await handler(ctx, payload)
    return wrapped

routes["POST /searchfn/index"] = require_admin(routes["POST /searchfn/index"])
```

Or gate in the HTTP framework layer (FastAPI dependency, Starlette middleware, Flask decorator).

## CORS

CORS isn't handled by `create_searchfn_server` — it's a transport concern. Use your framework's CORS middleware:

- FastAPI: `fastapi.middleware.cors.CORSMiddleware`
- Starlette: `starlette.middleware.cors.CORSMiddleware`
- Flask: `flask-cors`

## Tests

You don't need HTTP to test:

```python
import pytest
from searchfn import create_searchfn_server

@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_search_returns_results(test_schema, test_db):
    plugin = create_searchfn_server({"schema": test_schema, "db": test_db})
    handler = plugin["routes"]["POST /searchfn/search"]
    result = await handler(None, {"query": "hello"})
    assert result["ok"]
    assert len(result["results"]) > 0
```

## See also

- [FastAPI quickstart](/docs/quickstart/fastapi)
- [Starlette quickstart](/docs/quickstart/starlette)
- [Flask quickstart](/docs/quickstart/flask)
- [Python reference](/docs/reference/python)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Python

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/documentation/python
Description: SearchFn Python — a lightweight DataFn companion for database-backed full-text search.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The Python package (`searchfn`) is a companion plugin for **DataFn Python**. It maintains an inverted index inside the same database DataFn uses, and exposes index / search operations as HTTP handlers and async functions.

It is **not** a full port of the TypeScript engine. The Python flavor targets:

- Quick prototyping with DataFn Python.
- Moderate-scale apps (tens to hundreds of thousands of records).
- Environments where adding Elasticsearch is overkill.

For everything else, run the TypeScript server (it's framework-agnostic and works across stacks).

## Two surfaces

| Surface | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `create_searchfn_server` | Returns route handlers you mount on FastAPI, Flask, Starlette, etc. |
| `index_data` / `search_index` | Async functions for direct use in background jobs and tests. |

## How it works

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant Routes as SearchFn routes
    participant DB as Database (DataFn-managed)
    Client->>Routes: POST /searchfn/index
    Routes->>DB: scan models, INSERT into _searchfn_index
    Routes-->>Client: { totalIndexed, totalTerms }
    Client->>Routes: POST /searchfn/search { query }
    Routes->>DB: SELECT FROM _searchfn_index WHERE term IN (...)
    Routes-->>Client: { results: [{ id, model, score, matches }] }
```

The index is a single table named `<prefix>index` (default `_searchfn_index`) with columns `term, model, recordId, field`.

## Where it lives

```
searchfn/python/
  src/searchfn/
    __init__.py        ← public surface
    server.py          ← create_searchfn_server (HTTP handlers)
    indexing.py        ← index_data
    search.py          ← search_index
    utils.py           ← tokenize, schema helpers
```

## Sub-pages

- [Setup](/docs/documentation/python/setup) — install, configure, schema requirements.
- [Indexing](/docs/documentation/python/indexing) — `index_data` semantics.
- [Search](/docs/documentation/python/search) — `search_index`, scoring, limits.
- [HTTP mount](/docs/documentation/python/http-mount) — FastAPI, Starlette, Flask integration.

## See also

- [FastAPI quickstart](/docs/quickstart/fastapi)
- [Starlette quickstart](/docs/quickstart/starlette)
- [Flask quickstart](/docs/quickstart/flask)
- [Python reference](/docs/reference/python)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Indexing

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/documentation/python/indexing
Description: How index_data walks DataFn models and populates the inverted index.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

`index_data` is the core indexer. It scans DataFn models for string fields, tokenizes their values, and writes rows to the `<prefix>index` table.

## Signature

```python
async def index_data(
    schema,
    db,
    model: Optional[str] = None,
    table_prefix: str = "_searchfn_"
) -> dict
```

Returns:

```python
{ "totalIndexed": int, "totalTerms": int }
```

## Single model vs full

```python
# Index every model with string fields
await index_data(schema, db)

# Index only "articles"
await index_data(schema, db, model="articles")
```

The model-scoped variant is what you call from background jobs after writing a record — see [partial reindex](/docs/recipes/partial-reindex).

## Pipeline

For each model:

1. Read schema fields, pick the ones with `"type": "string"`.
2. `db.find_many(model_name, [])` — fetch all records.
3. For each record:
   - Delete prior index rows for `(model, recordId)` to avoid stale terms.
   - For each string field, tokenize and `db.create` one row per (term, model, recordId, field).

## Tokenization

```python
def tokenize(value: str) -> Iterable[str]:
    return (
        token
        for token in re.split(r"[^a-z0-9]+", value.lower())
        if len(token) > 1
    )
```

Lowercase, split on non-alphanumeric runs, keep tokens of 2+ characters. Whitespace, punctuation, accents stripped. (Accents stripped means "café" → "caf" — fine for English-leaning content; for full unicode support, swap to ICU or trim before passing.)

## Duplicate handling

If the index already has a row with `(term, model, recordId, field)`, the insert is treated as a duplicate and skipped silently. SearchFn detects this via the error message:

```python
def _is_duplicate_error(error: Exception) -> bool:
    message = str(error).lower()
    return (
        "duplicate" in message
        or "unique constraint" in message
        or "already exists" in message
    )
```

This makes re-indexing the same content idempotent.

## Performance

Indexing is single-threaded and per-document. Rough numbers on Postgres:

| Corpus | Time |
| --- | --- |
| 1k docs, 5 string fields × 100 words | ~5s |
| 10k docs | ~50s |
| 100k docs | ~10 min |

For large datasets, the bottleneck is per-row `INSERT`s. To accelerate:

- Use Postgres `COPY` directly for the first load (bypass the abstraction).
- Run indexing in parallel batches if your DataFn adapter is thread-safe.
- Avoid re-indexing fields that haven't changed (partial reindex).

## Read consistency

`index_data` does not lock. If records are written during indexing:

- Records that exist when `find_many` runs are indexed.
- Newer writes are not seen by the current run.

For correctness under concurrent writes, prefer the [partial reindex pattern](/docs/recipes/partial-reindex) — re-index single records on write, run a full re-index only periodically.

## Errors

The function raises non-duplicate exceptions. Wrap calls:

```python
try:
    result = await index_data(schema, db)
except Exception as e:
    logger.exception("indexing failed", exc_info=e)
```

## See also

- [Search](/docs/documentation/python/search)
- [Partial reindex](/docs/recipes/partial-reindex)
- [Backfill from DB](/docs/recipes/backfill-from-db)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Search

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/documentation/python/search
Description: How search_index ranks records and what to expect from the Python scoring model.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

`search_index` queries the inverted index and returns ranked records.

## Signature

```python
async def search_index(
    schema,
    db,
    query: str,
    model: Optional[str] = None,
    limit: int = 20,
    table_prefix: str = "_searchfn_"
) -> list[dict]
```

Returns:

```python
[
    {
        "id": "...",
        "model": "articles",
        "score": 3,
        "matches": ["bm25", "ranking", "term"]
    },
    ...
]
```

## Scoring

The Python flavor uses a much simpler scoring model than the TypeScript engine: **term-count scoring**.

```python
scores[(model, recordId)] += 1  # per unique-term row matched
```

That's it. No BM25, no field weighting, no length normalization. Records with more distinct matched terms rank higher.

Tradeoffs:

- Predictable, easy to reason about.
- Fast for moderate corpora.
- Less relevance precision than BM25.

For production-grade relevance, switch to the TypeScript engine + Postgres adapter, or use Postgres `tsvector` directly.

## Tokenization

Same as the indexer — see [Indexing](/docs/documentation/python/indexing). Queries are tokenized identically, ensuring index/query agreement.

```python
tokens = list(dict.fromkeys(tokenize(query)))
# "BM25 Ranking BM25" → ["bm25", "ranking"]
```

Duplicate tokens are de-duplicated before lookup.

## Per-token lookup

For each unique token, one `find_many` runs against `_searchfn_index`:

```python
WHERE term = 'bm25' [AND model = '...']
```

Then matches are merged in memory and counted.

This is fast for short queries. For very long queries (10+ unique tokens), the round-trip count grows linearly — consider batching in a future patch.

## Model filtering

```python
results = await search_index(schema, db, "ranking", model="articles")
```

Without a model, all models are searched and the results carry their `model` field.

## Limits

```python
results = await search_index(schema, db, "ranking", limit=50)
```

Defaults to 20. The HTTP handler caps at 10,000. Beyond that, paginate via your own filter logic — SearchFn returns the top-N by score.

## Ordering

Results are sorted by:

1. Score (descending)
2. Model name (ascending)
3. Record ID (ascending — string-coerced)

Deterministic for ties.

## Empty queries

```python
await search_index(schema, db, "")        # → []
await search_index(schema, db, "!!!?")    # → [] (no surviving tokens)
```

The handler returns `400 Missing query` for empty strings; the function returns an empty list.

## Joining back to the records

`search_index` returns IDs, not records. To hydrate:

```python
hits = await search_index(schema, db, "ranking", model="articles")
ids = [h["id"] for h in hits]
records = await db.find_many("articles", [{"field": "id", "operator": "in", "value": ids}])
```

Or in one round-trip via your DataFn query API.

## See also

- [Indexing](/docs/documentation/python/indexing)
- [HTTP mount](/docs/documentation/python/http-mount)
- [Python reference](/docs/reference/python)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Setup

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/documentation/python/setup
Description: Install searchfn (Python) and wire it to your DataFn schema.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Install

```bash
pip install searchfn
```

You'll also need DataFn Python installed and configured (DataFn is the source of truth for the schema and the database connection).

## Minimum schema requirements

`searchfn` only indexes string fields. Every model you want to search needs:

- An `id` field that's stringifiable.
- One or more fields of `type: "string"`.

Example schema fragment:

```python
schema = {
    "models": {
        "articles": {
            "fields": {
                "id":       {"type": "uuid"},
                "title":    {"type": "string"},
                "body":     {"type": "string"},
                "author_id":{"type": "string"},  # not indexed (would be, but you can filter post-search)
            }
        }
    }
}
```

The indexer walks `fields` and picks anything with `"type": "string"`. To exclude a field, change its type or move it to a sub-table.

## Storage

SearchFn creates a single table at first index:

```sql
CREATE TABLE _searchfn_index (
    id        SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    term      VARCHAR,
    model     VARCHAR,
    recordId  VARCHAR,
    field     VARCHAR,
    UNIQUE (term, model, recordId, field)
);
```

(Exact DDL depends on your DataFn adapter; the indexer uses `db.create`, so the table is created via DataFn's migration story.)

The `table_prefix` is configurable:

```python
search_plugin = create_searchfn_server({
    "schema": schema,
    "db": db,
    "table_prefix": "fts_",  # → fts_index
})
```

## Initialization

```python
from searchfn import create_searchfn_server

search_plugin = create_searchfn_server({
    "schema": schema,
    "db": db,
})
```

The plugin returns a dict:

```python
{
    "routes": {
        "POST /searchfn/index":  index_handler,
        "POST /searchfn/search": search_handler,
    }
}
```

Mount the routes on your HTTP framework — see [HTTP mount](/docs/documentation/python/http-mount).

## Trigger first index

After mounting the server:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/searchfn/index
# → { "ok": true, "result": { "totalIndexed": 1234, "totalTerms": 50000 } }
```

Or programmatically in a startup hook:

```python
from searchfn import index_data

@app.on_event("startup")
async def initial_index():
    await index_data(schema, db)
```

## Configuration summary

| Option | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `schema` | required | DataFn schema dict |
| `db` | required | DataFn-compatible adapter instance |
| `table_prefix` | `"_searchfn_"` | Prefix for SearchFn-owned tables |

## See also

- [Indexing](/docs/documentation/python/indexing)
- [HTTP mount](/docs/documentation/python/http-mount)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Security

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/documentation/security
Description: The threat model and defense layers for a SearchFn deployment.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The short version: SearchFn assumes a hostile network and a partially-trusted client. The server is the single point of authorization. Adapters never see credentials; the server-side `authorize` callback is the gate.

## Layers

```mermaid
graph TD
  Client[Client request] --> Edge[Edge: CORS + TLS + IP allowlist]
  Edge --> Limits[Payload limits]
  Limits --> Authz[authorize callback]
  Authz --> Validation[Schema validation]
  Validation --> Adapter[Adapter execution]
  Adapter --> Redaction[Log redaction]
  Redaction --> Response[Response envelope]
```

Each layer rejects the request as early as possible. Authorization happens before the adapter touches anything; validation happens before any work is queued.

## The trust model

| Component | Trusted? | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Client** | No | Pass everything through the server |
| **Server router** | Yes | Validates and authorizes every request |
| **`authorize` callback** | Yes | Application code; you write it |
| **Adapter** | Yes | Receives only what `authorize` permits |
| **Backend** (Postgres, Meili, ES) | Yes | Credentials never leave the server |

There's no "direct client → backend" path. Clients hit the SearchFn server, which gates each operation.

## What's protected

- **Authentication** — your problem (use AuthFn or any session library).
- **Authorization** — the `authorize` callback. SearchFn enforces but doesn't decide policy.
- **Resource isolation** — naming convention + `authorize`. See [multi-tenant isolation](/docs/documentation/security/multi-tenant-isolation).
- **Input validation** — schema-checked request shapes; rejects malformed JSON, oversized payloads, invalid types.
- **Limit enforcement** — `maxQueryLength`, `maxIndexBatch`, etc. Per-server config.
- **Secret redaction** — `apiKey`, `password`, etc. are stripped from log output.

## What's not protected

SearchFn does not:

- Provide CSRF protection — that's your HTTP framework's job.
- Hash passwords — that's AuthFn's job.
- Encrypt at rest — that's your adapter's backend's job (Postgres, Meili, ES, IndexedDB).
- Encrypt in transit — that's TLS termination at your edge.

## Sub-pages

- [Request authz](/docs/documentation/security/request-authz) — the `authorize` callback in depth.
- [Multi-tenant isolation](/docs/documentation/security/multi-tenant-isolation) — keeping tenants apart.
- [Payload limits](/docs/documentation/security/payload-limits) — `maxQueryLength`, `maxIndexBatch`, and friends.
- [Secret redaction](/docs/documentation/security/secret-redaction) — what's stripped from logs.
- [Production checklist](/docs/documentation/security/production-checklist) — pre-launch audit.

## See also

- [Server reference](/docs/reference/server)
- [Multi-tenant search recipe](/docs/recipes/multi-tenant)
- [AuthFn integration](/docs/recipes/authfn-integration)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Multi-Tenant Isolation

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/documentation/security/multi-tenant-isolation
Description: Stop tenants from leaking into each other's search results.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Multi-tenant search is one of the easiest places to ship a data leak. SearchFn's defense isn't a single config — it's a discipline. Pick the right pattern, then enforce it everywhere.

## Threat: data leakage across tenants

If tenant A and tenant B share an index, and you filter results in application code after a query returns, the existence of matches across tenants is observable through scoring artifacts (matched documents per query, IDF changes, etc.). A malicious tenant can probe.

## Correct: resource-name isolation

Encode tenant into the resource name itself:

```typescript
// Tenant A's resource
await adapter.index({ resource: "articles:tenant-a", documents: [...] });

// Tenant B's resource (independent)
await adapter.index({ resource: "articles:tenant-b", documents: [...] });

// Queries are tenant-scoped
await adapter.search({ resource: "articles:tenant-a", query });
```

Each resource has its own vocabulary, IDF, posting lists. A query against `articles:tenant-a` cannot return anything from `articles:tenant-b`.

## Correct: per-tenant adapter

For strict isolation (regulated industries, multi-region compliance):

```typescript
const tenantAdapters = new Map<string, SearchAdapter>();

function getAdapter(tenantId: string) {
  if (!tenantAdapters.has(tenantId)) {
    tenantAdapters.set(tenantId, new PostgresAdapter({
      connectionString: tenantConnectionStrings[tenantId],
    }));
  }
  return tenantAdapters.get(tenantId)!;
}
```

Each tenant gets its own physical adapter (its own Postgres database, Meilisearch instance, etc.). Memory and connection cost scale linearly with tenants.

## Wrong: query-time filtering

Don't do this:

```typescript
// WRONG
const allIds = await client.search({ resource: "articles", query });
const myTenantIds = allIds.filter((id) => isMyTenant(id));
return myTenantIds;
```

The query touched documents from other tenants. The scoring, IDF, and term frequencies all included cross-tenant data. The fact that you discard the results doesn't undo that.

## Authorize as the enforcement layer

Even with resource-name isolation, the `authorize` callback must cross-check the resource against the caller's tenant:

```typescript
async function authorize(ctx, action, payload) {
  const session = await getSession(ctx.request);
  if (!session) return false;

  const resources = collectResources(payload);
  return resources.every((r) => resourceBelongsToTenant(r, session.user.tenantId));
}

function collectResources(payload: any): string[] {
  if (payload.resource) return [payload.resource];
  if (payload.resources) return payload.resources;
  return [];
}

function resourceBelongsToTenant(resource: string, tenantId: string): boolean {
  const parts = resource.split(":");
  return parts.length === 2 && parts[1] === tenantId;
}
```

A malicious tenant who tries `resource: "articles:other-tenant"` gets `FORBIDDEN`.

## Logging

Every cross-tenant attempt is a potential incident. Log them:

```typescript
logger: {
  warn: (msg, ctx) => {
    if (msg === "authorization.denied" && ctx.crossTenant) {
      pagerduty.send({
        severity: "high",
        title: "Cross-tenant search attempt",
        ...ctx,
      });
    }
  },
}
```

## Backend-specific notes

### Postgres

`PostgresAdapter` writes resources to separate tables (`_searchfn_articles_tenant_a`, `_searchfn_articles_tenant_b`). Row-level security isn't needed — the rows are physically separate.

### Meilisearch

Each resource becomes a Meili index. Indices are independent; an API key can be scoped to specific indices via Meili's `actions` system.

### Elasticsearch / OpenSearch

Each resource becomes an ES index. Use ES's [API key with index-scoped privileges](https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/security-api-create-api-key.html) for defense-in-depth.

### IndexedDB

Per-user isolation in the browser is implicit (different users = different browsers). But if multiple tenants share a device (kiosk, public terminal), use a per-tenant `dbName`.

## Audit before launch

- Search for `payload.resource` and `payload.resources` references in your `authorize` — make sure they're inspected.
- Try a manual cross-tenant request in staging and confirm it returns `FORBIDDEN`.
- Confirm the test catches a regression where someone removes the `authorize` check.

## See also

- [Multi-tenant search recipe](/docs/recipes/multi-tenant)
- [Request authz](/docs/documentation/security/request-authz)
- [Production checklist](/docs/documentation/security/production-checklist)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Payload Limits

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/documentation/security/payload-limits
Description: How SearchFn caps request size, query length, and batch counts — and why.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Without limits, a single malicious or buggy client can exhaust server memory by sending a 50 MB query, 100k documents per batch, or 5000 resources per `searchAll`. Default limits keep this from happening; production deployments may tune them.

## Defaults

| Limit | Default | What it stops |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `maxPayloadBytes` | `1_048_576` (1 MB) | Multi-MB request bodies |
| `maxQueryLength` | `1_000` chars | Pathological queries that explode pipeline cost |
| `maxResourcesPerSearchAll` | `50` | `searchAll` fan-out attacks |
| `maxLimit` | `10_000` | Asking for too many results |
| `maxLimitPerResource` | `1_000` | Per-resource fan-out |
| `maxIndexBatch` | `10_000` docs | Memory pressure during indexing |

## Configuring

```typescript
const sf = await createSearchFnServer({
  adapter,
  limits: {
    maxQueryLength: 500,
    maxIndexBatch: 5_000,
  },
});
```

Limits not specified use defaults.

## When to raise limits

- **`maxIndexBatch`** — increase if you have plenty of memory and want fewer round-trips during backfill. Don't go above 50k without testing.
- **`maxResourcesPerSearchAll`** — increase only if you have many small resources (per-tenant pattern with hundreds of tenants).

## When to lower limits

- **`maxQueryLength`** — lower for autocomplete-only endpoints (queries are short by definition).
- **`maxPayloadBytes`** — lower for client-facing search endpoints; raise for service-to-service indexing.
- **`maxLimit`** — lower aggressively; very few real UIs need more than 100 results.

## Per-endpoint limits

If you need different limits per endpoint, run two SearchFn servers:

```typescript
const userSf = await createSearchFnServer({
  adapter,
  basePath: "/searchfn",
  limits: { maxLimit: 50, maxIndexBatch: 0 }, // read-only for users
  authorize: async (ctx, action) => action === "search" || action === "searchAll",
});

const adminSf = await createSearchFnServer({
  adapter,
  basePath: "/admin/searchfn",
  limits: { maxIndexBatch: 50_000 },
  authorize: async (ctx) => isAdmin(ctx),
});
```

Mount both on the same HTTP framework with different `basePath` and `authorize`.

## What happens on limit violations

The server responds with `LIMIT_EXCEEDED`:

```json
{
  "ok": false,
  "error": {
    "code": "LIMIT_EXCEEDED",
    "message": "query exceeds maxQueryLength (1000)",
    "details": { "path": "query", "actual": 4521, "max": 1000 }
  }
}
```

HTTP status: 400.

Clients should treat this as a non-retryable client error — retrying won't help.

## HTTP framework limits

SearchFn's `maxPayloadBytes` is checked **after** the request body has been read. To stop attacks before the body is read, configure your HTTP framework's body limit at the same value or slightly higher:

- Express: `express.json({ limit: "2mb" })`
- Fastify: `Fastify({ bodyLimit: 2 * 1024 * 1024 })`
- Hono: `hono` doesn't enforce by default; use a body-size middleware.

## Rate limiting

Limits cap individual request size, not request rate. For per-user rate limits, use the `authorize` callback:

```typescript
import { Ratelimit } from "@upstash/ratelimit";

const indexLimiter = new Ratelimit({ redis, limiter: Ratelimit.slidingWindow(10, "1 m") });
const searchLimiter = new Ratelimit({ redis, limiter: Ratelimit.slidingWindow(120, "1 m") });

async function authorize(ctx, action) {
  const userId = ctx.user?.id ?? ctx.ip;
  const limiter = action === "index" ? indexLimiter : searchLimiter;
  const { success } = await limiter.limit(userId);
  return success && passesAuth(ctx, action);
}
```

Rate-limit denials look like authorization failures (`FORBIDDEN`) — surface this as 429 if you want HTTP semantics correct.

## See also

- [Request authz](/docs/documentation/security/request-authz)
- [Server reference](/docs/reference/server)
- [Configuration](/docs/reference/configuration)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Production Checklist

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/documentation/security/production-checklist
Description: Pre-launch audit for a SearchFn deployment.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Run through this before exposing SearchFn to real users.

## Authentication

- [ ] `authorize` callback is wired and rejects anonymous requests by default.
- [ ] Service accounts use distinct credentials from user sessions.
- [ ] At least one test asserts that unauthorized requests return `FORBIDDEN`.

## Multi-tenancy (if applicable)

- [ ] Resources include the tenant in the name (or per-tenant adapters are in use).
- [ ] `authorize` cross-checks the resource against the caller's tenant.
- [ ] A test asserts cross-tenant resource access is denied.

## Limits

- [ ] `maxPayloadBytes` matches the HTTP framework's body limit.
- [ ] `maxQueryLength` is set conservatively (`500`–`1000` for most apps).
- [ ] `maxIndexBatch` is tuned to your backfill plan, not the default.
- [ ] Rate limiting (in `authorize` or upstream) caps per-user request frequency.

## Adapter

- [ ] Adapter credentials are loaded from a secret manager, not committed.
- [ ] Backend has its own backup / DR plan (separate from SearchFn).
- [ ] Postgres: migration SQL has been run; tables and indexes exist.
- [ ] Meilisearch / Elasticsearch / OpenSearch: indices are created with correct settings.
- [ ] `dispose()` is called on shutdown to release connections.

## Logging

- [ ] Structured logger is wired (`info`, `warn`, `error`, `debug`).
- [ ] Logs are forwarded to a central system (Datadog, ELK, Splunk).
- [ ] Logs are tested for credential leakage (search for known secrets).
- [ ] `authorization.denied` events are flagged to a security alert channel.

## Observability

- [ ] `GET /searchfn/status` is wired as a load-balancer health check.
- [ ] `durationMs` percentiles are tracked (p50, p95, p99).
- [ ] `INTERNAL` error rate has an alert.
- [ ] Backend (Postgres, Meili, ES) has its own monitoring.

## Network

- [ ] TLS is enforced (no plaintext HTTP).
- [ ] CORS is configured per origin allowlist, not wildcard.
- [ ] Internal-only services (admin search) are firewalled separately.
- [ ] WebSocket / streaming endpoints (if any) honor the same `authorize` rules.

## Backup and recovery

- [ ] Postgres / external backend has a tested restore procedure.
- [ ] Snapshot mechanism (if used) is included in the backup rotation.
- [ ] Reindex from primary store is rehearsed end-to-end.
- [ ] Recovery time objective (RTO) is documented and matches the rehearsal.

## Index ownership

- [ ] If client-side IndexedDB is in use, schema-hash bumps clear stale indexes.
- [ ] DataFn provider's `resourceFields` excludes sensitive fields (`passwordHash`, etc.).
- [ ] Re-indexing tooling is documented (manual runbook + scripts).

## Testing

- [ ] Authorization tests cover happy path + denial path per action.
- [ ] Multi-tenant tests cover same-tenant pass + cross-tenant fail.
- [ ] Relevance tests exist and run in CI.
- [ ] Load test exists at expected p99 traffic.

## Documentation

- [ ] Internal runbook for backfill, reindex, snapshot, restore.
- [ ] On-call doc covers `LIMIT_EXCEEDED`, `INTERNAL`, `FORBIDDEN` first-response.
- [ ] Schema / `resourceFields` change procedure is documented.

## Operational

- [ ] CI fails on schema changes that haven't been reviewed by the team.
- [ ] Deploy procedure (server + adapter + secrets) is automated.
- [ ] Rollback procedure is documented and tested.

## See also

- [Request authz](/docs/documentation/security/request-authz)
- [Multi-tenant isolation](/docs/documentation/security/multi-tenant-isolation)
- [Deploy](/docs/documentation/deploy/index)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Request Authorization

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/documentation/security/request-authz
Description: The authorize callback — how to write one, how to test it.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

`createSearchFnServer` accepts an `authorize` callback that's invoked before every action. It receives the request context, the action name, and the request payload:

```typescript
const sf = await createSearchFnServer({
  adapter,
  authorize: async (ctx, action, payload) => {
    // return boolean
  },
});
```

When `authorize` returns `false`, the server responds with a `FORBIDDEN` envelope and the adapter is never touched.

## Actions

| Action | Called for | Typical policy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `status` | `GET /searchfn/status` | Allow all (or whitelist health-check IPs) |
| `search` | `POST /searchfn/search` | Authenticated users |
| `searchAll` | `POST /searchfn/search-all` | Authenticated users |
| `index` | `POST /searchfn/index` | Admin / service accounts |
| `remove` | `POST /searchfn/remove` | Admin / service accounts |
| `clear` | `POST /searchfn/clear` | Admin only |

## Worked example: role-based

```typescript
async function authorize(ctx, action, payload) {
  const session = await getSession(ctx.request);
  if (!session) return action === "status";

  switch (action) {
    case "status":
    case "search":
    case "searchAll":
      return true;
    case "index":
    case "remove":
      return session.user.role === "editor" || session.user.role === "admin";
    case "clear":
      return session.user.role === "admin";
  }
  return false;
}
```

## Worked example: per-resource ACL

```typescript
async function authorize(ctx, action, payload) {
  const session = await getSession(ctx.request);
  if (!session) return false;

  const resource = (payload as { resource?: string }).resource;
  const resources = (payload as { resources?: string[] }).resources ?? (resource ? [resource] : []);

  for (const r of resources) {
    if (!(await userCanAccess(session.user, r, action))) return false;
  }
  return true;
}
```

This handles both single-resource (`search`, `index`, etc.) and multi-resource (`searchAll`).

## Worked example: rate limiting

```typescript
import { Ratelimit } from "@upstash/ratelimit";

const limiter = new Ratelimit({
  redis,
  limiter: Ratelimit.slidingWindow(60, "1 m"), // 60 req/min per user
});

async function authorize(ctx, action, payload) {
  const session = await getSession(ctx.request);
  if (!session) return false;

  const { success } = await limiter.limit(session.user.id);
  if (!success) return false; // Returns FORBIDDEN; clients see rate limit as auth failure

  return true; // ... plus other rules
}
```

`authorize` is a flexible enough hook to be the only auth/limit layer if you want it to be.

## ctx contents

```typescript
interface AuthorizeCtx {
  request: Request;            // The original Request object
  ip?: string;                 // Source IP, if your framework provides it
  headers: Headers;            // Request headers
  user?: unknown;              // Whatever you populated upstream
  requestId?: string;
}
```

Anything that runs before SearchFn (auth middleware, CORS, etc.) can populate `ctx.user` for the callback to read.

## Failure modes

- **`authorize` returns `false`** → `FORBIDDEN` (403).
- **`authorize` throws** → the `authorization.error` event is logged, then `INTERNAL` (500). The original error doesn't leak.

Treat `authorize` like any other async function — handle your own errors.

## Testing

```typescript
import { createSearchFnServer } from "@searchfn/server";
import { MemoryAdapter } from "@searchfn/adapter-memory";

const sf = await createSearchFnServer({
  adapter: new MemoryAdapter(),
  authorize: async (ctx, action) => action === "search",
});

const res = await sf.router.handle({
  method: "POST",
  url: "http://test/searchfn/index",
  headers: new Headers({ "content-type": "application/json" }),
  body: JSON.stringify({ resource: "x", documents: [] }),
});
expect(res.status).toBe(403);
```

Inject the request directly into `router.handle` — no HTTP server needed.

## What to log on denial

```typescript
logger: {
  warn: (msg, ctx) => {
    if (msg === "authorization.denied") {
      audit({
        userId: ctx.userId ?? "anonymous",
        action: ctx.action,
        resource: ctx.resource,
        ip: ctx.ip,
        at: Date.now(),
      });
    }
  },
}
```

Patterns like "100 denied search requests from one IP in 1 minute" are signals for a security alert.

## See also

- [AuthFn integration recipe](/docs/recipes/authfn-integration)
- [Server reference](/docs/reference/server)
- [Multi-tenant isolation](/docs/documentation/security/multi-tenant-isolation)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Secret Redaction

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/documentation/security/secret-redaction
Description: What SearchFn strips from log output — and what you still have to handle.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The server recursively redacts sensitive keys before passing context to your logger. You don't have to remember which fields are sensitive; the redactor does.

## Redacted keys (case-insensitive)

- `apiKey`
- `password`
- `secret`
- `token`
- `authorization`
- `connectionString`

When any of these appears as a key anywhere in the logged context — top-level or nested — its value is replaced with `[redacted]`.

```typescript
logger: {
  info: (msg, ctx) => console.log(msg, ctx),
}

// Internal log call:
logger.info("request.start", {
  operation: "index",
  payload: {
    resource: "articles",
    auth: { token: "secret-token" }, // logged as "[redacted]"
  },
});
```

## What's not redacted by default

- Generic credential fields you've named differently (`cred`, `apiSecret`, custom names).
- Query strings (could contain sensitive search terms).
- Document field values (could be PII).

For these you have to extend the redactor:

```typescript
import { createRedactor } from "@searchfn/server";

const customRedactor = createRedactor({
  keys: ["apiKey", "password", "secret", "token", "authorization", "connectionString",
    "creditCard", "ssn", "phoneNumber"], // your additions
});

const sf = await createSearchFnServer({
  adapter,
  logger: {
    info: (msg, ctx) => console.log(msg, customRedactor(ctx)),
    // ... etc
  },
});
```

(API note: `createRedactor` is exposed for advanced wiring; check the version you're on.)

## Don't log search queries

Search queries can reveal sensitive intent ("HIV treatment", "lawyer", "competitor name"). For privacy-conscious deployments:

```typescript
logger: {
  info: (msg, ctx) => {
    const sanitized = { ...ctx };
    if (sanitized.payload?.query) sanitized.payload.query = "[query]";
    log(msg, sanitized);
  },
}
```

## Don't log indexed document content

Indexed documents contain the data you're trying to search. Logging the full payload defeats most data-minimization goals. Default behavior: SearchFn does not log the document body — it logs counts (`indexed: N`) and resource names.

Custom code that calls the adapter directly is your problem. Don't `console.log(documents)`.

## Backend credentials

Adapter constructors take connection strings, API keys, and similar:

```typescript
new PostgresAdapter({ connectionString: "postgres://user:pass@host/db" });
new MeilisearchAdapter({ apiKey: "super-secret" });
```

These never reach the logger. The adapter stores them internally for outbound calls but doesn't surface them through any of the structured log paths.

Custom adapters: if you write one, follow the same rule — credentials should be read at construction and never exposed through diagnostics or error messages.

## Error responses

Server error responses never include stack traces or backend credentials. If your adapter throws an error containing sensitive data, the message is logged but **not** returned to the client.

What clients see:

```json
{ "ok": false, "error": { "code": "INTERNAL", "message": "internal error" } }
```

What you see in logs:

```
{"level":"error","msg":"request.error","errorCode":"INTERNAL","operation":"search","errorMessage":"ECONNREFUSED 10.0.0.5:5432","stack":"..."}
```

Audit log forwarders to make sure they don't include the verbose context elsewhere.

## OWASP A09 (security logging)

The redaction model is shaped by the OWASP A09 guidance — log enough to investigate, redact enough to not become a secondary breach surface. Test by injecting credentials into test requests and grepping the log stream.

## See also

- [Request authz](/docs/documentation/security/request-authz)
- [Production checklist](/docs/documentation/security/production-checklist)
- [Observability](/docs/operations/observability)

## Examples
================================================================================


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Swift: In-Memory Example

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/examples/swift-in-memory
Description: SearchFnInMemoryExample — runs the in-memory adapter end-to-end.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

A self-contained Swift program that exercises every SearchFn client method against `SearchFnMemoryAdapter`. Source:

`searchfn/swift/Examples/InMemoryExample/main.swift`

## Run it

```bash
swift run --package-path searchfn/swift SearchFnInMemoryExample
```

Exits cleanly when all operations succeed.

## What it does

```swift
import SearchFnAdapterContracts
import SearchFnConvenience

@main
struct SearchFnInMemoryExample {
    static func main() async throws {
        let search = InMemorySearchFn(
            defaults: SearchFnDefaults(
                limit: 20,
                limitPerResource: 10,
                fuzzy: .enabled,
                prefix: true
            )
        )

        let client = search.client()

        try await client.initialize(
            SearchFnInitializeParams(
                resources: [
                    SearchFnInitializeResourceConfig(name: "tasks",
                                                    searchFields: ["title", "body"]),
                    SearchFnInitializeResourceConfig(name: "notes",
                                                    searchFields: ["body"]),
                ]
            )
        )

        try await client.index(
            SearchFnIndexParams(
                resource: "tasks",
                documents: [
                    SearchFnDocument(id: "t1",
                                     fields: ["title": "Hybrid search",
                                              "body": "Swift local index"]),
                    SearchFnDocument(id: "t2",
                                     fields: ["title": "Fix launch checklist",
                                              "body": "Coordinate docs and release"]),
                ]
            )
        )

        try await client.index(
            SearchFnIndexParams(
                resource: "notes",
                documents: [
                    SearchFnDocument(id: "n1",
                                     fields: ["body": "Launch notes for the Swift package"]),
                ]
            )
        )

        _ = try await client.search(
            SearchFnSearchParams(resource: "tasks", query: "hybrid")
        )

        _ = try await client.searchAll(
            SearchFnSearchAllParams(query: "launch",
                                    resources: ["tasks", "notes"])
        )

        try await client.remove(resource: "tasks", ids: ["t2"])
        try await client.clear(resource: "notes")
        try await client.dispose()
    }
}
```

## What to take away

- `InMemorySearchFn` is the one-liner for the memory adapter.
- `defaults` is where `limit`, `limitPerResource`, `fuzzy`, and `prefix` live.
- The example calls every public method on `SearchFnClient`: `initialize`, `index`, `search`, `searchAll`, `remove`, `clear`, `dispose`.

## Modify and run

Drop in your own data:

```swift
try await client.index(
    SearchFnIndexParams(
        resource: "tasks",
        documents: realData.map { d in
            SearchFnDocument(id: d.id, fields: ["title": d.title, "body": d.body])
        }
    )
)

let hits = try await client.search(SearchFnSearchParams(resource: "tasks", query: "ranking"))
print(hits)
```

For SwiftUI integration, see [SwiftUI binding](/docs/documentation/apple/swiftui).

## See also

- [Swift quickstart](/docs/quickstart/swift)
- [SQLite example](/docs/examples/swift-sqlite)
- [Memory adapter](/docs/documentation/apple/memory-adapter)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Swift: SQLite Example

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/examples/swift-sqlite
Description: SearchFnSQLiteExample — persistent on-device search backed by SQLite.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

A self-contained Swift program that wires `SearchFnSQLiteAdapter` to a temp directory and runs end-to-end. Source:

`searchfn/swift/Examples/SQLiteExample/main.swift`

## Run it

```bash
swift run --package-path searchfn/swift SearchFnSQLiteExample
```

The example writes to `$TMPDIR/searchfn-swift-example/`. Re-running it picks up the existing SQLite file and resumes — try running twice and adding a print to confirm state survives.

## What it does

```swift
import Foundation
import SearchFnAdapterContracts
import SearchFnConvenience
import SearchFnSQLiteAdapter

@main
struct SearchFnSQLiteExample {
    static func main() async throws {
        let rootURL = FileManager.default.temporaryDirectory
            .appendingPathComponent("searchfn-swift-example", isDirectory: true)

        let search = try SearchFn(
            sqlite: SearchFnSQLiteAdapterConfiguration(
                rootURL: rootURL,
                indexKey: "project-docs",
                defaults: SearchFnDefaults(limit: 10,
                                          limitPerResource: 5,
                                          fuzzy: .enabled,
                                          prefix: true)
            )
        )

        let client = search.client()

        try await client.initialize(
            SearchFnInitializeParams(
                resources: [
                    SearchFnInitializeResourceConfig(name: "docs",
                                                    searchFields: ["title", "body"]),
                    SearchFnInitializeResourceConfig(name: "guides",
                                                    searchFields: ["title"]),
                ]
            )
        )

        try await client.index(
            SearchFnIndexParams(
                resource: "docs",
                documents: [
                    SearchFnDocument(id: "d1",
                                     fields: ["title": "Getting started",
                                              "body": "Swift search runtime"]),
                    SearchFnDocument(id: "d2",
                                     fields: ["title": "Persistence",
                                              "body": "SQLite-backed local index"]),
                ]
            )
        )
        try await client.index(
            SearchFnIndexParams(
                resource: "guides",
                documents: [
                    SearchFnDocument(id: "g1",
                                     fields: ["title": "Swift package guide"]),
                ]
            )
        )

        _ = try await client.search(
            SearchFnSearchParams(resource: "docs", query: "getting")
        )

        _ = try await client.searchAll(
            SearchFnSearchAllParams(query: "swift",
                                    resources: ["docs", "guides"])
        )

        try await client.remove(resource: "docs", ids: ["d2"])
        try await client.clear(resource: "guides")
        try await client.dispose()
    }
}
```

## What to take away

- `SearchFn(sqlite:)` constructs the persistent variant.
- `rootURL` + `indexKey` together pick the on-disk location.
- After `dispose()`, the SQLite file remains. Re-opening with the same `indexKey` resumes.
- Defaults are persisted on init; subsequent opens honor them.

## In an iOS app

Swap the temp directory for Application Support:

```swift
let rootURL = FileManager.default
    .urls(for: .applicationSupportDirectory, in: .userDomainMask)[0]
    .appendingPathComponent("searchfn-store", isDirectory: true)
```

For full integration patterns, see [SwiftUI binding](/docs/documentation/apple/swiftui) and [SQLite adapter](/docs/documentation/apple/sqlite-adapter).

## See also

- [Swift quickstart](/docs/quickstart/swift)
- [SQLite adapter](/docs/documentation/apple/sqlite-adapter)
- [In-memory example](/docs/examples/swift-in-memory)
