## Integrations
================================================================================


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### DataFn Integration

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/integrations/datafn
Description: Connect SearchFn adapters to DataFn as a search provider.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The `@searchfn/datafn-provider` package bridges any SearchFn adapter into DataFn's search provider interface. This lets DataFn use SearchFn for full-text search without coupling to a specific search backend.

## Installation

```bash
npm install @searchfn/datafn-provider @searchfn/adapter-meilisearch
```

## Usage

Create a search provider by passing any SearchFn adapter to `createSearchProvider`:

```typescript
import { createSearchProvider } from "@searchfn/datafn-provider";
import { MeilisearchAdapter } from "@searchfn/adapter-meilisearch";

const adapter = new MeilisearchAdapter({
  host: process.env.MEILI_URL!,
  apiKey: process.env.MEILI_API_KEY!,
});

const provider = createSearchProvider(adapter, {
  resourceFields: {
    tasks: ["title", "description"],
    notes: ["content", "tags"],
  },
});
```

Then pass the provider to your DataFn server:

```typescript
import { createDatafnServer } from "@datafn/server";

const server = await createDatafnServer({
  schema,
  db: drizzleAdapter({ db, dialect: "postgres" }),
  search: provider,
});
```

### Client-Side Setup

Pass the same provider (or a client-appropriate adapter) to `createDatafnClient` for local-first search:

```typescript
import { createDatafnClient } from "@datafn/client";
import { createSearchProvider } from "@searchfn/datafn-provider";
import { IndexedDbAdapter } from "@searchfn/adapter-indexeddb";

const searchProvider = createSearchProvider(
  new IndexedDbAdapter({
    dbName: "my-app-search",
    defaults: { prefix: true, fuzzy: 0.2 },
  }),
  {
    resourceFields: {
      tasks: ["title", "description"],
      notes: ["content", "tags"],
    },
  },
);

const client = createDatafnClient({
  schema,
  clientId,
  storage,
  searchProvider,
});
```

With `searchProvider` configured on the client, DFQL `search` blocks and `client.search()` calls execute locally using the IndexedDB adapter. The client falls back to server search when the local index is not yet ready.

## Configuration

| Option | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `resourceFields` | `Record<string, string[]>` | Maps resource names to the record fields that should be indexed for search. Falls back to all fields except `id` when omitted. |

### Resource Fields

The `resourceFields` option controls which record fields become searchable. When DataFn indexes a record, only the fields listed here are sent to the search adapter:

```typescript
const provider = createSearchProvider(adapter, {
  resourceFields: {
    tasks: ["title", "description"],
    notes: ["content"],
  },
});
```

If `resourceFields` is omitted or a resource is not listed, the provider indexes all record fields except `id`.

## Provider Methods

The provider implements DataFn's `SearchProvider` interface:

| Method | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `search` | Search a single resource. Calls `adapter.search` and returns IDs as strings. |
| `searchAll` | Search across resources. Uses `adapter.searchAll` when available, otherwise runs per-resource searches concurrently (max 10) and merges results by score. |
| `updateIndices` | Called by DataFn on mutations. For `upsert`, maps records to search documents using `resourceFields` and calls `adapter.index`. For `delete`, calls `adapter.remove`. |
| `initialize` | Delegates to `adapter.initialize` when the adapter supports it. |
| `dispose` | Delegates to `adapter.dispose` when the adapter supports it. |

## Behavior

- **Abort signals** — all provider methods forward abort signals to the underlying adapter.
- **searchAll fallback** — if the adapter does not implement `searchAll`, the provider runs per-resource `search` calls concurrently (up to 10 at a time) and merges results with deterministic score-based ordering.
- **ID coercion** — the provider returns all IDs as strings to match DataFn's ID format.

## Adapter Recommendations

| Use case | Recommended adapter |
| --- | --- |
| Development and tests | `MemoryAdapter` |
| Small production apps | `PostgresAdapter` |
| User-facing search | `MeilisearchAdapter` |
| Large-scale search | `ElasticsearchAdapter` |



================================================================================
## Operations
================================================================================


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Observability

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/operations/observability
Description: Structured logging, health checks, and failure classification for SearchFn.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Structured Logging

Pass a `logger` to `createSearchFnServer` to receive structured log events for every operation:

```typescript
const server = await createSearchFnServer({
  adapter,
  logger: {
    info: (msg, ctx) => console.log(JSON.stringify({ level: "info", msg, ...ctx })),
    warn: (msg, ctx) => console.warn(JSON.stringify({ level: "warn", msg, ...ctx })),
    error: (msg, ctx) => console.error(JSON.stringify({ level: "error", msg, ...ctx })),
    debug: (msg, ctx) => console.debug(JSON.stringify({ level: "debug", msg, ...ctx })),
  },
});
```

### Log Events

The server emits these event names:
- `request.start`
- `request.end`
- `request.error`
- `authorization.denied`
- `authorization.error`
- `server.close`

### Log Fields

Each log event includes:

| Field | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `operation` | `string` | The action being performed (`search`, `index`, `remove`, etc.) |
| `adapter` | `string` | Adapter name (`memory`, `postgres`, `meilisearch`, etc.) |
| `durationMs` | `number` | Time taken for the operation in milliseconds |
| `status` | `number` | HTTP status code from the response |
| `success` | `boolean` | Whether the operation succeeded |
| `errorCode` | `string?` | Error code if the operation failed |

Sensitive values are automatically redacted before logging. See [Security](/docs/operations/security) for details.

## Health Endpoint

`GET /searchfn/status` provides a readiness check for load balancers and monitoring:

```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "result": {
    "adapter": "postgres",
    "capabilities": {
      "persistent": true,
      "searchAll": true,
      "fuzzy": true,
      "fieldBoosts": false
    },
    "uptimeMs": 84200
  }
}
```

Use this endpoint for:
- Kubernetes readiness probes
- Load balancer health checks
- Monitoring dashboards

## Failure Classification

Errors fall into five categories. Use these to build alerts and dashboards:

| Category | Error codes | Cause | Action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Validation | `DFQL_INVALID`, `LIMIT_EXCEEDED` | Malformed request or exceeded limits | Fix client-side request construction |
| Authorization | `FORBIDDEN` | Auth callback denied access | Check credentials and permissions |
| Unsupported | `DFQL_UNSUPPORTED` | Adapter doesn't support the operation | Use a different adapter or remove unsupported options |
| Runtime | `INTERNAL` | Unexpected backend failure | Check backend health and logs |
| Cancellation | `DFQL_ABORTED` | Client cancelled the request | No action needed (expected behavior) |

### Alerting Recommendations

- **Alert on `INTERNAL` errors** — these indicate backend problems that need investigation.
- **Monitor `LIMIT_EXCEEDED` rates** — a spike may indicate a client bug or abuse.
- **Track `durationMs` percentiles** — degrading latency can signal backend capacity issues.
- **Ignore `DFQL_ABORTED`** — these are normal when users navigate away or cancel searches.



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Security

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/operations/security
Description: Authorization, secret handling, and credential management for SearchFn.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Authorization

`createSearchFnServer` supports a per-action `authorize` callback. It is called before every operation with the request context, action name, and payload:

```typescript
const server = await createSearchFnServer({
  adapter,
  authorize: async (ctx, action, payload) => {
    if (action === "status") return true;
    if (action === "search" || action === "searchAll") return !!ctx.user;
    return ctx.user?.role === "admin";
  },
});
```

### Actions

| Action | Endpoint | Typical policy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `status` | `GET /searchfn/status` | Allow all (health checks) |
| `search` | `POST /searchfn/search` | Authenticated users |
| `searchAll` | `POST /searchfn/search-all` | Authenticated users |
| `index` | `POST /searchfn/index` | Admin or service accounts |
| `remove` | `POST /searchfn/remove` | Admin or service accounts |
| `clear` | `POST /searchfn/clear` | Admin only |

Unauthorized requests return a `FORBIDDEN` error envelope with no details about the denial reason.

## Secret Redaction

The server automatically redacts sensitive values in structured logs. The following keys are recursively redacted:

- `apiKey`
- `password`
- `secret`
- `token`
- `authorization`
- `connectionString`

Error responses never include backend credentials, connection strings, or internal stack traces.

## Credential Management

| Adapter | Credential | Storage recommendation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PostgresAdapter | Connection string (DSN) | Secure secret store or encrypted environment variable |
| MeilisearchAdapter | API key | Environment-level secret |
| Elasticsearch/OpenSearch | API key or username/password | Secure runtime secret store |

Never hardcode credentials in application code. Use environment variables at minimum, and a dedicated secret manager (AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, etc.) for production deployments.



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Setup

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/operations/setup
Description: Deploy SearchFn in production with proper configuration, limits, and resilience.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Deployment Steps

1. **Choose an adapter** — pick the adapter that matches your infrastructure. See [Adapters](/docs/reference/adapters) for a comparison.
2. **Run backend infrastructure** — set up Postgres, Meilisearch, or Elasticsearch/OpenSearch if using a server-side adapter.
3. **Run migrations** — for PostgresAdapter, execute the migration SQL to create required tables and indexes.
4. **Initialize resources** — call `initialize()` with your resource definitions before indexing traffic.
5. **Create the server** — use `createSearchFnServer()` to expose search over HTTP.
6. **Mount the router** — attach the server router to your HTTP framework using a `@superfunctions/http` adapter.

```typescript
import { createSearchFnServer } from "@searchfn/server";
import { PostgresAdapter } from "@searchfn/adapter-postgres";

const server = await createSearchFnServer({
  adapter: new PostgresAdapter({
    connectionString: process.env.SEARCH_DB_URL!,
  }),
  basePath: "/searchfn",
});

// Mount server.router with Express, Fastify, Hono, etc.
```

## Default Limits

The server enforces these limits by default. Override them in the `limits` configuration:

| Limit | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `maxQueryLength` | `1,000` | Maximum search query string length. |
| `maxLimit` | `10,000` | Maximum `limit` parameter value. |
| `maxLimitPerResource` | `1,000` | Maximum `limitPerResource` parameter value. |
| `maxResourcesPerSearchAll` | `50` | Maximum resources in a `searchAll` request. |
| `maxIndexBatch` | `10,000` | Maximum documents per index request. |
| `maxPayloadBytes` | `1,048,576` | Maximum request body size (1 MB). |

```typescript
const server = await createSearchFnServer({
  adapter,
  limits: {
    maxQueryLength: 500,
    maxIndexBatch: 5000,
  },
});
```

## Resilience

For external adapters (Postgres, Meilisearch, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch), configure timeouts and retries to handle transient failures:

```typescript
const adapter = new PostgresAdapter({
  connectionString: process.env.SEARCH_DB_URL!,
  queryTimeoutMs: 15000,
  retry: {
    maxRetries: 3,
    baseDelayMs: 200,
    maxDelayMs: 10000,
  },
});
```

- Use conservative timeouts that match your SLA requirements.
- Bounded retries with exponential backoff and jitter prevent thundering herd problems.
- Monitor retry rates to detect degraded backends early.

## Environment Variables

Keep all credentials in environment variables or a secret store:

| Variable | Used by | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `SEARCH_DB_URL` | PostgresAdapter | Postgres connection string |
| `MEILI_URL` | MeilisearchAdapter | Meilisearch endpoint |
| `MEILI_API_KEY` | MeilisearchAdapter | Meilisearch API key |
| `ES_NODE` | ElasticsearchAdapter | Elasticsearch/OpenSearch endpoint |
| `ES_API_KEY` | ElasticsearchAdapter | Elasticsearch API key |



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Troubleshooting

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/operations/troubleshooting
Description: Diagnose and resolve common SearchFn errors with error codes and backend-specific playbooks.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Error Reference

| Error Code | Cause | Resolution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `DFQL_INVALID` | Invalid request shape, missing required fields, or empty query string | Validate the request payload before sending. Check that `resource`, `query`, and `documents` fields are present and correctly typed. |
| `LIMIT_EXCEEDED` | Query length, result limit, resource count, or batch size exceeds configured maximums | Reduce the request size or increase server limits in the `limits` configuration. |
| `DFQL_ABORTED` | The caller aborted the request via `AbortSignal` | Expected behavior when users cancel searches. Retry from the client when appropriate. |
| `DFQL_UNSUPPORTED` | Adapter does not support the requested operation or configuration | Check your adapter's capabilities. For Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, verify the `engine` value is `"elasticsearch"` or `"opensearch"`. |
| `FORBIDDEN` | Authorization callback denied the request | Verify the user's credentials and permissions. Check the `authorize` callback logic. |
| `INTERNAL` | Unexpected backend or runtime failure | Check the structured logs for details. Inspect backend health (database connectivity, service availability). |

## Common Issues

### Search returns no results

1. Verify that `initialize()` was called with the correct `searchFields`.
2. Verify that documents were indexed with matching field names.
3. Check that the `resource` name matches between `index` and `search` calls.
4. Try disabling `fuzzy` to rule out fuzzy matching issues.

### `initialize` not called

Calling `index` or `search` before `initialize` may cause unexpected behavior. Always call `initialize()` with your resource definitions before other operations.

### Adapter disposed

Calling any method after `dispose()` throws `SEARCH_ADAPTER_DISPOSED`. Call `initialize()` again to reinitialize the adapter.

## Backend Playbooks

### Postgres

| Symptom | Check |
| --- | --- |
| Connection timeouts | Verify `connectionString` and network access to the database |
| Slow queries | Check that migration SQL was run (tables and indexes exist) |
| Missing results | Verify the target `schema` matches your database setup |
| Retry exhaustion | Increase `retry.maxRetries` or `retry.maxDelayMs` |

### Meilisearch

| Symptom | Check |
| --- | --- |
| `FORBIDDEN` errors | Verify the API key has the correct permissions (search, documents, indexes) |
| Missing results | Check the Meilisearch dashboard for index status and task queue |
| Timeout errors | Verify `host` is reachable and increase `requestTimeoutMs` if needed |
| Wrong results | Verify `indexPrefix` matches across your adapter instances |

### Elasticsearch / OpenSearch

| Symptom | Check |
| --- | --- |
| `DFQL_UNSUPPORTED` | Verify `engine` is set to `"elasticsearch"` or `"opensearch"` |
| Connection errors | Verify `node` URL and authentication credentials |
| Missing indexes | Ensure `initialize()` was called to create indexes |
| Cluster health | Check cluster status via `/_cluster/health` endpoint |

## Top 15 failure modes

A curated list, ordered by frequency in production deployments.

### 1. "Search returns no results, indexing claims success"

Tokenization mismatch between index and query. The most common cause is normalization differences across SearchFn versions.

Check:

```typescript
import { tokenize } from "@searchfn/core";

console.log(tokenize("Foo Bar")); // ["foo", "bar"]
```

Both index and search must use the same tokenizer. If you set `pipeline.tokenize` to a custom function, ensure it's applied at both index and query time.

### 2. "Index size grew past available RAM"

You're on `MemoryAdapter` with too many docs, or you indexed all fields when you only meant a few. Fix:

- Switch to a persistent adapter ([Postgres](/docs/reference/adapters/postgres) is the easy first step).
- Reduce `searchFields` to the ones you actually query.

### 3. "First request after deploy is slow"

Cold cache. The first 100 queries after a fresh start re-populate Postgres' OS cache or the LRU caches in the JS engine. Warm with a `status` ping and a representative query.

See [cache tuning](/docs/documentation/performance/cache-tuning).

### 4. "Query latency spiked at 9am"

Cache eviction, not load. Check:

- Postgres `shared_buffers` hit ratio (drops mean the working set outgrew RAM).
- Meilisearch task queue (`/tasks?status=processing`).
- Concurrent index operations stealing CPU from queries.

### 5. "Re-indexing is taking hours"

Sequential single-doc inserts. Fix:

- Batch with 500–2000 docs per call.
- Run 4 batches in parallel.
- For very large backfills, use the [backfill from DB recipe](/docs/recipes/backfill-from-db).

### 6. "Got `LIMIT_EXCEEDED` on a normal query"

Server-side limits are stricter than you think. Common culprits:

- `query` over 1024 characters (configurable via `limits.maxQueryLength`).
- `limit` over 1000 (configurable via `limits.maxLimit`).
- Indexing batch over `maxBatchSize` for your adapter.

See [configuration reference](/docs/reference/configuration).

### 7. "Got `FORBIDDEN` from authorize callback"

Your `authorize` returned `false` or threw. Add structured logging:

```typescript
authorize: async ({ method, resource, request }) => {
  const result = await myAuthCheck(...);
  if (!result) console.warn("denied", { method, resource });
  return result;
},
```

### 8. "Adapter disposed errors"

You called `dispose()` and then made another call. In serverless, `dispose` is rarely needed — let the adapter live with the process. In tests, recreate the adapter per test.

### 9. "Fuzzy queries are extremely slow"

Fuzzy is 5–20x slower than exact, especially on large vocabularies. Fix:

- Use fuzzy only after exact returns no results.
- Limit fuzzy to terms ≥ 4 characters.
- Use `fuzzy: 1` instead of `fuzzy: 2` (2 edits is much slower).

### 10. "Postgres adapter: connection pool exhausted"

Each Lambda/Vercel function creates its own pool. Fix:

- Use a connection pooler (Neon's, Supabase's, pgBouncer).
- Set `poolSize: 1` per Lambda.

### 11. "Meilisearch: task queue backing up"

You're indexing faster than Meili can process. Symptoms:

- `/tasks?status=processing` always non-empty.
- Search queries stay fast, but writes don't reflect for minutes.

Fix: slow down indexing, or scale up the Meili instance.

### 12. "Elasticsearch: too many shards"

You created a separate index per tenant and crossed ES's per-cluster shard limit. Fix:

- Combine small tenants into a shared index with a `tenant_id` filter.
- Use [multi-tenant isolation](/docs/recipes/multi-tenant) pattern.

### 13. "Swift app: index file grew unexpectedly"

SQLite WAL not checkpointed. Fix:

- The SQLite adapter handles this automatically. If you're seeing growth, you probably have multiple processes opening the same indexKey — not supported.
- Confirm a single owner per indexKey.

### 14. "Build fails with `<N ms` JSX error"

MDX confuses `<N ms` with a JSX tag. This bit our own docs build (see DataFn build notes). Fix in your MDX content:

- Wrap in backticks: `` `<10 ms` ``.
- Or escape: `&lt;10 ms`.

### 15. "Tests pass locally, fail in CI"

Likely a port collision, missing binary, or different tokenization (locale-sensitive). Check:

- CI runs Node 20+.
- No locale-dependent collation (force `LANG=en_US.UTF-8`).
- Database/Meilisearch fixtures reset between test runs.

## Where to look

- Structured logger output (one line per operation).
- Adapter health endpoints (`/searchfn/status` on the server; `/health` on Meilisearch; `/_cluster/health` on ES).
- Apple `SearchFnDiagnosticsSink` events.
- Postgres `pg_stat_statements`.

If none of these turn up a culprit, file an issue with the failing request shape (redacted) and the server log line for that request.



================================================================================
## Quickstart
================================================================================


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Bun

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/quickstart/bun
Description: SearchFn on Bun's native HTTP server.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Bun's native `Bun.serve` handles requests with a single fetch handler, so SearchFn slots in directly.

## 1. Install

```bash
bun add @searchfn/server @searchfn/adapter-memory
```

## 2. Run

```typescript
import { createSearchFnServer } from "@searchfn/server";
import { MemoryAdapter } from "@searchfn/adapter-memory";

const sf = await createSearchFnServer({
  adapter: new MemoryAdapter(),
  basePath: "/searchfn",
});

await sf.adapter.initialize?.({
  resources: [{ name: "messages", searchFields: ["body"] }],
});

Bun.serve({
  port: 3000,
  fetch: async (req) => {
    if (new URL(req.url).pathname.startsWith("/searchfn/")) {
      return sf.router.handle({
        method: req.method,
        url: req.url,
        headers: req.headers,
        body: req.body,
      });
    }
    return new Response("Not found", { status: 404 });
  },
});
```

`Bun.serve` accepts native `Request`s, and `sf.router.handle` returns one — no shim needed.

## 3. Smoke test

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/searchfn/index \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{ "resource": "messages", "documents": [{ "id": "m-1", "fields": { "body": "ship the docs already" } }] }'

curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/searchfn/search \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{ "resource": "messages", "query": "docs" }'
```

## Production

For Bun on Fly or Railway:

- Use `@searchfn/adapter-postgres` for persistence (in-memory loses state on every cold start).
- Set up a tiny startup script to call `initialize()` against your resource list.

## Next steps

- [Server reference](/docs/reference/server)
- [Deploy: Fly](/docs/documentation/deploy/fly)

### Express

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/quickstart/express
Description: Mount SearchFn into an Express app in under 10 minutes.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 1. Install

```bash
npm install express @searchfn/server @searchfn/adapter-memory
```

## 2. Mount

```typescript
import express from "express";
import { createSearchFnServer } from "@searchfn/server";
import { MemoryAdapter } from "@searchfn/adapter-memory";

const sf = await createSearchFnServer({
  adapter: new MemoryAdapter(),
  basePath: "/searchfn",
});

await sf.adapter.initialize?.({
  resources: [{ name: "products", searchFields: ["name", "description"] }],
});

const app = express();
app.use(express.json({ limit: "2mb" }));

app.all("/searchfn/*", async (req, res) => {
  const response = await sf.router.handle({
    method: req.method,
    url: req.originalUrl,
    headers: new Headers(req.headers as Record<string, string>),
    body: JSON.stringify(req.body),
  });
  res.status(response.status);
  response.headers.forEach((v, k) => res.setHeader(k, v));
  res.send(await response.text());
});

app.listen(3000);
```

## 3. Index + search

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/searchfn/index \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{ "resource": "products", "documents": [{ "id": "p-1", "fields": { "name": "Notebook", "description": "Black A5" } }] }'

curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/searchfn/search \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{ "resource": "products", "query": "notebook" }'
```

## Production

Use `@searchfn/adapter-postgres` for persistence, set `authorize` to gate writes to admin/service principals, and add an `express.json({ limit })` matching the server's `maxPayloadBytes`.

## Next steps

- [Server reference](/docs/reference/server)
- [Security](/docs/documentation/security/index)
- [Deploy](/docs/documentation/deploy/index)

### FastAPI

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/quickstart/fastapi
Description: Mount the Python SearchFn server inside a FastAPI app.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 1. Install

```bash
pip install fastapi uvicorn searchfn datafn
```

## 2. Set up SearchFn alongside DataFn

`app.py`:

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
from searchfn import create_searchfn_server
from datafn.db import PostgresAdapter
from schema import schema  # your DataFn schema

db = PostgresAdapter(connection_string=os.environ["SEARCH_DB_URL"])

search_plugin = create_searchfn_server({
    "schema": schema,
    "db": db,
    "table_prefix": "_searchfn_",
})

app = FastAPI()

for path, handler in search_plugin["routes"].items():
    @app.api_route(path, methods=["POST"], name=f"sf-{path}")
    async def route(request: Request, _handler=handler):
        body = await request.json()
        return await _handler(body)
```

The Python SearchFn server stores its inverted index inside your existing Postgres database, alongside the DataFn data. No additional infrastructure required for moderate-scale apps.

## 3. Run

```bash
uvicorn app:app --reload
```

## 4. Index

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/searchfn/index \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{ "model": "products" }'
```

This scans all rows in `products`, tokenizes the string fields, and populates `_searchfn_index`.

## 5. Search

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/searchfn/search \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{ "query": "fast laptop", "limit": 10 }'
```

## When to use the TypeScript adapters instead

The Python package is optimized for the "DataFn + Postgres" case. If you need an external search service (Meilisearch, Elasticsearch), stand up the TypeScript server in a sidecar and have FastAPI call it. The Python package and TypeScript server share the same envelope contract, so client code stays portable.

## Next steps

- [Python reference](/docs/reference/python)
- [DataFn integration](/docs/integrations/datafn)

### Fastify

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/quickstart/fastify
Description: SearchFn on Fastify with a single route registration.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 1. Install

```bash
npm install fastify @searchfn/server @searchfn/adapter-memory
```

## 2. Register the route

```typescript
import Fastify from "fastify";
import { createSearchFnServer } from "@searchfn/server";
import { MemoryAdapter } from "@searchfn/adapter-memory";

const sf = await createSearchFnServer({
  adapter: new MemoryAdapter(),
  basePath: "/searchfn",
});

await sf.adapter.initialize?.({
  resources: [{ name: "books", searchFields: ["title", "author"] }],
});

const app = Fastify({ bodyLimit: 2 * 1024 * 1024 });

app.all("/searchfn/*", async (request, reply) => {
  const response = await sf.router.handle({
    method: request.method,
    url: request.url,
    headers: new Headers(request.headers as Record<string, string>),
    body: request.body ? JSON.stringify(request.body) : undefined,
  });
  reply.status(response.status);
  response.headers.forEach((v, k) => reply.header(k, v));
  return response.text();
});

await app.listen({ port: 3000 });
```

## 3. Smoke test

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/searchfn/index \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{ "resource": "books", "documents": [{ "id": "b-1", "fields": { "title": "Gödel Escher Bach", "author": "Hofstadter" } }] }'

curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/searchfn/search \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{ "resource": "books", "query": "godel" }'
```

Fuzzy matching is on by default — the typo-corrected hit comes back.

### Flask

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/quickstart/flask
Description: Mount SearchFn into a Flask app.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 1. Install

```bash
pip install flask searchfn datafn
```

## 2. App

```python
from flask import Flask, request, jsonify
import asyncio
import os

from searchfn import create_searchfn_server
from datafn.db import PostgresAdapter
from schema import schema

db = PostgresAdapter(connection_string=os.environ["SEARCH_DB_URL"])

search_plugin = create_searchfn_server({
    "schema": schema,
    "db": db,
})

app = Flask(__name__)

for path, handler in search_plugin["routes"].items():
    def make_view(_handler):
        def view():
            return jsonify(asyncio.run(_handler(request.get_json())))
        return view
    app.add_url_rule(path, endpoint=f"sf{path}", view_func=make_view(handler), methods=["POST"])

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(port=8000)
```

Flask is synchronous; the wrapper bridges Python's async SearchFn into Flask's sync request lifecycle via `asyncio.run`. For higher throughput consider Starlette or FastAPI.

## 3. Smoke test

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/searchfn/index -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"model":"products"}'
curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/searchfn/search -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"query":"laptop"}'
```

### Hono

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/quickstart/hono
Description: SearchFn on Hono with the Memory adapter for dev and Postgres for prod.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This guide gets a Hono server indexing and searching in under 10 minutes. The same shape works on Bun, Deno, or Node.

## 1. Install

```bash
npm install hono @searchfn/server @searchfn/adapter-memory
```

For production with Postgres:

```bash
npm install @searchfn/adapter-postgres
```

## 2. Mount SearchFn on Hono

```typescript
import { Hono } from "hono";
import { createSearchFnServer } from "@searchfn/server";
import { MemoryAdapter } from "@searchfn/adapter-memory";

const sf = await createSearchFnServer({
  adapter: new MemoryAdapter(),
  basePath: "/searchfn",
});

await sf.adapter.initialize?.({
  resources: [
    { name: "articles", searchFields: ["title", "body"] },
  ],
});

const app = new Hono();

app.all("/searchfn/*", async (c) => {
  const res = await sf.router.handle({
    method: c.req.method,
    url: c.req.url,
    headers: c.req.raw.headers,
    body: c.req.raw.body,
  });
  return new Response(res.body, { status: res.status, headers: res.headers });
});

export default app;
```

`@searchfn/server` exposes a generic `router` that adapts to any HTTP framework through small request/response shims. The example above is a 10-line shim; if you use `@superfunctions/http`'s Hono adapter, you can drop the shim entirely.

## 3. Run

```bash
npx tsx --watch server.ts
```

Server listens on the default Hono port (3000).

## 4. Index your first documents

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/searchfn/index \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "resource": "articles",
    "documents": [
      { "id": "a-1", "fields": { "title": "Hello SearchFn", "body": "Get started in 10 minutes" } },
      { "id": "a-2", "fields": { "title": "BM25 in practice", "body": "Why ranking matters" } }
    ]
  }'
```

## 5. Search

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/searchfn/search \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{ "resource": "articles", "query": "ranking", "limit": 5 }'
```

```json
{ "ok": true, "result": { "ids": ["a-2"] } }
```

## 6. Promote to Postgres for production

Swap the adapter:

```typescript
import { PostgresAdapter } from "@searchfn/adapter-postgres";

const sf = await createSearchFnServer({
  adapter: new PostgresAdapter({
    connectionString: process.env.SEARCH_DB_URL!,
  }),
  basePath: "/searchfn",
});
```

Run the [Postgres adapter migration SQL](/docs/reference/adapters/postgres) once. Everything else stays the same.

## Next steps

- [Authorization](/docs/documentation/security/request-authz) — gate `/searchfn/*` per user/role
- [Deploy](/docs/documentation/deploy/index) — production hosting
- [DataFn integration](/docs/integrations/datafn) — use this server as a DataFn search backend

### Next.js

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/quickstart/nextjs
Description: SearchFn in Next.js (App Router) — server route for search + IndexedDB on the client.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 1. Install

```bash
npm install @searchfn/server @searchfn/adapter-postgres @searchfn/client @searchfn/adapter-indexeddb
```

## 2. Server route

`app/searchfn/[...path]/route.ts`:

```typescript
import { createSearchFnServer } from "@searchfn/server";
import { PostgresAdapter } from "@searchfn/adapter-postgres";

const sf = await createSearchFnServer({
  adapter: new PostgresAdapter({ connectionString: process.env.SEARCH_DB_URL! }),
  basePath: "/searchfn",
});

await sf.adapter.initialize?.({
  resources: [{ name: "tasks", searchFields: ["title", "description"] }],
});

const handler = (request: Request) =>
  sf.router.handle({
    method: request.method,
    url: request.url,
    headers: request.headers,
    body: request.body,
  });

export const GET = handler;
export const POST = handler;
```

Run the [Postgres migration](/docs/reference/adapters/postgres) once.

## 3. Client side

`lib/search.ts`:

```typescript
"use client";
import { createIndexedDbSearchClient } from "@searchfn/client";

export const search = createIndexedDbSearchClient({
  adapterConfig: { dbName: "app-search" },
  defaults: { limit: 20, fuzzy: true },
});
```

## 4. Use in a component

```tsx
"use client";
import { useState } from "react";
import { search } from "@/lib/search";

export function SearchBox() {
  const [q, setQ] = useState("");
  const [ids, setIds] = useState<string[]>([]);

  return (
    <>
      <input
        value={q}
        onChange={async (e) => {
          setQ(e.target.value);
          setIds(await search.search({ resource: "tasks", query: e.target.value }));
        }}
      />
      <ul>{ids.map((id) => <li key={id}>{id}</li>)}</ul>
    </>
  );
}
```

## 5. Server actions for indexing

```typescript
"use server";
export async function indexTask(t: { id: string; title: string; description: string }) {
  await fetch("/searchfn/index", {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "content-type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify({ resource: "tasks", documents: [{ id: t.id, fields: { title: t.title, description: t.description } }] }),
  });
}
```

For a tighter loop, call the server adapter directly from a server action instead of going over HTTP.

## Edge runtime

The MemoryAdapter and PostgresAdapter both work on Node.js. For Edge runtimes (Vercel Edge, Cloudflare Workers), use Meilisearch or Elasticsearch via HTTP — direct DB drivers don't run on Edge. See [Deploy: Cloudflare Workers](/docs/documentation/deploy/cloudflare-workers).

- [Cross-resource ranking recipe](/docs/recipes/cross-resource-ranking)
- [Server reference](/docs/reference/server)

### Starlette

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/quickstart/starlette
Description: Mount SearchFn into a Starlette app.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 1. Install

```bash
pip install starlette uvicorn searchfn datafn
```

## 2. App

```python
from starlette.applications import Starlette
from starlette.routing import Route
from starlette.requests import Request
from starlette.responses import JSONResponse

from searchfn import create_searchfn_server
from datafn.db import PostgresAdapter
from schema import schema

db = PostgresAdapter(connection_string=os.environ["SEARCH_DB_URL"])

search_plugin = create_searchfn_server({
    "schema": schema,
    "db": db,
})

def wrap(handler):
    async def endpoint(request: Request):
        body = await request.json()
        return JSONResponse(await handler(body))
    return endpoint

routes = [Route(path, wrap(handler), methods=["POST"]) for path, handler in search_plugin["routes"].items()]

app = Starlette(routes=routes)
```

## 3. Run

```bash
uvicorn app:app --reload
```

## Smoke test

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/searchfn/index -d '{"model": "products"}'
curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/searchfn/search -d '{"query": "laptop"}'
```

- [Security: authorization](/docs/documentation/security/request-authz)

### SvelteKit

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/quickstart/sveltekit
Description: SearchFn in a SvelteKit app — IndexedDB on the client, Postgres on the server.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This guide sets up SearchFn in two places: an `IndexedDbAdapter` for offline-first browser search, and a server-side `PostgresAdapter` for shared search state.

## 1. Install

```bash
npm install @searchfn/client @searchfn/adapter-indexeddb @searchfn/server @searchfn/adapter-postgres
```

## 2. Server route

`src/routes/searchfn/+server.ts`:

```typescript
import { json } from "@sveltejs/kit";
import { createSearchFnServer } from "@searchfn/server";
import { PostgresAdapter } from "@searchfn/adapter-postgres";
import { SEARCH_DB_URL } from "$env/static/private";

const sf = await createSearchFnServer({
  adapter: new PostgresAdapter({ connectionString: SEARCH_DB_URL }),
  basePath: "/searchfn",
});

await sf.adapter.initialize?.({
  resources: [{ name: "notes", searchFields: ["title", "body"] }],
});

export const GET = async ({ request }) =>
  sf.router.handle({ method: "GET", url: request.url, headers: request.headers });

export const POST = async ({ request }) =>
  sf.router.handle({
    method: "POST",
    url: request.url,
    headers: request.headers,
    body: request.body,
  });
```

Run the Postgres migrations once — see the [PostgresAdapter reference](/docs/reference/adapters/postgres).

## 3. Client (offline-first)

`src/lib/search.ts`:

```typescript
import { createIndexedDbSearchClient } from "@searchfn/client";

export const search = createIndexedDbSearchClient({
  adapterConfig: { dbName: "notes-search" },
  defaults: { limit: 20, fuzzy: true },
});

await search.initialize?.({
  resources: [{ name: "notes", searchFields: ["title", "body"] }],
});
```

## 4. Use in a Svelte component

```svelte
<script lang="ts">
  import { search } from "$lib/search";
  let query = "";
  let ids: string[] = [];

  async function run() {
    ids = await search.search({ resource: "notes", query, limit: 10 });
  }
</script>

<input bind:value={query} on:input={run} placeholder="Search notes..." />
<ul>
  {#each ids as id}
    <li>{id}</li>
  {/each}
</ul>
```

The browser search runs against the local IndexedDB index. Sync the index from the server on app boot, or use [DataFn integration](/docs/integrations/datafn) if your data already lives in DataFn.

### Swift

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/quickstart/swift
Description: SearchFn on iOS, macOS, watchOS — in-memory or SQLite-backed local search.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The Swift package is standalone — it doesn't require the SearchFn TypeScript server. Same engine concepts: tokenize, BM25, fuzzy, optional persistence.

## 1. Add the package

In `Package.swift`:

```swift
.package(url: "https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions", from: "0.2.0"),
.product(name: "SearchFnConvenience", package: "super-functions"),
```

Or in Xcode → File → Add Packages → `https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions`.

## 2. In-memory client

```swift
import SearchFnConvenience
import SearchFnAdapterContracts

let search = InMemorySearchFn(
    defaults: SearchFnDefaults(
        limit: 20,
        limitPerResource: 10,
        fuzzy: .enabled,
        prefix: true
    )
)

let client = search.client()

try await client.initialize(SearchFnInitializeParams(
    resources: [
        SearchFnInitializeResourceConfig(name: "tasks", searchFields: ["title", "body"])
    ]
))

try await client.index(SearchFnIndexParams(
    resource: "tasks",
    documents: [
        SearchFnDocument(id: "t-1", fields: ["title": "Hybrid search", "body": "Swift local index"]),
        SearchFnDocument(id: "t-2", fields: ["title": "Groceries", "body": "Milk and bread"]),
    ]
))

let ids = try await client.search(
    SearchFnSearchParams(resource: "tasks", query: "hybrid")
)
```

## 3. SQLite-backed (persistent)

```swift
import Foundation
import SearchFnConvenience
import SearchFnSQLiteAdapter

let rootURL = FileManager.default.urls(for: .applicationSupportDirectory, in: .userDomainMask)[0]
    .appendingPathComponent("searchfn-store", isDirectory: true)

let search = try SearchFn(sqlite: SearchFnSQLiteAdapterConfiguration(
    rootURL: rootURL,
    indexKey: "project-docs"
))

let client = search.client()
// initialize, index, search the same way
```

The SQLite adapter persists the inverted index under `<rootURL>/<indexKey-hashed>/searchfn.sqlite`. Reopening with the same `indexKey` resumes from where you left off.

## 4. SwiftUI

```swift
import SwiftUI
import SearchFnConvenience

struct SearchView: View {
    let client: SearchFnClient
    @State private var query = ""
    @State private var ids: [String] = []

    var body: some View {
        TextField("Search", text: $query)
            .onChange(of: query) { _, new in
                Task {
                    let result = try await client.search(
                        SearchFnSearchParams(resource: "tasks", query: new)
                    )
                    ids = result.map(String.init(describing:))
                }
            }
        List(ids, id: \.self) { Text($0) }
    }
}
```

- [Apple runtime deep-dive](/docs/documentation/apple/index)
- [Swift reference](/docs/reference/swift)

## Recipes
