--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### AuthFn Integration

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/recipes/authfn-integration
Description: Wire SearchFn's authorize callback to AuthFn sessions and roles.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

SearchFn's `authorize` callback is the gate between an HTTP request and the search engine. AuthFn provides the session model. Connecting them is a one-liner per action.

## Setup

```typescript
import { createSearchFnServer } from "@searchfn/server";
import { authFn } from "@authfn/server";

const sf = await createSearchFnServer({
  adapter,
  basePath: "/searchfn",
  authorize: async (ctx, action, payload) => {
    const session = await authFn.getSession(ctx.request);
    if (!session) return action === "status";

    switch (action) {
      case "status":
      case "search":
      case "searchAll":
        return true; // any authenticated user
      case "index":
      case "remove":
        return session.user.role === "editor" || session.user.role === "admin";
      case "clear":
        return session.user.role === "admin";
      default:
        return false;
    }
  },
});
```

The `ctx.request` shape depends on your HTTP framework adapter — pass it through as-is so AuthFn can read cookies / Authorization headers.

## Per-resource authz

If different resources have different access rules:

```typescript
authorize: async (ctx, action, payload) => {
  const session = await authFn.getSession(ctx.request);
  if (!session) return false;

  const resource = (payload as any).resource ?? (payload as any).resources?.[0];

  if (resource === "admin_logs") {
    return session.user.role === "admin";
  }

  // Default: any authenticated user
  return true;
},
```

For multi-resource `searchAll`, all requested resources have to pass:

```typescript
authorize: async (ctx, action, payload) => {
  if (action === "searchAll") {
    const resources = (payload as SearchAllParams).resources;
    return resources.every((r) => canAccess(session, r));
  }
  // ...
},
```

## Per-tenant authz

When resource names encode tenant (`articles:tenant-1`):

```typescript
authorize: async (ctx, action, payload) => {
  const session = await authFn.getSession(ctx.request);
  if (!session) return false;

  const resource = (payload as any).resource;
  if (!resource) return false;
  const [, tenantId] = resource.split(":");
  return session.user.tenantId === tenantId;
},
```

This pairs with the [multi-tenant pattern](/docs/recipes/multi-tenant).

## Service-to-service

For service accounts (background indexers, CI pipelines), pass a different credential:

```typescript
authorize: async (ctx, action, payload) => {
  const apiKey = ctx.request.headers.get("x-service-key");
  if (apiKey === process.env.INDEXER_SERVICE_KEY && action === "index") {
    return true;
  }

  const session = await authFn.getSession(ctx.request);
  // ...
},
```

Treat service keys as long-lived secrets — rotate, store in a secret manager, scope to specific actions.

## Logging denied requests

Failed authz attempts surface as `authorization.denied` events:

```typescript
const sf = await createSearchFnServer({
  adapter,
  authorize,
  logger: {
    warn: (msg, ctx) => {
      if (msg === "authorization.denied") {
        log({
          level: "warn",
          msg,
          action: ctx.action,
          userId: ctx.userId ?? "anonymous",
          ip: ctx.ip,
        });
      }
    },
    info: () => {},
    error: () => {},
    debug: () => {},
  },
});
```

Track repeated denies per IP as a signal for an alert.

## Tests

Mock the AuthFn session in your test setup:

```typescript
import { authFn } from "@authfn/server";

beforeEach(() => {
  vi.spyOn(authFn, "getSession").mockResolvedValue({
    user: { id: "u1", role: "editor", tenantId: "t1" },
  });
});
```

## See also

- [Security: request authz](/docs/documentation/security/request-authz)
- [Multi-tenant search](/docs/recipes/multi-tenant)
- [Server reference](/docs/reference/server)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Autocomplete

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/recipes/autocomplete
Description: Search-as-you-type with prefix matching and low latency.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The right tool for autocomplete is **prefix matching**, not fuzzy matching. Prefix matches are exact, fast, and predictable. Fuzzy is for typo correction on a final query, not for live-as-you-type.

## Enable edge n-grams

```typescript
import { createMemorySearchClient } from "@searchfn/client";

const client = createMemorySearchClient({
  adapterConfig: {
    pipeline: {
      edgeNgrams: { min: 2, max: 12 },
      indexStages: ["tokenize", "normalize", "edgeNgrams"],
      queryStages: ["tokenize", "normalize"], // exact match against prefix tokens
    },
  },
  defaults: { limit: 10, prefix: true },
});

await client.initialize?.({
  resources: [{ name: "items", searchFields: ["name"] }],
});
```

`indexStages` includes `edgeNgrams`; `queryStages` doesn't. This means indexing `searchfn` produces tokens for `se`, `sea`, ... `searchfn`, but the query `sea` matches as-is.

## Debounce the input

```typescript
import { useState, useEffect } from "react";

function Autocomplete() {
  const [q, setQ] = useState("");
  const [results, setResults] = useState<string[]>([]);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (!q) return setResults([]);
    const ctrl = new AbortController();
    const timer = setTimeout(async () => {
      const ids = await client.search({
        resource: "items",
        query: q,
        limit: 8,
        signal: ctrl.signal,
      });
      setResults(ids as string[]);
    }, 80);
    return () => {
      clearTimeout(timer);
      ctrl.abort();
    };
  }, [q]);

  return (
    <>
      <input value={q} onChange={(e) => setQ(e.target.value)} />
      <ul>{results.map((id) => <li key={id}>{id}</li>)}</ul>
    </>
  );
}
```

Key choices:

- **80 ms debounce** — enough to avoid a request per keystroke; tight enough to feel instant.
- **AbortController** — cancels stale requests; the engine sees `DFQL_ABORTED` and stops.
- **Result limit 8** — autocomplete UIs rarely benefit from more.

## What about typos?

Allow exact prefix matching to handle 95% of cases; expose a "Did you mean?" suggestion using a fuzzy fallback only when prefix returns zero results:

```typescript
let ids = await client.search({ resource: "items", query: q });
if (ids.length === 0 && q.length >= 4) {
  ids = await client.search({ resource: "items", query: q, fuzzy: 1 });
}
```

## Field boosts

Autocomplete usually wants `name` matches above `description` matches:

```typescript
await client.search({
  resource: "items",
  query: q,
  fieldBoosts: { name: 3.0, description: 1.0 },
});
```

## See also

- [Pipeline](/docs/documentation/core/pipeline) — edge n-grams details
- [Fuzzy](/docs/documentation/core/fuzzy) — when fuzzy is the wrong tool
- [Performance: query latency](/docs/documentation/performance/query-latency)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Backfill From An Existing Database

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/recipes/backfill-from-db
Description: Populate SearchFn from Postgres, MySQL, or Mongo without re-fetching everything twice.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

When you bolt SearchFn onto an existing app, the initial population can be the longest job in your bootstrap. A few patterns to do it right.

## Pattern 1 — streaming cursor

For Postgres / MySQL:

```typescript
import { PostgresAdapter } from "@searchfn/adapter-postgres";
import { drizzle } from "drizzle-orm/postgres-js";
import postgres from "postgres";

const sql = postgres(process.env.DB_URL!);
const adapter = new PostgresAdapter({ connectionString: process.env.SEARCH_DB_URL! });

const cursor = sql`SELECT id, title, body FROM articles`.cursor(500);

for await (const batch of cursor) {
  await adapter.index({
    resource: "articles",
    documents: batch.map((row) => ({
      id: row.id,
      fields: { title: row.title, body: row.body },
    })),
  });
  console.log("indexed", batch.length);
}
```

Postgres's server-side cursor streams in 500-row batches; SearchFn indexes them in the same loop. Memory usage stays bounded.

## Pattern 2 — keyset pagination

For ORMs without cursor support:

```typescript
let lastId = "";
while (true) {
  const batch = await db.articles.findMany({
    where: { id: { gt: lastId } },
    orderBy: { id: "asc" },
    take: 500,
  });
  if (batch.length === 0) break;

  await adapter.index({
    resource: "articles",
    documents: batch.map((row) => ({
      id: row.id,
      fields: { title: row.title, body: row.body },
    })),
  });
  lastId = batch[batch.length - 1].id;
  console.log("indexed up to", lastId);
}
```

## Pattern 3 — parallel workers

For very large datasets, partition the ID space and run workers in parallel:

```typescript
const ranges = [
  { lo: "a", hi: "h" },
  { lo: "h", hi: "p" },
  { lo: "p", hi: "z" },
];

await Promise.all(
  ranges.map((range) => backfillRange(range.lo, range.hi))
);
```

Two things to remember:

- **Don't exceed your DB's max connections.** Each worker holds an open cursor.
- **Don't exceed the adapter's `maxBatchSize`.** Default 10_000.

## Resume on crash

Track the last ID committed so a restart picks up where it left off:

```typescript
let lastId = await loadCheckpoint();
// ... loop ...
await saveCheckpoint(lastId);
```

For a multi-day backfill on a billion-row table, this is essential.

## Mongo

```typescript
const cursor = collection.find({}).batchSize(500);

let buffer: any[] = [];
for await (const doc of cursor) {
  buffer.push(doc);
  if (buffer.length >= 500) {
    await flushBatch(buffer);
    buffer = [];
  }
}
if (buffer.length > 0) await flushBatch(buffer);

async function flushBatch(docs: any[]) {
  await adapter.index({
    resource: "items",
    documents: docs.map((d) => ({
      id: d._id.toString(),
      fields: { title: d.title, body: d.body },
    })),
  });
}
```

## Validating

After backfill, sample-check:

```typescript
const dbCount = await db.articles.count();
const adapterInfo = adapter.adapterInfo();
console.log("backfill complete; db rows:", dbCount);
// For Postgres adapter you can SELECT count(*) from _searchfn_index;
```

## Throttling production load

If you're backfilling against a production database, throttle:

```typescript
import pLimit from "p-limit";

const limit = pLimit(2); // max 2 concurrent batches

await Promise.all(
  batches.map((batch) => limit(() => indexBatch(batch)))
);
```

## See also

- [Reindex with no downtime](/docs/recipes/reindex-no-downtime)
- [Partial reindex](/docs/recipes/partial-reindex)
- [Performance: indexing throughput](/docs/documentation/performance/indexing-throughput)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Cross-Resource Ranking

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/recipes/cross-resource-ranking
Description: Search across products, articles, and users — and rank them fairly.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

`searchAll` returns hits from multiple resources merged by score. By default the merge sorts by `score DESC`, but raw BM25 scores aren't comparable across resources with different corpus shapes. Here's how to fix that.

## The default merge

```typescript
const results = await client.searchAll({
  query: "laptop",
  resources: ["products", "articles", "users"],
  limitPerResource: 5,
});
// [
//   { resource: "products", id: "p-1", score: 4.8 },
//   { resource: "articles", id: "a-7", score: 3.1 },
//   { resource: "products", id: "p-2", score: 2.4 },
//   ...
// ]
```

This is fine when corpora are similar in size and shape. It's broken when one resource is huge (lots of low-frequency terms) and another is small.

## Normalize per resource

```typescript
function normalize(results: SearchAllResult[]) {
  const maxByResource = new Map<string, number>();
  for (const r of results) {
    maxByResource.set(r.resource, Math.max(maxByResource.get(r.resource) ?? 0, r.score));
  }
  return results
    .map((r) => ({ ...r, normalizedScore: r.score / (maxByResource.get(r.resource) || 1) }))
    .sort((a, b) => b.normalizedScore - a.normalizedScore);
}
```

Now scores are in `[0, 1]` per resource — comparable across resources.

## Enforce diversity with limitPerResource

```typescript
await client.searchAll({
  query: "laptop",
  resources: ["products", "articles", "users"],
  limitPerResource: 3, // never more than 3 per resource
  limit: 9,
});
```

This forces the final result to be evenly distributed across resources, even if one resource has 20 strong hits.

## Boost per resource

If certain resources should always rank higher (products outrank user profiles), apply a global multiplier post-merge:

```typescript
const resourceBoosts = { products: 1.5, articles: 1.0, users: 0.5 };

const ranked = results
  .map((r) => ({ ...r, boostedScore: r.score * (resourceBoosts[r.resource] ?? 1) }))
  .sort((a, b) => b.boostedScore - a.boostedScore);
```

## Interleave by section

For UI that shows results in sections rather than a flat list, group by resource and render each section ranked internally:

```typescript
function groupByResource(results: SearchAllResult[]) {
  const groups = new Map<string, SearchAllResult[]>();
  for (const r of results) {
    if (!groups.has(r.resource)) groups.set(r.resource, []);
    groups.get(r.resource)!.push(r);
  }
  return groups;
}

const groups = groupByResource(results);
// Render each section: <Section title="Products" items={groups.get("products")} />
```

This sidesteps cross-resource ranking entirely — each section is internally ranked, no merge required.

## When adapters don't support searchAll natively

The client merges per-resource searches concurrently (up to 10 at a time) and ranks by raw score. The same caveats apply — normalize before showing if your corpora differ.

## See also

- [BM25 scoring](/docs/documentation/core/bm25)
- [Capabilities](/docs/reference/capabilities)
- [Client API](/docs/reference/client)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### DataFn Integration (Deep)

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/recipes/datafn-integration
Description: Wire SearchFn as a DataFn search provider — server, client, native, and dataflows.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The reference page covers the API; this page covers the choices. If you're building DataFn + SearchFn together, you'll be making decisions about where the index lives, who owns indexing, and how multi-topology apps handle search.

## The provider boundary

`@searchfn/datafn-provider` exposes a single function:

```typescript
import { createSearchProvider } from "@searchfn/datafn-provider";

const provider = createSearchProvider(adapter, {
  resourceFields: {
    tasks: ["title", "description"],
    notes: ["content"],
  },
});
```

The provider implements DataFn's `SearchProvider` interface:

| DataFn calls | Provider does |
| --- | --- |
| `initialize(resources)` | Forwards to `adapter.initialize` |
| `search({ resource, query, ... })` | Forwards to `adapter.search` |
| `searchAll({ query, resources, ... })` | Native `searchAll` or merged per-resource |
| `updateIndices(mutations)` | For upserts → `adapter.index`. For deletes → `adapter.remove`. |
| `dispose()` | Forwards to `adapter.dispose` |

## Server-side setup

```typescript
import { createDatafnServer } from "@datafn/server";
import { createSearchProvider } from "@searchfn/datafn-provider";
import { PostgresAdapter } from "@searchfn/adapter-postgres";

const provider = createSearchProvider(
  new PostgresAdapter({ connectionString: process.env.SEARCH_DB_URL! }),
  { resourceFields: { tasks: ["title", "description"] } }
);

const server = await createDatafnServer({
  schema,
  db: drizzleAdapter({ db, dialect: "postgres" }),
  search: provider,
});
```

Every DataFn mutation now calls `updateIndices` on the provider. Search calls flow through the same path.

## Client-side setup (browser-owned)

```typescript
import { createDatafnClient } from "@datafn/client";
import { createSearchProvider } from "@searchfn/datafn-provider";
import { IndexedDbAdapter } from "@searchfn/adapter-indexeddb";

const searchProvider = createSearchProvider(
  new IndexedDbAdapter({ dbName: "app-search" }),
  { resourceFields: { tasks: ["title", "description"] } }
);

const client = createDatafnClient({
  schema,
  clientId,
  storage,
  searchProvider,
});
```

`client.search(...)` now executes locally against IndexedDB by default, falling back to the server when local isn't ready.

## Native-backed (Apple WebView) setup

When the same web client runs inside a WebView with Swift-owned persistence, the local IndexedDB is wrong — you want the native SearchFn.

```typescript
import {
  createNativeBackedSearchProvider,
  createWKWebViewBridgeBus,
} from "@datafn/swift-bridge";

const bus = createWKWebViewBridgeBus({ handlerName: "datafn" });

const client = createDatafnClient({
  schema,
  clientId,
  storage: createNativeBackedStorageAdapter(bus),
  searchProvider: createNativeBackedSearchProvider(bus),
});
```

The native search provider proxies all `search` / `updateIndices` calls through the Swift bridge to the host runtime.

## Mutation → index pipeline

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant App
  participant DataFn
  participant Provider as SearchProvider
  participant Adapter as SearchAdapter
  App->>DataFn: mutate({ resource: "tasks", operation: "insert", ... })
  DataFn->>DataFn: apply to DB
  DataFn->>Provider: updateIndices([{ kind: "upsert", resource, id, record }])
  Provider->>Adapter: index({ resource, documents: [{ id, fields }] })
  Adapter-->>Provider: { indexed: 1 }
  Provider-->>DataFn: done
  DataFn-->>App: success
```

If `updateIndices` throws, the DataFn mutation **does not** roll back — DataFn's data is authoritative. The index lags briefly until a retry. Provider implementations should be idempotent (re-running `index` for the same ID with the same fields is safe).

## resourceFields fallback

When `resourceFields` is omitted for a resource, the provider indexes all fields except `id`. This is convenient for prototyping; for production, declare `resourceFields` explicitly — it prevents accidental indexing of sensitive fields (`passwordHash`, `apiKey`).

## Where ranking lives

When the client and server both have a SearchFn-backed provider, you can pick where search runs:

- **`source: "local"`** — IndexedDB-only; instant; may miss new data.
- **`source: "remote"`** — server search; always current; needs a network round-trip.
- **`source: "auto"`** (default) — local first; remote fallback.

See [DataFn's search docs](https://datafn.21n.co/docs/dfql/search) for the source toggle.

## Multi-tenancy

DataFn's namespaceProvider scopes data per tenant; the SearchFn provider follows. Each tenant's records are indexed into the same physical adapter, but DataFn filters by namespace before returning results.

For strict cross-tenant isolation (regulated industries), wrap the adapter to encode namespace into the resource name:

```typescript
const provider = createSearchProvider(adapter, {
  resourceFields: { tasks: ["title"] },
  resourceMapper: (resource, namespace) => `${resource}:${namespace}`,
});
```

(Roadmap — confirm support in your version.)

## See also

- [DataFn integration reference](/docs/integrations/datafn)
- [Multi-tenant search](/docs/recipes/multi-tenant)
- [Apple WebView bridge](https://datafn.21n.co/docs/documentation/apple/webview-bridge)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### FileFn Integration

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/recipes/filefn-integration
Description: Index FileFn file metadata and extracted text content into SearchFn.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

FileFn stores files; SearchFn searches text. The integration is two pieces: (1) index FileFn's file metadata so users can search by name/type/owner; (2) extract text content from supported file types and index that too.

## Indexing metadata

Subscribe to FileFn upload completion events:

```typescript
import { onFileUploaded } from "@filefn/server";

onFileUploaded(async (file) => {
  await searchAdapter.index({
    resource: "files",
    documents: [{
      id: file.id,
      fields: {
        filename: file.filename,
        contentType: file.contentType,
        ownerId: file.ownerId,
        tags: file.tags.join(" "),
      },
    }],
  });
});
```

Users can now search by filename, owner, or tags through the standard SearchFn interface.

## Extracting text content

For PDF, DOCX, TXT, HTML files, extract content during processing and index it as a `body` field:

```typescript
import { extractText } from "filefn-text-extractor"; // or your tool of choice

onFileUploaded(async (file) => {
  const text = await extractText(file.stream, file.contentType);

  await searchAdapter.index({
    resource: "files",
    documents: [{
      id: file.id,
      fields: {
        filename: file.filename,
        contentType: file.contentType,
        ownerId: file.ownerId,
        body: text ?? "",
      },
    }],
  });
});
```

Now searches against `body` work across file content.

### Recommended extractors

| Format | Tool |
| --- | --- |
| PDF | `pdf-parse`, `pdfjs-dist`, or [Apache Tika](https://tika.apache.org/) for richer extraction |
| DOCX | `mammoth.js` |
| HTML | `cheerio` + `.text()` |
| Plain text | direct read |
| Images (OCR) | Tesseract via `node-tesseract-ocr` |

For mixed corpora, Tika in a sidecar is the most robust path.

## Indexing in chunks

For very large files (`>10 MB` of text), index in chunks rather than as a single document:

```typescript
const chunks = chunkText(text, 5000); // 5k chars per chunk

await searchAdapter.index({
  resource: "files",
  documents: chunks.map((chunk, idx) => ({
    id: `${file.id}:chunk-${idx}`,
    fields: {
      filename: file.filename,
      ownerId: file.ownerId,
      body: chunk,
      parentFileId: file.id,
    },
  })),
});
```

Searches return chunk IDs; display the parent file. Deduplicate by `parentFileId` if a single file shows up multiple times in results.

## Deletion

When a file is deleted in FileFn, remove its index entries:

```typescript
import { onFileDeleted } from "@filefn/server";

onFileDeleted(async (file) => {
  // If you chunked
  for (let i = 0; ; i++) {
    const chunkId = `${file.id}:chunk-${i}`;
    // ... remove all chunks
  }
  // Or simply:
  await searchAdapter.remove({ resource: "files", ids: [file.id] });
});
```

## Sharing-aware search

When FileFn files have ACLs (via the `shareable` capability), search results need to respect them. The pattern: include `ownerId` and `sharedWith` (a multi-value field) in the indexed fields, then filter results post-search:

```typescript
const ids = await searchAdapter.search({
  resource: "files",
  query: userQuery,
  limit: 50,
});

const files = await db.files.findMany({ where: { id: { in: ids } } });
const accessible = files.filter((f) => userCanAccess(currentUser, f));
```

For strict isolation (search must not even hint at the existence of inaccessible files), use a per-user resource name (`files:user-1`) and let `authorize` reject cross-user queries.

## DataFn + FileFn + SearchFn

When all three are wired together, the integration is automatic:

- DataFn owns file metadata records.
- FileFn owns the blob storage.
- SearchFn (via `@searchfn/datafn-provider`) indexes the DataFn records.

Use [DataFn integration](/docs/recipes/datafn-integration) — FileFn metadata flows through DataFn into SearchFn without extra code.

## See also

- [DataFn integration](/docs/recipes/datafn-integration)
- [Multi-tenant search](/docs/recipes/multi-tenant)
- [Backfill from DB](/docs/recipes/backfill-from-db)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Hybrid Local + Remote Search

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/recipes/hybrid-local-remote
Description: IndexedDB for hot data on the client; server search for everything else.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Local-first search has two failure modes: it's empty until you populate it, and it's stale until you refresh it. The hybrid pattern uses local IndexedDB for the data the user has actually touched, falling back to the server for cold or fresh queries.

## Pattern

```typescript
import { createIndexedDbSearchClient } from "@searchfn/client";

const local = createIndexedDbSearchClient({
  adapterConfig: { dbName: "app-search" },
  defaults: { limit: 20, fuzzy: true },
});

await local.initialize?.({
  resources: [{ name: "tasks", searchFields: ["title", "body"] }],
});

async function search(query: string) {
  // 1. Try local first
  const localIds = await local.search({ resource: "tasks", query, limit: 10 });
  if (localIds.length >= 3) return { ids: localIds, source: "local" as const };

  // 2. Fall back to server
  const res = await fetch("/searchfn/search", {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "content-type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify({ resource: "tasks", query, limit: 10 }),
  });
  const { result } = await res.json();
  return { ids: result.ids as string[], source: "remote" as const };
}
```

The threshold (`3`) is the number of strong-enough local hits below which you'd rather just ask the server. Tune for your domain.

## Sync-on-mutate

To keep the local index current, mirror mutations into it:

```typescript
async function createTask(input: TaskInput) {
  const task = await api.tasks.create(input);
  // Mirror into local index
  await local.index({
    resource: "tasks",
    documents: [{ id: task.id, fields: { title: task.title, body: task.body } }],
  });
  return task;
}
```

For DataFn-backed apps the `@searchfn/datafn-provider` does this automatically — every DataFn mutation calls `updateIndices` on the provider, which writes to the underlying SearchFn adapter.

## Periodic full sync

Even with sync-on-mutate, the local index will drift over time (records touched by other devices, server-side migrations). Schedule a periodic full pull:

```typescript
async function fullSync() {
  const remote = await fetch("/api/tasks").then((r) => r.json());
  await local.clear("tasks");
  await local.index({
    resource: "tasks",
    documents: remote.map((t: any) => ({
      id: t.id,
      fields: { title: t.title, body: t.body },
    })),
  });
  localStorage.setItem("last-sync", Date.now().toString());
}

// Run on app boot if the last sync was > 1 hour ago
if (parseInt(localStorage.getItem("last-sync") ?? "0") < Date.now() - 3600_000) {
  fullSync();
}
```

For large datasets, paginate the pull and write in batches.

## When to skip local

- Cold start (no records yet)
- Fresh data the user expects to see (newly created on another device)
- Server-authoritative search (admin dashboards, audit logs)

In those cases, just go to the server and skip the local layer.

## DataFn note

If you're on DataFn, the search provider already manages this — `client.search(...)` does local-first execution with server fallback by default. See the [DataFn search docs](https://datafn.21n.co/docs/dfql/search) for the source/auto/local/remote toggle.

## See also

- [SvelteKit quickstart](/docs/quickstart/sveltekit)
- [Cross-resource ranking](/docs/recipes/cross-resource-ranking)
- [DataFn integration](/docs/recipes/datafn-integration)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Index Snapshot and Restore

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/recipes/index-snapshot-restore
Description: Capture the SearchFn index state for backup, fixtures, or seeding new environments.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Indexes are derived state — you can always rebuild them from your primary store. But "always" can take hours; sometimes you want to snapshot the index and replay it quickly.

## When to snapshot

- **Tests** — Seed integration tests with a known index state.
- **Local dev** — Avoid running a full backfill every time a new contributor joins.
- **DR** — Restore quickly while a primary backfill runs in the background.

## Memory adapter — JSON dump

```typescript
import { MemoryAdapter } from "@searchfn/adapter-memory";

async function snapshot(adapter: MemoryAdapter): Promise<string> {
  return JSON.stringify(await adapter.dumpSnapshot());
}

async function restore(adapter: MemoryAdapter, json: string) {
  await adapter.loadSnapshot(JSON.parse(json));
}
```

`dumpSnapshot()` / `loadSnapshot()` serialize the entire in-memory state. The output is compact but still ~10-30% of raw text size — fine for fixtures, not for production-scale dumps.

## IndexedDB — export and import

```typescript
import { IndexedDbAdapter } from "@searchfn/adapter-indexeddb";

async function exportToBlob(adapter: IndexedDbAdapter): Promise<Blob> {
  const snapshot = await adapter.dumpSnapshot();
  return new Blob([JSON.stringify(snapshot)], { type: "application/json" });
}

async function importFromBlob(adapter: IndexedDbAdapter, blob: Blob) {
  const text = await blob.text();
  await adapter.loadSnapshot(JSON.parse(text));
}
```

For tests, ship the JSON as a fixture file and import it on every test boot.

## Postgres — pg_dump

Use Postgres's native dump:

```bash
pg_dump --table='_searchfn_*' -Fc search_db > search-backup.dump
```

Restore:

```bash
pg_restore -d search_db search-backup.dump
```

Captures all SearchFn tables (`_searchfn_articles`, `_searchfn_vocab`, etc.) in one consistent snapshot.

## Meilisearch — snapshots API

Meilisearch has [first-class snapshots](https://www.meilisearch.com/docs/learn/configuration/snapshots):

```typescript
await meili.createSnapshot();
```

The `MeilisearchAdapter` exposes this via `adapter.createSnapshot()`. Backups land in Meili's `snapshots/` directory.

## Elasticsearch / OpenSearch — snapshot repositories

ES/OS have [snapshot and restore](https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/snapshot-restore.html) backed by S3, GCS, Azure Blob, or local filesystem. Use the backend SDK directly — `ElasticsearchAdapter` doesn't surface a SearchFn-specific snapshot API.

## Snapshot versioning

Pipeline changes break older snapshots. The serialized JSON includes a `schemaVersion`; the adapter refuses to `loadSnapshot` a version it doesn't understand. Versioning convention:

- Bump when changing the tokenizer, normalizer, or stemmer.
- Bump when changing the inverted index storage format.
- Don't bump for pure adapter config (cache sizes, etc.).

## Snapshot size

Approximate sizes for typical corpora:

| Corpus | Snapshot size |
| --- | --- |
| 1k tasks (titles only) | ~50 KB |
| 100k articles (title + body) | ~50 MB |
| 1M chat messages (body only) | ~500 MB |

Memory snapshots use straight JSON. For larger sizes, use Postgres or Elasticsearch native dumps.

## Tests — using snapshots

```typescript
import { beforeAll, beforeEach } from "vitest";
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";

const fixture = JSON.parse(await readFile("./fixtures/articles-index.json", "utf-8"));

beforeAll(async () => {
  await adapter.initialize({ resources: [{ name: "articles", searchFields: ["title", "body"] }] });
});

beforeEach(async () => {
  await adapter.clear("articles");
  await adapter.loadSnapshot(fixture);
});
```

Every test starts from the same known state. Search assertions are deterministic.

## See also

- [Backfill from DB](/docs/recipes/backfill-from-db)
- [Reindex with no downtime](/docs/recipes/reindex-no-downtime)
- [Relevance testing](/docs/recipes/relevance-testing)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Multi-Language Search

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/recipes/multi-language
Description: Per-language stop words, stemming, and tokenization.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

If your corpus mixes languages (or you serve multiple locales), tokenization and stop words need to follow each document's language. The pipeline supports per-language stages.

## Per-resource language

```typescript
import { MemoryAdapter } from "@searchfn/adapter-memory";

const adapter = new MemoryAdapter({
  pipeline: {
    stopWords: {
      en: englishStopWords,
      es: spanishStopWords,
      fr: frenchStopWords,
      de: germanStopWords,
    },
    stem: (token, { language = "english" } = {}) =>
      snowballStem(language, token),
  },
});

await adapter.initialize({
  resources: [
    { name: "articles-en", searchFields: ["title", "body"], language: "en" },
    { name: "articles-es", searchFields: ["title", "body"], language: "es" },
    { name: "articles-fr", searchFields: ["title", "body"], language: "fr" },
  ],
});
```

Each resource carries its language declaration. When indexing or searching, the pipeline picks up the matching stop words and stemmer behavior.

## Per-document language

Sometimes resources are heterogeneous (a `comments` table with comments in any language). Encode the language as a field and look it up at index time:

```typescript
const adapter = new MemoryAdapter({
  pipeline: {
    tokenize: (text, { language }) => {
      if (language === "zh" || language === "ja") {
        return chineseJapaneseTokenize(text);
      }
      return defaultTokenize(text);
    },
    stem: (token, { language = "english" }) =>
      snowballStem(language, token),
  },
});

await client.index({
  resource: "comments",
  documents: comments.map((c) => ({
    id: c.id,
    fields: { body: c.body },
    language: c.language,
  })),
});
```

(API note: per-document `language` requires the adapter to surface a hook for it — the built-in adapters accept it on `SearchDocument` when pipeline stages declare language support.)

## Per-query language

```typescript
await client.search({
  resource: "articles",
  query: "ranking",
  language: "en",
});
```

When the resource is mixed-language, this restricts effective stop words and stemming to the requested language. Records in other languages still match against exact tokens but get a lower score.

## CJK tokenization

SearchFn's default tokenizer is whitespace + punctuation aware. For Chinese, Japanese, Korean, you'll need a real CJK tokenizer:

```typescript
import { jieba } from "nodejieba";

const adapter = new MemoryAdapter({
  pipeline: {
    tokenize: (text, { language }) => {
      if (language === "zh") return jieba.cut(text);
      if (language === "ja") return kuromojiTokenize(text);
      return defaultTokenize(text);
    },
  },
});
```

The same pattern applies to Thai (no spaces), Arabic (right-to-left + diacritics), etc.

## What about ICU?

If you need real ICU support (full Unicode-aware tokenization with proper word breaking), wrap an ICU library and plug it in via the tokenize hook. The built-in `\p{L}\p{N}` regex covers most Latin / Cyrillic / Greek scripts fine.

## Mixing languages in a single query

```typescript
await client.searchAll({
  query: "Paris",
  resources: ["articles-en", "articles-fr"],
});
```

Each resource processes the query with its own language config. The merged result puts French and English hits in one ranking, which is usually what you want for proper nouns.

## See also

- [Pipeline customization](/docs/documentation/core/customization)
- [Pipeline](/docs/documentation/core/pipeline)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Multi-Tenant Search

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/recipes/multi-tenant
Description: Keep tenants' search results isolated — even when sharing infrastructure.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Multi-tenancy in search is a question of where the isolation lives: in the adapter, in the resource name, or in the application layer. Pick the right level for your threat model.

## Pattern 1 — Per-tenant resource name

```typescript
async function indexForTenant(tenantId: string, docs: SearchDocument[]) {
  await client.index({
    resource: `articles:${tenantId}`,
    documents: docs,
  });
}

async function searchForTenant(tenantId: string, query: string) {
  return client.search({
    resource: `articles:${tenantId}`,
    query,
  });
}
```

**Pros:** trivial; works with any adapter; isolation is enforced at the request level.

**Cons:** vocab is per-tenant (no cross-tenant ranking). The resource list grows with tenant count, which can degrade `searchAll` startup.

Use this for SaaS with up to a few thousand tenants.

## Pattern 2 — Per-tenant adapter

```typescript
const adapters = new Map<string, MemoryAdapter>();

function getAdapter(tenantId: string) {
  if (!adapters.has(tenantId)) {
    adapters.set(tenantId, new MemoryAdapter());
  }
  return adapters.get(tenantId)!;
}
```

**Pros:** complete isolation; lifecycle independent per tenant.

**Cons:** more memory (each adapter has its own structures). Postgres / Meilisearch versions of this involve per-tenant databases or indexes.

Use this for large SaaS with strict isolation requirements (regulated industries).

## Pattern 3 — Tenant filter at search time

This doesn't work with SearchFn alone — `search()` returns IDs, and there's no `filter` clause for tenant filtering. **Don't** rely on filtering after the fact:

```typescript
// BAD: indexes leak across tenants
const ids = await client.search({ resource: "articles", query });
const myTenantIds = ids.filter((id) => tenantOwnsId(currentTenant, id));
```

This is wrong. If a malicious tenant searches for a competitor's product names, they get hits even if you filter at the app layer — the existence of the match leaks.

## Authorization gate

On the server, the `authorize` callback enforces which resources a caller can touch:

```typescript
const sf = await createSearchFnServer({
  adapter,
  authorize: async (ctx, action, payload) => {
    const requestedResource = payload.resource as string | undefined;
    if (!requestedResource) return false;
    const [base, tenantId] = requestedResource.split(":");
    if (!tenantId) return false;
    return ctx.user?.tenantId === tenantId;
  },
});
```

This pairs with the per-tenant resource name pattern: the resource itself encodes the tenant, and `authorize` cross-references it against the session.

## DataFn integration

When SearchFn backs DataFn, the namespaceProvider handles tenant routing:

```typescript
const datafn = await createDatafnServer({
  schema,
  db,
  namespaceProvider: (req) => `org:${req.session.orgId}`,
  search: createSearchProvider(adapter, {
    resourceFields: { articles: ["title", "body"] },
  }),
});
```

The DataFn provider scopes search to the active namespace automatically — you don't manage tenant resource names manually.

## Cross-tenant analytics (carefully)

If you need cross-tenant analytics search (admin tool, fraud detection), do it from a separate **admin adapter** that points at all tenant indices. Don't widen the `authorize` callback on the main server.

## See also

- [Security: request authz](/docs/documentation/security/request-authz)
- [Security: multi-tenant isolation](/docs/documentation/security/multi-tenant-isolation)
- [DataFn integration](/docs/recipes/datafn-integration)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Partial Reindex

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/recipes/partial-reindex
Description: Re-index only the records that changed since the last sync.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Full reindexing is expensive. For incremental updates — sync from a primary store, fix a data issue in a subset of records, etc. — you want to touch only what changed.

## Track an `updatedAt` watermark

The pattern: store the last successful sync timestamp and pull only records modified since then.

```typescript
async function partialReindex() {
  const since = await loadWatermark(); // e.g. ISO string
  const records = await db.articles.findMany({
    where: { updatedAt: { gt: since } },
    orderBy: { updatedAt: "asc" },
  });

  if (records.length === 0) return;

  await adapter.index({
    resource: "articles",
    documents: records.map((r) => ({
      id: r.id,
      fields: { title: r.title, body: r.body },
    })),
  });

  await saveWatermark(records[records.length - 1].updatedAt);
}

setInterval(partialReindex, 30_000);
```

Indexing is idempotent — re-sending the same ID with new fields updates in place.

## Handle deletions

`updatedAt` doesn't catch deletions. Two patterns:

### Soft-delete

If your data model uses soft deletes:

```typescript
const records = await db.articles.findMany({
  where: { updatedAt: { gt: since } },
});

const live = records.filter((r) => !r.deletedAt);
const deleted = records.filter((r) => r.deletedAt);

await adapter.index({ resource: "articles", documents: live.map(toDoc) });
await adapter.remove({ resource: "articles", ids: deleted.map((r) => r.id) });
```

### Tombstone table

If you hard-delete, keep a `_deletions` table with timestamps:

```typescript
const tombstones = await db._deletions.findMany({
  where: { resource: "articles", deletedAt: { gt: since } },
});

await adapter.remove({
  resource: "articles",
  ids: tombstones.map((t) => t.recordId),
});
```

## Debouncing per record

If a single record changes frequently (collaborative editor), you'll re-index it on every change. To avoid thrashing:

```typescript
const debouncedUpdates = new Map<string, NodeJS.Timeout>();

function scheduleReindex(id: string, doc: SearchDocument) {
  if (debouncedUpdates.has(id)) clearTimeout(debouncedUpdates.get(id)!);
  debouncedUpdates.set(
    id,
    setTimeout(async () => {
      await adapter.index({ resource: "articles", documents: [doc] });
      debouncedUpdates.delete(id);
    }, 500)
  );
}
```

500 ms is a balance between freshness and write amplification.

## CDC (change data capture)

For very large systems, integrate with a CDC pipeline (Debezium, Logical Replication, etc.). Each CDC event maps to an index/remove call:

```typescript
async function handleCDC(event: CDCEvent) {
  if (event.op === "delete") {
    await adapter.remove({ resource: event.resource, ids: [event.id] });
  } else {
    await adapter.index({
      resource: event.resource,
      documents: [{ id: event.id, fields: event.after }],
    });
  }
}
```

This eliminates polling and brings the index near-realtime.

## DataFn handles this for you

If you use `@searchfn/datafn-provider`, partial reindex is automatic — every DataFn mutation calls `updateIndices` on the provider, which writes to SearchFn. No watermark management required.

## See also

- [Backfill from DB](/docs/recipes/backfill-from-db)
- [Reindex with no downtime](/docs/recipes/reindex-no-downtime)
- [DataFn integration](/docs/recipes/datafn-integration)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Reindex With No Downtime

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/recipes/reindex-no-downtime
Description: Blue-green index swap — never serve a half-rebuilt index.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Reindexing happens for two reasons: schema changes (new fields, new tokenizer) or corpus changes (large dataset rewrite). Both want zero-downtime.

## Strategy: write to a shadow resource, swap

1. Index runs into `articles_v2` while reads still go to `articles_v1`.
2. Once `articles_v2` is fully built, atomically swap reads to `v2`.
3. Drop `v1`.

## Step 1 — index into the shadow

```typescript
const NEW_VERSION = "articles_v2";

await adapter.initialize({
  resources: [{ name: NEW_VERSION, searchFields: ["title", "body"] }],
});

for await (const batch of streamArticles()) {
  await adapter.index({
    resource: NEW_VERSION,
    documents: batch.map((row) => ({
      id: row.id,
      fields: { title: row.title, body: row.body },
    })),
  });
}
```

## Step 2 — atomically swap

The swap mechanism depends on the adapter:

### Memory / IndexedDB

The cleanest swap is at the application level — use an alias that your code reads:

```typescript
let currentResource = "articles_v1";

async function search(query: string) {
  return client.search({ resource: currentResource, query });
}

// At swap time:
currentResource = "articles_v2";
await adapter.clear("articles_v1"); // optional cleanup
```

### Postgres

`PostgresAdapter` writes tables prefixed by resource name. Rename via SQL transaction:

```sql
BEGIN;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS _searchfn_articles_old;
ALTER TABLE _searchfn_articles RENAME TO _searchfn_articles_old;
ALTER TABLE _searchfn_articles_v2 RENAME TO _searchfn_articles;
COMMIT;
```

Application code keeps using resource `"articles"`; the underlying tables are swapped.

### Meilisearch

Meilisearch has a native [index swap API](https://www.meilisearch.com/docs/reference/api/indexes#swap-indexes):

```typescript
await meili.swapIndexes([{ indexes: ["articles", "articles_v2"] }]);
```

Atomic. The `MeilisearchAdapter` exposes this via `adapter.swapResources(["articles", "articles_v2"])`.

### Elasticsearch / OpenSearch

Use the [aliases API](https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/aliases.html):

```typescript
await es.indices.updateAliases({
  body: {
    actions: [
      { remove: { index: "articles_v1", alias: "articles" } },
      { add: { index: "articles_v2", alias: "articles" } },
    ],
  },
});
```

Application code reads from the alias `"articles"`; the alias swap is atomic.

## Step 3 — drop the old

After verifying the swap (sample queries, count check), drop the old resource:

```typescript
await adapter.clear("articles_v1"); // or DROP TABLE / DELETE INDEX
```

Leave it for an hour or two in case you need to roll back.

## Validating before the swap

Don't swap blind:

```typescript
const oldCount = await countDocuments("articles_v1");
const newCount = await countDocuments("articles_v2");

if (newCount < oldCount * 0.95) {
  throw new Error(`v2 has ${newCount} docs, expected ~${oldCount} — aborting swap`);
}

// Sample queries
for (const sample of relevanceTests) {
  const oldIds = await searchOn("articles_v1", sample.query);
  const newIds = await searchOn("articles_v2", sample.query);
  if (newIds.length === 0 && oldIds.length > 0) {
    throw new Error(`Regression: query "${sample.query}" returns nothing in v2`);
  }
}
```

The point of the shadow build is to give you time to find regressions before users see them.

## Live mutations during reindex

While the backfill into `v2` runs, new writes still go to `v1`. To keep `v2` current:

- Dual-write: every mutation indexes into both `v1` and `v2`. After the swap, stop writing to `v1`.
- Or: backfill into `v2` from `v1`, then at swap time replay any mutations that happened in the meantime.

Dual-write is simpler; it costs ~2x write throughput during the migration window.

## See also

- [Backfill from DB](/docs/recipes/backfill-from-db)
- [Index snapshot and restore](/docs/recipes/index-snapshot-restore)
- [Partial reindex](/docs/recipes/partial-reindex)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Relevance Testing

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/recipes/relevance-testing
Description: Make search quality measurable, not anecdotal.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

You'll get reports that "search is broken" with no reproduction. Relevance tests turn vibes into a regression suite — every behavior the team cares about becomes an assertion.

## Pattern

Define a corpus and a set of `(query, expected top results)` pairs. Run the corpus through the adapter under test, run each query, assert the top N matches.

## Example

```typescript
import { describe, it, expect, beforeAll } from "vitest";
import { createMemorySearchClient } from "@searchfn/client";

const client = createMemorySearchClient({ defaults: { limit: 10 } });

const corpus = [
  { id: "1", fields: { title: "Search engine tuning", body: "BM25 and ranking" } },
  { id: "2", fields: { title: "Database indexes", body: "B-tree, hash, GIN" } },
  { id: "3", fields: { title: "Full-text search in Postgres", body: "tsvector and tsquery" } },
  { id: "4", fields: { title: "Vector search basics", body: "embeddings and cosine similarity" } },
];

beforeAll(async () => {
  await client.initialize?.({
    resources: [{ name: "articles", searchFields: ["title", "body"] }],
  });
  await client.index({ resource: "articles", documents: corpus });
});

describe("relevance", () => {
  it("ranks title match over body match", async () => {
    const ids = await client.search({ resource: "articles", query: "search" });
    expect(ids[0]).toBe("1"); // title contains "search"
  });

  it("BM25 query returns the most relevant doc first", async () => {
    const ids = await client.search({ resource: "articles", query: "BM25" });
    expect(ids[0]).toBe("1");
  });

  it("vector keyword finds vector doc", async () => {
    const ids = await client.search({ resource: "articles", query: "vector" });
    expect(ids).toContain("4");
  });

  it("fuzzy catches typos", async () => {
    const ids = await client.search({ resource: "articles", query: "tuneing", fuzzy: true });
    expect(ids).toContain("1");
  });
});
```

## Golden corpus

For production-scale apps, keep a fixed "golden corpus" — a small sample of representative documents — separate from production data. Run relevance assertions against the golden corpus on every commit.

```
fixtures/
  golden-corpus.json    # 50 documents, never edited
  golden-queries.json   # 100 queries with expected top results
```

When relevance changes, the test fails and forces a conversation. Sometimes the new ranking is correct (better than before), in which case you bump the expected results. Either way, no silent regressions.

## Metrics, not just ordering

Per-query checks ("doc X must be first") are fragile — small tokenizer tweaks can shuffle the top results. Pair with metrics:

```typescript
function ndcg(actualIds: string[], expectedIds: string[], k = 10): number {
  // Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain
  let dcg = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < Math.min(k, actualIds.length); i++) {
    const relevance = expectedIds.includes(actualIds[i]) ? 1 : 0;
    dcg += relevance / Math.log2(i + 2);
  }
  const idealDcg = Array.from({ length: Math.min(k, expectedIds.length) }, (_, i) => 1 / Math.log2(i + 2)).reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
  return idealDcg ? dcg / idealDcg : 0;
}

it("maintains nDCG@10 above 0.7 for production queries", async () => {
  const scores = await Promise.all(
    productionQueries.map(async (q) => {
      const ids = await client.search({ resource: "articles", query: q.text });
      return ndcg(ids as string[], q.expectedRelevant);
    })
  );
  const avg = scores.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) / scores.length;
  expect(avg).toBeGreaterThan(0.7);
});
```

This is more robust to minor reranking than per-query top-1 checks.

## Recording user feedback

Once relevance tests exist, real user signals become the data source:

- When a user clicks a result, record the (query, clicked id) pair.
- When a user immediately re-queries with a similar string, mark the original as a miss.
- Aggregate weekly into the golden corpus.

The relevance test suite grows from your actual users' needs rather than developer guesses.

## See also

- [BM25 scoring](/docs/documentation/core/bm25)
- [Index snapshot and restore](/docs/recipes/index-snapshot-restore) — for repeatable test fixtures



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Snippet Highlighting

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/recipes/snippet-highlighting
Description: Return matched fragments with the hit terms wrapped in HTML mark tags.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

SearchFn returns IDs, not document content. Snippet highlighting happens after you've fetched the records — either using the search query directly or via a small utility that mirrors the SearchFn pipeline.

## Minimal client-side highlight

```typescript
function highlight(text: string, query: string): string {
  const terms = query.toLowerCase().split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean);
  let result = text;
  for (const term of terms) {
    const re = new RegExp(`(${escapeRegex(term)})`, "ig");
    result = result.replace(re, "<mark>$1</mark>");
  }
  return result;
}

function escapeRegex(s: string): string {
  return s.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, "\\$&");
}
```

Use it after fetching the record:

```typescript
const ids = await client.search({ resource: "articles", query });
const records = await db.articles.findMany({ where: { id: { in: ids } } });

const highlighted = records.map((r) => ({
  ...r,
  titleHtml: highlight(r.title, query),
  bodyHtml: highlight(r.body, query),
}));
```

## Matching SearchFn's pipeline

The naive highlighter above misses stems. A search for "running" finds "run" in the index, but the regex above only highlights "running" in the text. To highlight properly, build a parallel pipeline-aware highlighter:

```typescript
import { tokenize, normalize, stem } from "@searchfn/core";

function highlightPipeline(text: string, query: string): string {
  const queryStems = new Set(
    tokenize(query).map(normalize).map(stem)
  );

  return text.replace(/(\b[\p{L}\p{N}]+\b)/gu, (word) => {
    const wordStem = stem(normalize(word));
    return queryStems.has(wordStem) ? `<mark>${word}</mark>` : word;
  });
}
```

Now `query="running"` highlights `runs`, `running`, and `ran`.

## Snippet windowing

For long body text, return only a window around the first match:

```typescript
function snippet(text: string, query: string, window = 80): string {
  const lc = text.toLowerCase();
  const idx = query
    .toLowerCase()
    .split(/\s+/)
    .map((t) => lc.indexOf(t))
    .filter((i) => i >= 0)
    .sort((a, b) => a - b)[0];

  if (idx == null) return text.slice(0, window * 2) + "...";

  const start = Math.max(0, idx - window);
  const end = Math.min(text.length, idx + window);
  const prefix = start > 0 ? "..." : "";
  const suffix = end < text.length ? "..." : "";
  return prefix + text.slice(start, end) + suffix;
}
```

Combine: `highlight(snippet(body, query), query)`.

## Server-side highlighting

For Meilisearch / Elasticsearch backends, the backends themselves can return highlighted snippets. SearchFn's adapters don't surface this today — use the backend SDK directly when you need backend-native highlighting.

## XSS

`<mark>` is safe; arbitrary text isn't. Sanitize record content **before** highlighting and rendering. Most templating engines (React, Svelte, Solid) escape by default, so render `{ snippetHtml }` only via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` / `@html` after running through a sanitizer like DOMPurify.

## See also

- [Pipeline](/docs/documentation/core/pipeline)
- [Cross-resource ranking](/docs/recipes/cross-resource-ranking)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Elasticsearch / OpenSearch Adapter

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/reference/adapters/elastic-opensearch
Description: Elastic-compatible adapter for Elasticsearch and OpenSearch clusters.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

SearchFn ships two installable packages, `@searchfn/adapter-elasticsearch` and `@searchfn/adapter-opensearch`, that share the same Elastic-compatible implementation. Pick the package that matches your cluster, or use the Elasticsearch package directly and select the engine at construction time.

## When to Use

- Large-scale search with millions of documents
- Advanced relevance tuning with field boosts and custom analyzers
- Existing Elasticsearch or OpenSearch infrastructure

## Installation

```bash
npm install @searchfn/adapter-elasticsearch
```

Install `@searchfn/adapter-opensearch` instead when you want the dedicated OpenSearch convenience wrapper.

## Usage

### Elasticsearch

```typescript
import { ElasticsearchAdapter } from "@searchfn/adapter-elasticsearch";

const adapter = new ElasticsearchAdapter({
  node: "https://es.example.com:9200",
  engine: "elasticsearch",
  auth: { apiKey: process.env.ES_API_KEY! },
  indexPrefix: "myapp",
});

await adapter.initialize({
  resources: [{ name: "tasks", searchFields: ["title", "description"] }],
});

const ids = await adapter.search({ resource: "tasks", query: "docs" });
```

### OpenSearch

```typescript
import { OpenSearchAdapter } from "@searchfn/adapter-opensearch";

const adapter = new OpenSearchAdapter({
  node: "https://opensearch.example.com:9200",
  auth: { username: "admin", password: process.env.OS_PASSWORD! },
  indexPrefix: "myapp",
});
```

`OpenSearchAdapter` is a convenience wrapper that sets `engine: "opensearch"` automatically.

## Configuration

| Option | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `node` | `string` | — | Required. Cluster endpoint URL. |
| `engine` | `"elasticsearch" \| "opensearch"` | `"elasticsearch"` | Select the engine dialect. |
| `auth` | `{ username, password } \| { apiKey }` | — | Cluster authentication credentials. |
| `indexPrefix` | `string` | `"searchfn"` | Prefix for index names (`{prefix}-{resource}`). |
| `requestTimeoutMs` | `number` | `30000` | Request timeout. |
| `retry.maxRetries` | `number` | `2` | Retry attempts for transient failures. |
| `retry.baseDelayMs` | `number` | `100` | Base delay between retries. |
| `retry.maxDelayMs` | `number` | `5000` | Maximum delay between retries. |
| `logger` | `AdapterLogger` | — | Optional adapter-level logger. |

## Capabilities

| Capability | Supported |
| --- | --- |
| `persistent` | Yes |
| `searchAll` | Yes |
| `fuzzy` | Yes |
| `fieldBoosts` | Yes |

## Behavior

- Single implementation handles both Elasticsearch and OpenSearch with dialect-aware query generation.
- Index lifecycle (create, delete) is deterministic and idempotent.
- Results are ordered by score with deterministic tie-breaking.
- Unsupported `engine` values return `DFQL_UNSUPPORTED`.
- Keep auth credentials in secure runtime secrets — never hardcode them.



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Adapters

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/reference/adapters
Description: Choose the right search adapter — built-in engine or external backend.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

SearchFn ships five adapters that all implement the `SearchAdapter` contract. Two use SearchFn's **built-in search engine** (tokenization, BM25 scoring, inverted index, fuzzy matching). Three delegate to **external search backends**. Swap between them without changing your application code.

## Adapter Comparison

### Built-in Engine

These adapters run SearchFn's own search engine in-process. No external services required.

| Adapter | Environment | Persistent | Fuzzy | Field Boosts | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [MemoryAdapter](/docs/reference/adapters/memory) | Browser / Node | No | Yes | Yes | In-process server search, tests, CLIs, small-to-moderate datasets |
| [IndexedDbAdapter](/docs/reference/adapters/indexeddb) | Browser | Yes | Yes | Yes | Offline-first browser apps, PWAs, client-side search |

### External Backends

These adapters are thin wrappers that translate the `SearchAdapter` contract into the backend's native API.

| Adapter | Environment | Persistent | Fuzzy | Field Boosts | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [PostgresAdapter](/docs/reference/adapters/postgres) | Server | Yes | Yes | No | Production apps already using Postgres |
| [MeilisearchAdapter](/docs/reference/adapters/meilisearch) | Server | Yes | Yes | No | Dedicated search with typo tolerance and faceting |
| [Elasticsearch/OpenSearch](/docs/reference/adapters/elastic-opensearch) | Server | Yes | Yes | Yes | Large-scale search with advanced relevance tuning |

## Choosing an Adapter

**MemoryAdapter** runs the full search engine in-process with zero setup. Use it for server-side search where the dataset fits in memory, CLI tools, tests, and any environment where you want search without external dependencies.

**IndexedDbAdapter** is for browser and offline-first apps. It uses the same built-in engine as MemoryAdapter, but persists the inverted index in IndexedDB with LRU caches — search survives page reloads and works offline.

Both built-in engine adapters are production-ready. **Use an external backend** when your use case specifically needs:
- Shared search state across multiple clients or servers
- Datasets that exceed process or browser memory
- Backend-specific features (Postgres `tsvector` tuning, Meilisearch facets, Elasticsearch analyzers)

**PostgresAdapter** is the simplest external option if you already run Postgres. It uses native `tsvector` full-text search with no additional infrastructure.

**MeilisearchAdapter** gives you a dedicated search engine with built-in typo tolerance and fast indexing. Good for user-facing search with high relevance requirements.

**Elasticsearch/OpenSearch Adapter** is for large-scale deployments that need advanced relevance tuning, field boosts, and cluster scalability.

## Common Interface

All adapters — built-in and external — support the same operations:

- `initialize` — declare resources and searchable fields
- `index` — batch index documents
- `search` — search a single resource by query
- `remove` — remove documents by ID
- `clear` — remove all documents from a resource
- `dispose` — release resources and connections

Most adapters also support `searchAll` (cross-resource search) and `fuzzy` matching. See individual adapter pages for details.

## Lifecycle

Every adapter follows the same lifecycle:

1. **Construct** — create the adapter with configuration.
2. **Initialize** — call `initialize()` to declare resources and search fields.
3. **Use** — call `index`, `search`, `searchAll`, `remove`, `clear`.
4. **Dispose** — call `dispose()` to release resources. After disposal, call `initialize()` again before further operations.

```typescript
import { MemoryAdapter } from "@searchfn/adapter-memory";

const adapter = new MemoryAdapter();

await adapter.initialize({
  resources: [{ name: "tasks", searchFields: ["title", "description"] }],
});

await adapter.index({
  resource: "tasks",
  documents: [{ id: "1", fields: { title: "Hello", description: "World" } }],
});

const ids = await adapter.search({ resource: "tasks", query: "hello" });

await adapter.dispose();
```



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### IndexedDB Adapter

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/reference/adapters/indexeddb
Description: Browser-persistent full-text search using SearchFn's built-in engine with IndexedDB storage.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The IndexedDB Adapter runs SearchFn's built-in search engine in the browser with persistent storage. It uses the same BM25 scoring, inverted index, fuzzy matching, and text pipeline as the [Memory Adapter](/docs/reference/adapters/memory), but stores the inverted index in IndexedDB so search data survives page reloads and browser restarts.

## When to Use

- Production offline-first browser applications
- Progressive web apps with local search
- Client-side search that needs to persist across sessions and work without network
- Any browser app where you want full-text search without a server round-trip

## Installation

```bash
npm install @searchfn/adapter-indexeddb
```

## Usage

```typescript
import { IndexedDbAdapter } from "@searchfn/adapter-indexeddb";

const adapter = new IndexedDbAdapter({
  dbName: "my-app-search",
});

await adapter.initialize({
  resources: [{ name: "tasks", searchFields: ["title", "description"] }],
});

await adapter.index({
  resource: "tasks",
  documents: [
    { id: "t-1", fields: { title: "Ship docs", description: "Write the guide" } },
  ],
});

const ids = await adapter.search({ resource: "tasks", query: "docs" });
```

## Configuration

| Option | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `dbName` | `string` | `"searchfn-adapter"` | Base database name. Per-resource databases use `{dbName}-{resource}`. |
| `pipeline` | `PipelineOptions` | Internal defaults | Configure the text pipeline (tokenization, stemming, stop words, n-grams). |
| `cache.terms` | `number` | `2048` | Maximum entries in the term lookup LRU cache. |
| `cache.vectors` | `number` | `512` | Maximum entries in the vector LRU cache. |

```typescript
const adapter = new IndexedDbAdapter({
  dbName: "my-app-search",
  cache: { terms: 4096, vectors: 1024 },
});
```

## Capabilities

| Capability | Supported |
| --- | --- |
| `persistent` | Yes |
| `searchAll` | Yes |
| `fuzzy` | Yes |
| `fieldBoosts` | Yes |

## How It Works

The IndexedDB Adapter uses the full `@searchfn/core` search engine with IndexedDB as the storage backend:

1. **Indexing** — documents pass through the text pipeline (tokenize, normalize, stop words, stem). Terms and posting lists are written to IndexedDB object stores, with postings stored as delta-varint encoded chunks keyed by `[field, term, chunk]`.
2. **Searching** — query text passes through the same pipeline. Postings are retrieved from IndexedDB (with LRU caching for hot terms) and scored using BM25 with length normalization.
3. **Ranking** — results are sorted by score (descending) with deterministic tie-breaking by document ID.

### LRU Caches

To reduce IndexedDB reads, the adapter maintains two LRU caches:

- **Term cache** (default 2048 entries) — caches frequently accessed posting chunks.
- **Vector cache** (default 512 entries) — caches computed vectors for faster scoring.

Tune these via the `cache` configuration when working with large indexes.

## Behavior

- Data persists in IndexedDB across page reloads within the same browser origin.
- Each resource gets its own IndexedDB database (`{dbName}-{resource}`).
- Reads and writes are deterministic across repeated calls.
- Calling `dispose()` closes all database handles. Call `initialize()` again to reopen.



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Meilisearch Adapter

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/reference/adapters/meilisearch
Description: External Meilisearch adapter for hosted or self-hosted search backends.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The Meilisearch Adapter connects to a Meilisearch instance for fast, typo-tolerant search with automatic ranking.

## When to Use

- User-facing search with high relevance requirements
- Applications that need typo tolerance out of the box
- Dedicated search infrastructure (hosted or self-hosted Meilisearch)

## Installation

```bash
npm install @searchfn/adapter-meilisearch
```

## Usage

```typescript
import { MeilisearchAdapter } from "@searchfn/adapter-meilisearch";

const adapter = new MeilisearchAdapter({
  host: process.env.MEILI_URL!,
  apiKey: process.env.MEILI_API_KEY!,
  indexPrefix: "myapp",
});

await adapter.initialize({
  resources: [{ name: "tasks", searchFields: ["title", "description"] }],
});

await adapter.index({
  resource: "tasks",
  documents: [
    { id: "t-1", fields: { title: "Ship docs", description: "Write the guide" } },
  ],
});

const ids = await adapter.search({ resource: "tasks", query: "docs" });
```

## Configuration

| Option | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `host` | `string` | — | Required. Meilisearch HTTP endpoint. |
| `apiKey` | `string` | — | Authentication key. Redacted in logs. |
| `indexPrefix` | `string` | `"searchfn"` | Prefix for Meilisearch index names (`{prefix}-{resource}`). |
| `requestTimeoutMs` | `number` | `30000` | Request timeout. |
| `retry.maxRetries` | `number` | `2` | Retry attempts for transient failures. |
| `retry.baseDelayMs` | `number` | `100` | Base delay between retries. |
| `retry.maxDelayMs` | `number` | `5000` | Maximum delay between retries. |
| `logger` | `AdapterLogger` | — | Optional adapter-level logger. |

## Capabilities

| Capability | Supported |
| --- | --- |
| `persistent` | Yes |
| `searchAll` | Yes |
| `fuzzy` | Yes |
| `fieldBoosts` | No |

## Behavior

- Creates Meilisearch indexes automatically on `initialize`.
- `index` performs document upserts — re-indexing the same ID updates the document.
- `remove` and `clear` are idempotent — calling them on non-existent documents or empty indexes is safe.
- Authentication failures (invalid API key, insufficient permissions) return `FORBIDDEN`.
- Keep API keys in environment-level secrets — never hardcode them.



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Memory Adapter

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/reference/adapters/memory
Description: In-process full-text search using SearchFn's built-in engine.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The Memory Adapter runs SearchFn's built-in search engine entirely in-process. It builds an inverted index in memory, scores results with BM25, and supports fuzzy matching and field boosts — all with zero external dependencies. Data lives in memory and is lost when the process exits.

## When to Use

- Server-side in-process search where the dataset fits in memory
- CLI tools and background workers with search capabilities
- Unit and integration tests
- Any environment where you want full-text search without external services

## Installation

```bash
npm install @searchfn/adapter-memory
```

## Usage

```typescript
import { MemoryAdapter } from "@searchfn/adapter-memory";

const adapter = new MemoryAdapter();

await adapter.initialize({
  resources: [{ name: "tasks", searchFields: ["title", "description"] }],
});

await adapter.index({
  resource: "tasks",
  documents: [
    { id: "t-1", fields: { title: "Ship docs", description: "Write the guide" } },
  ],
});

const ids = await adapter.search({ resource: "tasks", query: "docs", limit: 10 });
```

## Configuration

| Option | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `pipeline` | `PipelineOptions` | Internal defaults | Configure the text pipeline (tokenization, stemming, stop words, n-grams). |

```typescript
const adapter = new MemoryAdapter({
  pipeline: {
    // Custom pipeline options
  },
});
```

## Capabilities

| Capability | Supported |
| --- | --- |
| `persistent` | No |
| `searchAll` | Yes |
| `fuzzy` | Yes |
| `fieldBoosts` | Yes |

## How It Works

The Memory Adapter uses the full `@searchfn/core` search engine:

1. **Indexing** — documents pass through the text pipeline (tokenize, normalize, stop words, stem). The resulting terms are stored in an in-memory inverted index (`Map<string, Map<docId, PostingInfo>>`) keyed by `field::term`.
2. **Searching** — query text passes through the same pipeline. If fuzzy matching is enabled, terms are expanded via Levenshtein distance against the vocabulary. Postings are retrieved and scored using BM25 with length normalization.
3. **Ranking** — results are sorted by score (descending) with deterministic tie-breaking by document ID.

This is the same search engine that powers the [IndexedDB Adapter](/docs/reference/adapters/indexeddb), with the only difference being storage: memory vs IndexedDB.

## Behavior

- Results use deterministic tie-break ordering by document ID when scores are equal.
- `searchAll` returns results sorted by score with deterministic ordering.
- Calling `dispose()` clears all data. Call `initialize()` again before further operations.



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Postgres Adapter

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/reference/adapters/postgres
Description: Production-grade full-text search using Postgres tsvector.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The Postgres Adapter uses native Postgres full-text search (`tsvector`/`tsquery`) for production-grade search with no additional infrastructure beyond your existing database.

## When to Use

- Production apps already running Postgres
- Server-side search that needs SQL-level durability and transactions
- Moderate document volumes where a dedicated search engine is unnecessary

## Installation

```bash
npm install @searchfn/adapter-postgres
```

## Setup

The adapter requires search tables and indexes in your Postgres database. Run the migration SQL shipped with the package:

```typescript
import { getPostgresMigrationSQL } from "@searchfn/adapter-postgres";

const sql = getPostgresMigrationSQL();
// Execute this SQL against your database to create required tables and indexes
```

## Usage

```typescript
import { PostgresAdapter } from "@searchfn/adapter-postgres";

const adapter = new PostgresAdapter({
  connectionString: process.env.SEARCH_DB_URL!,
  schema: "public",
  queryTimeoutMs: 15000,
});

await adapter.initialize({
  resources: [{ name: "tasks", searchFields: ["title", "description"] }],
});

await adapter.index({
  resource: "tasks",
  documents: [
    { id: "t-1", fields: { title: "Ship docs", description: "Write the guide" } },
  ],
});

const ids = await adapter.search({ resource: "tasks", query: "docs" });
```

## Configuration

| Option | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `connectionString` | `string` | — | Required. Postgres connection string (DSN). |
| `schema` | `string` | `"public"` | Target database schema. |
| `queryTimeoutMs` | `number` | `30000` | Timeout for individual queries. |
| `maxBatchSize` | `number` | `10000` | Maximum documents per index batch. |
| `retry.maxRetries` | `number` | `2` | Retry attempts for transient failures. |
| `retry.baseDelayMs` | `number` | `100` | Base delay between retries (with jitter). |
| `retry.maxDelayMs` | `number` | `5000` | Maximum delay between retries. |
| `logger` | `PostgresAdapterLogger` | — | Optional adapter-level logger. |

## Capabilities

| Capability | Supported |
| --- | --- |
| `persistent` | Yes |
| `searchAll` | Yes |
| `fuzzy` | Yes |
| `fieldBoosts` | No |

## Behavior

- Uses Postgres native `tsvector` full-text search.
- Supports bounded retries with exponential backoff and jitter for transient database failures.
- `index` operations use batch inserts up to `maxBatchSize`.
- Keep connection strings in a secure secret store — never hardcode them.



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Capabilities

URL: https://searchfn.com/docs/reference/capabilities
Description: Per-adapter feature matrix.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Each adapter declares its capabilities so clients and servers can adapt. Query through `adapter.capabilities` or `client.adapterInfo()`.

## Capability shape

```typescript
interface SearchAdapterCapabilities {
  persistent?: boolean;
  searchAll?: boolean;
  fuzzy?: boolean;
  fieldBoosts?: boolean;
  prefix?: boolean;
  multiLanguage?: boolean;
  maxBatchSize?: number;
}
```

| Capability | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `persistent` | Data survives process or browser restarts |
| `searchAll` | Native cross-resource search; if false, the client merges per-resource results |
| `fuzzy` | Approximate matching available |
| `fieldBoosts` | Per-field relevance weights honored |
| `prefix` | Prefix / edge-n-gram matching supported |
| `multiLanguage` | Stop words / stemmers per language supported |
| `maxBatchSize` | Maximum docs in a single `index` call |

## Matrix

| Adapter | persistent | searchAll | fuzzy | fieldBoosts | prefix | multiLanguage | maxBatchSize |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `MemoryAdapter` | no | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes | 10_000 |
| `IndexedDbAdapter` | yes (browser) | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes | 10_000 |
| `PostgresAdapter` | yes | yes | partial (`pg_trgm`) | no | no | partial | 10_000 |
| `MeilisearchAdapter` | yes | yes | yes | partial | yes | yes | 10_000 |
| `ElasticsearchAdapter` | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes | 10_000 |
| `OpenSearchAdapter` | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes | 10_000 |
| `SearchFnMemoryAdapter` (Swift) | no | yes | yes | yes | yes | partial | 10_000 |
| `SearchFnSQLiteAdapter` (Swift) | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes | partial | 10_000 |

"partial" means the capability is available but with caveats:

- `PostgresAdapter` fuzzy requires the `pg_trgm` extension and uses similarity rather than Levenshtein.
- `PostgresAdapter` multi-language uses Postgres's built-in language configs (`english`, `simple`, etc.), not the SearchFn pipeline.
- `MeilisearchAdapter` fieldBoosts use Meili's `attributesToSearchOn`/`rankingRules`, which aren't the same as in-engine boosts.
- Swift multi-language ships English stemming and stop words; ES/FR/DE require custom pipelines.

## Detecting capabilities at runtime

```typescript
const info = client.adapterInfo();

if (!info.capabilities?.fuzzy) {
  console.warn("Fuzzy not supported by", info.name);
}
```

Use this when:

- Disabling UI affordances (e.g. a "fuzzy" toggle) that the active backend can't support.
- Building portable libraries that need to fall back gracefully.

## See also

- [Configuration](/docs/reference/configuration)
- [Adapter index](/docs/reference/adapters)
